This knock-in strain provides a reliable, endogenously tagged red fluorescent peroxisome marker for investigating peroxisome dynamics, metabolic regulation, and organelle contact sites in vivo .

title: Systematic CRISPR screens decode regulators of primary human pathogenic Th17 cell differentiation and activation.
authors: Wang, Yuan; Yu, Zekun; Wang, Lixin; Zhang, Junshi; Wang, Wanting; Luo, Ban; Huang, Bochen; Zhang, Fanmeng; Zhang, Lu; Shen, Chenchen; Zhou, Biao; Li, Kecheng; Yang, Xuanming
abstract: T-helper 17 (Th17) cells mediate host defense against bacterial and fungal pathogens at mucosal and skin interfaces. However, they are also involved in the pathogenesis of diverse autoimmune and inflammatory diseases. To accelerate candidate discovery in the pathogenic Th17 pathway, we have customized druggable CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) and interference (CRISPRi) sgRNA libraries. With an optimized Th17 differentiation protocol, we performed customized CRISPRa and CRISPRi screens in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) to identify potential regulators controlling the function of pathogenic Th17 cells. Coupled with next-generation sequencing, our screens identified previously reported and undiscovered genes involved in pathogenic Th17 cell differentiation and activation. Among them, the regulatory roles of heme oxygenase 1 and CD28 were verified by sgRNA-based and small-molecule inhibitor-based functional experiments in vitro. Our study provided a useful resource for mapping key genes of pathogenic Th17 cell function and potential immunotherapy targets for treating Th17-related immune disorders.

title: Cellular morphology emerges from polygenic, distributed transcriptional variation.
authors: Paylakhi, Seyedehzahra; Geurgas, Rafael; Yasko, Antionette; Wedow, Robbee; Tegtmeyer, Matthew
abstract: Height and disease risk are canonical polygenic traits, but whether an analogous architecture governs cellular phenotypes remains unclear. Here, we show that cellular morphology behaves as a polygenic systems phenotype by integrating cross-modal modeling, perturbation profiling, and human genetic variation. An adversarially aligned autoencoder trained on four perturbation datasets predicted morphology from gene expression and generalized without retraining to matched RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and cell painting profiles from 100 genetically diverse induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) donors. Seventeen morphological features were strongly predicted, particularly those capturing organelle distribution and cytoskeletal architecture. Predictive signal was broadly distributed across genes, with weak individual gene-morphology correlations. Independent CRISPR perturbations supported model-prioritized genes including TIAM1, RAB31, and ABCC5, while genetic analyses identified variant-gene-morphology associations involving PDHX, SLC11A2, and MAPKAPK5. These findings extend polygenic models of complex traits to cellular architecture and provide a framework for interpreting cross-modal prediction in functional genomics.

title: Modern cell-based assays for biomedical research: from conventional methods to AI-driven high content analysis.
authors: Venkataramaiah, Chintha
abstract: In vitro cell-based assays are fundamental tools in biomedical research, supporting investigations of cellular physiology, disease mechanisms, drug discovery, toxicology, regenerative medicine, and precision therapeutics. However, conventional two-dimensional (2D) cell culture models often fail to recapitulate the structural complexity and physiological functions of native tissues, prompting the development of advanced platforms, including three-dimensional (3D) cultures, organoids, organ-on-a-chip technologies, and microphysiological systems. Recent advances in cell viability and cytotoxicity assessment, functional cellular analysis, molecular profiling, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based functional genomics, high-content imaging, flow cytometry, single-cell and spatial multi-omics, and automated high-throughput screening have expanded the analytical capabilities of cell-based assays. Furthermore, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted image analysis and computational biology has enhanced cellular phenotyping, biomarker discovery, and mechanistic investigation, with the potential to improve the prediction of therapeutic efficacy and toxicity. Nevertheless, challenges related to physiological relevance, technical variability, inadequate standardization, high operational costs, scalability, poor reproducibility, cell-line misidentification, batch-to-batch variation, and inconsistent reporting continue to hinder translational applications. Future progress will depend on integrating physiologically relevant models with AI-driven analytics, spatial multi-omics, digital pathology, automated screening, and microphysiological systems. Standardized protocols, harmonized reporting practices, and interdisciplinary collaboration will be essential to improve reproducibility, strengthen regulatory acceptance, advance precision medicine, and reduce reliance on animal experimentation. In this context, this review critically evaluates conventional and emerging in vitro cell-based assays, emphasizing their biological principles, analytical capabilities, translational applications, and practical limitations, while highlighting future opportunities to improve predictive accuracy, reproducibility, and clinical translation.

title: MSX2 is an ERalpha-associated transcription factor that sustains proliferative capacity and is associated with favorable prognosis in luminal breast cancer.
authors: Turan, Gamze; Kansiz, Elif; Korkmaz, Gozde; Ozkan Coskun, Hande
journal: Turkish journal of biology = Turk biyoloji dergisi
abstract: BACKGROUND/AIM: Breast cancer (BC) is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy among women and exhibits substantial molecular heterogeneity. Luminal tumors represent the largest molecular subtype and are primarily driven by estrogen receptor alpha (ERalpha), a hormone-dependent transcription factor (TF) that regulates gene expression programs controlling proliferation, differentiation, and endocrine response. Herein, the study aimed to identify functionally relevant TFs regulated by ERalpha as part of a complex regulatory program in luminal BC. MATERIALS AND METHODS: An integrative transcriptomic approach was applied to identify TFs regulated by ERalpha in luminal BC. Differential gene expression analysis was integrated with RNA-seq data obtained from estrogen receptor 1 (ESR1) gene knockdown conditions. Network and enrichment analyses were conducted to reveal ERalpha-centered transcriptional programs. Key TFs acting as potential ERalpha-regulated mediators were evaluated for subtype-specific expression in BC patient cohorts and for associations with patient survival. MCF7 and T47D cells underwent a time course of hormone deprivation, and the gene expression patterns of two TF candidates were assessed. Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats-associated protein 9 (CRISPR-Cas9)-mediated gene knockout experiments were performed to interrogate the functional roles of the ERalpha-regulated candidate TFs. RESULTS: The integrative transcriptomic analysis identified 95 ERalpha-associated candidate genes. Network and enrichment analyses highlighted ERalpha-centered regulatory pathways with nine genes encoding TFs. Among these TFs, Msh homeobox 2 (MSX2) displayed a subtype-associated expression pattern in BC patients and was associated with favorable survival outcomes. Hormone deprivation significantly altered the expression of MSX2 in BC cell lines, which pinpoints the functional regulation by ERalpha. Time-course evaluation of MSX2 under hormone-deprived conditions confirmed that MSX2 may be regulated by ERalpha. Furthermore, functional interrogation using CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene disruption demonstrated that the loss of MSX2 significantly impaired the proliferative capacity and viability of luminal BC cells. CONCLUSION: These functional assessments identified MSX2 as an underexplored ERalpha-associated TF and suggest that the ERalpha-MSX2 regulatory relationship may contribute to transcriptional programs associated with luminal BC identity and cellular fitness.

title: Synchronized Optimal Transport Reconstructs Coupled Transcriptomic and Chromatin Dynamics.
authors: Wang, Jingfeng; Zhao, Yanxiang; Nie, Qing; Cang, Zixuan
abstract: Single-cell RNA and ATAC data collected across developmental stages provide time-course snapshots of transcriptional and regulatory states. Since sequencing is destructive, trajectories between these snapshots must be inferred from independently sampled cell populations. Existing approaches typically infer continuous dynamics in a single modality or integrate RNA and ATAC in a shared representation. Here we present Cross-Omics Aligned Trajectory Inference (COATI), which extends unbalanced synchronized dynamical optimal transport to time-dependent cross-modal maps for reconstructing coupled trajectories in distinct RNA and ATAC state spaces. We evaluated COATI on synthetic benchmarks and four developmental datasets using held-out-stage reconstruction and lineage analyses. COATI improved reconstruction of cell populations at held-out stages, including recovery of chromatin-state heterogeneity within cell types, and better preserved developmental lineage relationships. The unbalanced formulation allows the inference of population mass changes, which were shown to associate with DNA-replication programs at early stages and lineage-maturation programs later in development. The coupled trajectories enabled analysis of lineage-specific transcriptional and chromatin changes and their temporal relationships during development. Lineage responses inferred by COATI agreed with independent CRISPR perturbation results, and the inferred regulatory patterns were consistent with independent epigenetic data.

title: Hypoxia-inducible factor 2-alpha promotes fitness of cytokine-activated human natural killer cells.
authors: Feldman, H Alex; VonHandorf, Andrew; Alianiello, Kate E; English, Krista L; Reighard, Seth D; Brunner, Hermine I; Kottyan, Leah C; Weirauch, Matthew T; Kaufman, Kenneth M; Waggoner, Stephen N
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Natural Killer (NK) cells are innate effector cells with potent antiviral, antitumor, and immunoregulatory functions that are relevant for the treatment of human diseases. There is a pressing need to better understand the mechanisms governing cellular fitness and functional persistence of NK cells to generate NK cell-based therapeutics of sufficient durability to achieve meaningful clinical benefit. Given the central role of interleukin-2 (IL-2) and IL-15 in the survival and proliferation of NK cells, we sought to identify transcription factors induced by these cytokines that are essential for maintaining the fitness of human NK cells. Culture in IL-2 or IL-15 increased protein expression of hypoxia inducible factor 2 alpha (HIF-2alpha, encoded by EPAS1 ) but not HIF-1alpha in NK cells from healthy human blood donors. Unexpectedly, induction of HIF-2alpha was independent of limiting oxygen. CRISPR targeting of EPAS1 or pharmacological inhibition of HIF-2alpha protein expression markedly compromised the survival of cytokine-activated human NK cells. In contrast, inhibition of canonical HIF-2alpha transcription factor activity via blocking HIF-2alpha /HIF-1beta heterodimer formation had no apparent effects on NK cell viability, function, or metabolic fitness. These results suggest that cytokines, rather than hypoxia, activate an unconventional HIF-1beta independent, HIF-2alpha pathway that helps to maintain NK cells during cellular activation, revealing the potential promise of manipulating HIF-2alpha to improve the efficacy of adoptive NK cell therapies. KEY POINTS: Cytokine activation of human NK cells induces hypoxia-independent HIF-2alpha protein expressionConventional HIF-2alpha/HIF-1beta heterodimer driven gene regulation is dispensable in NK cellsAn unconventional activity of HIF-2alpha promotes survival of cytokine-activated NK cells.

title: Creation of genomic chimeras via megabase scale genome expansion.
authors: Sanfiorenzo, Charles; Zhang, Raymond J; Wythes, George; Wang, Megan; Huang, Jianyi; Hur, Jeongsoo; Lipschitz, Mikel; Zhou, Jie; Swift, Russell; Gerber, Bryan; Wang, Kaihang
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: An organism's physiology is controlled by its genomic content. Building genomic chimeras would enable melding of the diverse functions and properties of life. However, prior arts in genome synthesis are limited to reconstituting pre-existing functions within a singular genome rather than combining diverse genomic functions across multiple distinct genomes. Existing methods are also prohibitively expensive, labor intensive, and time consuming, and thus fundamentally not scalable for creating large synthetic chimeric genomes. To address all these limitations, we invented Additive Conjugative-CAST Engineering (ACE) combining conjugation with CRISPR-associated transposition (CAST) to deliver and integrate up to half a genome per step from a donor cell into a precisely defined position in the recipient's genome. We have demonstrated ACE's capability to integrate at least a 2-megabase donor genomic segment in a single step and at least 3 megabase in two consecutive steps. Importantly, we confirmed ACE's generality through the creation of multiple genomic chimeras across species, genus, and at least order barriers. With ACE, we further demonstrate such chimeric organisms, or what we call genome expanded organisms (GEOs), can be stably forged from at least three starting bacterial strains, and can be stably maintained to express all their acquired genomic parts in a single chimera. ACE offers a new paradigm of creating artificial lifeforms to combine desired properties and potentially create novel functions beyond the constraints of nature. ACE also offers a unique perspective to probe unexplored plasticity in genome architecture and expression patterns of novel, massively expanded genomes.

title: Druggable CSNK2A1-MeCP2 regulatory axis links Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome with MECP2 -related disorders.
authors: Anderson, Ashley G; Chamakuri, Srinivas; Meyer-Schuman, Rebecca; Chu, Elizabeth Hai-Yen; Revelli, Jean-Pierre; Kim, Jiyoen; Zaghlula, Manar; Veeraragavan, Surabi; Young, Damian W; Zoghbi, Huda Y
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: The brain is exquisitely sensitive to methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MeCP2) abundance. Too little causes Rett syndrome (RTT), too much causes MECP2 duplication syndrome (MDS), and in both, severity tracks with the amount of functional MeCP2. Even modest deviations are detrimental, yet how MeCP2 abundance is controlled remains poorly understood. Using genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens, we identified hundreds of proteins regulating MeCP2, revealing a casein kinase 2 alpha 1 (CSNK2A1)-driven regulatory axis stabilizing MeCP2. We show this axis is druggable and therapeutically relevant, using a novel CSNK2A1 inhibitor in human cells and targeting Csnk2a1 in an MDS mouse model. We further connect CSNK2A1-MeCP2 regulatory disruption to Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome (OCNDS), caused by mutations in CSNK2A1 , finding  approximately 50% less hippocampal MeCP2 in an OCNDS mouse model. Together, these data identify a druggable regulatory axis modulating MeCP2 and implicate MeCP2 dysregulation in the molecular pathogenesis of OCNDS and potentially other neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: RNA Polymerase Backtracking Promotes Type III-A CRISPR DNA Targeting.
authors: Hernandez Viera, Angel J; Gross, Naomi; Tran, Patricia Q; Shahin, Omar; Kosmopoulos, James C; Anantharaman, Karthik; Mo, Charlie Y
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Type III CRISPR-Cas systems provide transcription-dependent immunity against mobile genetic elements, yet the mechanism underlying their DNA targeting remains unclear. Although the type III effector Cas10-Csm functions as a single-stranded DNase in vitro , type III systems eliminate double-stranded DNA targets in vivo , suggesting that transcription generates critical DNA substrates. Here, we show that conserved RNA polymerase anti-backtracking factors, such as GreA, selectively inhibit DNA-targeting of type III immunity. GreA overexpression abolishes protection against both phages and conjugative plasmids, whereas mutations that disrupt GreA anti-backtracking activity eliminate this effect. In contrast, immunity mediated by the type II CRISPR-Cas system or the auxiliary type III RNase Csm6 remain unaffected, demonstrating that GreA specifically suppresses Cas10-dependent DNA interference. These findings identify RNA polymerase backtracking as a key determinant of Cas10-Csm activity and support a model in which arrested transcription complexes generate substrates for DNA degradation, opening up new anti-CRISPR strategies against type III.

title: Resolving how genetic perturbations act through gene regulatory paths.
authors: Ren, Lixin; Duren, Zhana
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Perturb-seq measures transcriptional responses to thousands of genetic perturbations, but each gene's response mixes the contributions of many regulatory paths, so how a perturbation acts cannot be resolved from expression alone, however large the model. Here we present REGA-perturb, which supplies this missing information rather than adding model complexity: reference epigenomes define a scaffold of possible transcription factor (TF)-regulatory element-gene paths, and perturbation responses, pooled through shared latent programs, determine how each path is used, requiring only RNA measurements. Across three CRISPR interference screens totaling 2.4 million cells, REGA-perturb inferred TF-target relationships that agreed with ChIP-seq binding with a gain over random more than four times that of the best existing method, separated candidate direct from indirect targets, and predicted targets of TFs withheld from training. It also inferred perturbation-induced changes in TF activity not reflected in TF transcript levels, and resolved perturbation-specific regulatory rewiring in which opposing regulatory changes cancel at the expression level.

title: Mapping the regulatory wiring of endothelial cell differentiation reveals a critical role for Hippo mechanosignaling.
authors: Nguyen, Tri C; King, Hunter D; Amgalan, Dulguun; Pushkarev, Olga; Mo, Yanyan Alexandra; Munger, Chad J; McCreery, Chloe; Gupta, Revant; Zeng, Tony; Zhou, Ronghao; Conley, Stephanie D; Batta, Surya Prakash Rao; Sheth, Maya U; Mattei, Eugenio; Masaltseva, Anastasiia; Kang, Helen Y; Ma, X Rosa; Tran, Ngoc; Gaskell, Liz; Shoresh, Noam; Orlova, Valeria; Kundaje, Anshul; Sumanas, Saulius; Ang, Lay Teng; Loh, Kyle M; Engreitz, Jesse M
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: At each step of development, stem cells encounter a branching decision to differentiate into one type of cell or another. This decision is executed through the action of competing gene programs that specify different cellular identities. Consequently, creating a comprehensive map of the gene programs that drive each branching step of human cell differentiation remains a long-sought goal of developmental and stem cell biology. Here, we introduce a framework combining genome-wide CRISPR screens, single-cell readouts, and gene program inference to systematically discover and characterize regulators of cell differentiation. This framework includes a method for CRISPR perturbations paired with single-cell RNA-seq called circular capture Perturb-seq (CC-Perturb-seq), which improves gRNA detection from split-pool combinatorial indexing protocols and enables perturbing many candidate regulators to map their effects on gene programs. We applied this framework to map how human pluripotent stem cells differentiate into arterial endothelial cells (ECs), and identified 174 regulators that promote or inhibit EC differentiation. By tracking gene programs across three stages of differentiation, we resolved when and how regulators divert cells toward alternative fates. This map revealed an unexpected requirement for the Hippo mechanosignaling pathway in EC specification. During lateral mesoderm differentiation, Hippo mechanosignaling was required to activate ETV2 , the master transcriptional regulator of endothelial identity. Inhibiting Hippo blocked ETV2 even in the presence of VEGF and diverted progenitors to a mesenchymal fate in vitro . Likewise, Hippo signaling was required for maximal etv2 expression in developing zebrafish embryos. Conversely, pharmacologically activating the Hippo pathway increased the purity of both arterial and venous EC differentiation in vitro . Our framework thus identifies novel regulators of endothelial cell differentiation, improves stem-cell differentiation protocols via manipulation of mechanosignaling, and provides a generalizable platform for mapping the regulatory wiring of human development.

title: A large, distinct family of RNase H fold nucleases associated with numerous defense systems in prokaryotes.
authors: Wolf, Yuri I; Arshad, Kanza; Kannatey-Asibu, Kwame; Theisen, Rachel Q; Kitzinger, Katherine A; Jain, Preeti V; Koonin, Eugene V; Makarova, Kira S; Ledvina, Hannah E
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: During the last decade, systematic efforts aimed at the characterization of prokaryotic immunity resulted in the discovery of several hundred distinct defense systems in bacteria and archaea. This suggests that the common defense systems were already known and only rare ones remained to be identified. Here we present a genomic census and analysis of a vast family of bacterial and archaeal proteins (known as Domain of Unknown Function, DUF3800) that contain a distinct variant of the RNase H fold and are encoded in a striking 15% of the available complete prokaryotic genomes. Most of these proteins are encoded in defense islands, often in a close association with known defense systems, hence the designation WARD ( W eaponized A ntiphage R Nase-dependent D efense). The WARDs display a broad variety of protein domain architectures and genomic contexts, including a strong link to restriction-modification, CRISPR-Cas, retrons, and non-coding RNAs, suggestive of a substantial diversity in defense mechanisms. We experimentally tested 10 WARDs, mostly, encoded by standalone genes, and found that 9 of these conferred robust protection against diverse phages in Escherichia coli . Therefore, WARDs appear to represent the third most abundant defense system type in prokaryotes.

title: NanoPAMDA enables rapid PAM characterization of metagenome-derived Cas9 effectors.
authors: Genel, Ibrahim; Suren, Ceren; Kurt, Ibrahim C
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 orthologs remain functionally underexplored despite the rapidly growing scale of publicly available metagenomic sequencing data. Here, we applied a multi-stage computational discovery pipeline to two independent sources of metagenomic sequence data, a multi-biome collection of 620,185 metagenome-assembled genomes spanning 17 public catalogs, and raw sequencing reads from human microbiome studies assembled de novo, to identify novel Cas9 orthologs. Candidates were filtered for guide RNA architectural plausibility, sequence novelty, conservation of catalytic residues, and structural integrity, yielding 14 candidates spanning both data sources for experimental characterization. To determine PAM preference at scale, we developed a cost-effective Nanopore long-read-based adaptation of the high-throughput PAM determination assay (NanoPAMDA), enabling rapid, time-resolved, kinetic PAM profiling across many candidates in parallel. One Cas9 effector, E10, showed PAM-specific activity in vitro and was catalytically active in E. coli . Together, these findings demonstrate a scalable, long-read sequencing-based framework for discovering and biochemically characterizing novel Cas9 orthologs from metagenomic data.

title: Therapeutic vulnerabilities of the drug-resistant fungal meningitis pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans.
authors: Huang, Manning Y; Hecht, Patrick; Cesar, Kyle; Ciranni, Massimiliano; Wei, Angela L; Boucher, Michael J; Briner, Sydney L; Lortal, Lea; Nayak, Veda; Ankur, Ankur; Wang, Tuo; Doering, Tamara L; Pastore, Vito Paolo; Madhani, Hiten D
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Treatment options are limited for the priority fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans . We describe CRISPR-insert, a scalable gene inactivation method for global interrogation of drug targets. Genome-wide screens using this methodology combined with machine learning predict 1,297 essential genes under liberal criteria. Unexpectedly absent from this list is FKS1 , encoding the target of echinocandin drugs to which C. neoformans is resistant. Contrary to longstanding literature, targeted deletion shows that FKS1 is not essential. Solid-state NMR reveals that fks1 Delta mutants lack beta-1,3-glucan, arguing against compensation by another synthase. We experimentally test essentiality predictions for genes lacking human orthologs, identifying high-priority drug target candidates. To uncover targets for combination therapies, we establish genome-scale quantitative genetic interaction mapping. We use this method to uncover synthetic lethal dependencies of echinocandin resistance determinants, including the druggable calcineurin and Cdc50-Apt1 pathways. CRISPR-insert illuminates therapeutic vulnerabilities of an invasive fungal pathogen.

title: ExPert infers causal perturbations from cell states across biological and clinical contexts.
authors: Schwartz, Leon; Schlamowitz, Jacob L; Kuznets-Speck, Benjamin; Johnson, Conor W; Das, Diptatanu; Grody, Emanuelle I; Bai, Tao; Sun, Hanxiao; Senthilkumar, Irish; Primavera, Gillian; Jung, Jaekwon; Kuusik, Britta; Grant, Rogan A; Rojas, Enrique; Abdrabou, Abdalla M; Peiffer, Brandon; Sun, Zhaoli; Diehl, Anna Mae; Marr, Carsten; Chandel, Navdeep S; Mithal, Divakar S; Weinberg, Samuel E; Adli, Mazhar; Kalsotra, Auinash; Prashnani, Ekta; Goyal, Yogesh
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Pooled single-cell CRISPR screens have driven substantial effort toward models predicting the response to a perturbation. We posed the inverse question: which perturbation produced an observed cell state? Here we developed ExPert (Extracting Perturbations), which learns one prototype per perturbation in a latent space shared by 12 cellular contexts, trained on 8,964 perturbations and 19.5 million cells, and ranks 19,895 candidate genes per query, over half absent from training. ExPert more than doubled held-out-context recall over the best existing method with 1,000-fold less compute, and transferred without retraining to drugs, protein degradation and combinations. In alcohol-associated liver disease it implicated mRNA export, unchanged in expression, and we experimentally confirmed nuclear poly(A) retention and isoform switching. In primary mitochondrial disease it recovered the affected complex from blood, localized the signal to monocytes, and flagged a misdiagnosed control. Perturbation atlases can thus be queried in reverse, from state to likely driver.

title: An Isogenic iPSC Model of LMNA p.R482W Recapitulates Adipocyte Dysfunction in Familial Partial Lipodystrophy Type 2.
authors: Borrego Alvarez, Aluet; Wasielewski, Will O; Gobble, McKinlee R S; Grupe, Michael; Ali, Lina M; Buchser, William; Boggs-Bailey, Lauren; Baldridge, Dustin; Maung, Jessica N; Nishii, Akira; MacDougald, Ormond A; Oral, Elif A; Stone, Stephen I
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Familial partial lipodystrophy type 2 (FPLD2) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by pathogenic variants in LMNA , most commonly p.R482W, and is characterized by selective loss of subcutaneous adipose tissue, severe insulin resistance, and dyslipidemia. The cellular mechanisms underlying adipocyte dysfunction in FPLD2 remain incompletely understood, in part because existing in vitro models rely on patient-derived, non-isogenic cell lines or require non-physiologic transgene overexpression to achieve adipogenic differentiation. Here, we describe a CRISPR/Cas9-edited isogenic iPSC model of FPLD2 in which the heterozygous LMNA c.1444C>T (p.R482W) variant was introduced into a healthy donor-derived iPSC line. Using a transgene-free mesenchymal progenitor differentiation protocol, we generated LMNA (p.R482W) and isogenic control adipocytes and characterized their transcriptomic and functional phenotypes. Bulk RNA-sequencing demonstrated strong concordance in adipogenesis gene expression between genotypes during differentiation (Pearson rho = 0.968), yet LMNA (p.R482W) adipocytes exhibited significant downregulation of key adipogenic, lipid-handling, and extracellular matrix genes compared to isogenic controls. Functionally, LMNA (p.R482W) adipocytes showed markedly impaired glucose uptake under both basal and insulin-stimulated conditions, consistent with severe insulin resistance. Seahorse extracellular flux analysis revealed a globally quiescent metabolic state with significantly reduced oxygen consumption rate (126.5 vs. 261.5 pmol/min, p < 0.0001) and extracellular acidification rate (27.6 vs. 46.7 mpH/min, p < 0.0001). To validate these findings in human tissue, gene set enrichment analysis results from the iPSC model were compared to single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data from subcutaneous white adipose tissue biopsies of individuals with FPLD2 carrying the LMNA p.R482W variant. Across 37 mutually significant pathways, 59.5% were concordant between the iPSC model and human adipose tissue, including the pathways most central to FPLD2 pathophysiology: adipogenesis, fatty acid metabolism, oxidative phosphorylation, and inflammatory response. These findings establish this isogenic iPSC system as a faithful cellular model of FPLD2 adipocyte biology and a platform for functional characterization of LMNA variants of uncertain significance.

title: Regulation of the Epstein-Barr Epigenome by Histone Variant MacroH2A.
authors: Castro-Munoz, Leonardo Josue; Yoon, Leena; Karisetty, Bhanu Chandra; Bharti, Aradhana; Tempera, Italo; Soldan, Samantha S; Lieberman, Paul
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Histone variants play an important role in regulating chromatin dynamics of Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV). Here, we investigate the role of histone variant macroH2A in EBV chromatin structure, gene expression and copy number control during latent infection. ChIP-seq analysis in EBV (+) SNU719 gastric carcinoma and Mutu I Burkitt lymphoma cells revealed that macroH2A was most enriched at repetitive DNA elements, including oriLyt, BHLF1, LF3 and terminal repeat (TR) regions of the EBV genome. MacroH2A depletion in EBV-associated gastric cancer cell line SNU719 led to a small increase in some viral lytic genes and increase in viral DNA copy number. RNAseq transcriptomics after macroH2A depletion identified major perturbations in cellular gene pathways, including beta-catenin/TCF signaling and chromatin remodeling. Depletion of macroH2A during EBV lytic reactivation reduced EBV lytic gene activation, but increased EBV DNA copy number. Previous study demonstrated a colocalization and cooperative binding between histone variant H2A.Z and EBNA1. We now show that depletion of macroH2A causes an increase in both H2A.Z and EBNA1 at oriP and cellular binding sites for EBNA1. We also found that gammaH2AX localizes to oriP and that this depends on macroH2A. Finally, we show that CRISPR/Cas9 knockout of macroH2A increases the replication and episome maintenance of oriP-containing plasmids. Taken together, these findings indicate that macroH2A localizes to the repetitive elements of EBV, including oriLyt, and can function to limit H2A.Z and EBNA1 binding at oriP, which alters DNA damage signaling at oriP and limits episomal replication. These findings provide a novel role for macroH2A in maintaining EBV copy number and genome integrity.

title: Loss of CDKN2A remodels Golgi morphology to create a lipid peroxidation vulnerability.
authors: Amalric, Amandine; Yang, Baixue; Scarpati, Rebecca; Uboveja, Apoorva; Zheng, Ruiying; Tom, Alex; Cole, Aidan R; Huacachino, Andrea Andress; Liu, Qin; Snyder, Nathaniel W; Kossenkov, Andrew V; Aird, Katherine M; Buj, Raquel
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Loss of the tumor suppressor CDKN2A /p16 occurs in  approximately 50% of human cancers, yet no therapies specifically target tumors with complete loss or reduced CDKN2A /p16 expression (hereafter CDKN2A /p16 (Low) ). Identifying selective vulnerabilities in CDKN2A /p16 (Low) tumors therefore represents a critical unmet need. Here, we identify altered Golgi morphology as a vulnerability in CDKN2A /p16 (Low) melanoma. A CRISPR knockout screen revealed that genes associated with Golgi membranes are essential for CDKN2A /p16 (Low) cell survival. CDKN2A /p16 knockdown in human and murine cancer cells was associated with striking Golgi compaction. CDKN2A /p16 knockdown sensitized cells to pharmacologic Golgi disruption via lipid peroxidation both in vitro and in vivo . Notably, reduced Retinoblastoma -associated protein ( RB1 ) expression did not recapitulate the increased sensitivity to Golgi disruption, supporting a role for non-canonical p16 functions in this vulnerability. Together, these findings uncover a previously unrecognized link between CDKN2A /p16 (Low) status and Golgi remodeling, revealing a Golgi-associated metabolic vulnerability in CDKN2A /p16 (Low) melanomas.

title: Inferring gene regulatory networks from single-cell perturbation data by optimizing causal reach of latent mediator dynamics.
authors: Qian, Weizhou; Song, Yuxuan; Welch, Joshua D
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Resolving the causal structure of gene regulatory networks is central to understanding cellular regulation. Pooled CRISPR screens with single-cell RNA readouts measure the transcriptional consequences of many interventions in parallel, providing a powerful resource for causal discovery. Combinatorial designs that perturb multiple regulators per cell increase throughput and can reveal responses that single-gene perturbations do not. However, inferring causal gene networks from these experiments remains challenging because gene regulatory interactions are nonlinear, dynamic, and often involve feedback. Thus, attributing the combined effect of several perturbations to individual regulators remains difficult. Additionally, transcriptional regulation is ultimately carried out by proteins, while single-cell perturbation datasets generally measure only RNA levels. Existing methods often simplify regulatory dynamics or rely on assumptions that conflict with gene regulation, such as acyclicity. Moreover, current evaluation practices usually rely on expression prediction error, which is readily computable in real datasets, but does not necessarily reflect graph quality. A complementary metric is needed to assess inferred regulatory connections using observed perturbation responses in real data. To address these challenges, we present CausalODE, a differentiable framework for learning causal graphs from single-cell perturbation data. Our approach incorporates three central insights to improve upon previous methods. First, genes that are differentially expressed when a gene is perturbed should be downstream of the target gene in the regulatory network; we quantify this property with a metric we term causal reach. Second, causal interactions involve transient cellular responses in RNA transcription, splicing, and degradation. Third, gene regulatory interactions are mediated by proteins, whose levels are not directly measured in single-cell RNA-seq experiments. Building on these insights, CausalODE learns a graph that optimizes the causal reach metric, captures transient cellular responses to perturbation, and explicitly models the latent dynamics of protein levels. Together, these components allow nonlinear responses, feedback loops, and time-lagged regulation. Across simulated Perturb-seq datasets with different sparsities and graph structures, CausalODE improves AUPRC and precision among top-ranked edges compared with baselines and competing methods, while achieving competitive AUROC. We introduce a metric to evaluate the causal reach of inferred graphs on real data by measuring how well the graphs explain differentially expressed genes in single-cell perturbation experiments. Using this metric, CausalODE outperforms the strongest competing method or baseline by approximately 60% on the CaRPool-seq knockdown dataset and 80% on the Norman et al. activation dataset. Its top-ranked edges generally show greater enrichment for high-confidence evidence from cell-type-matched ChIP-seq, CollecTRI, and regulatory STRING than those of other methods. The inferred graphs also distin-guish non-additive from approximately additive genetic interactions in held-out perturbation pairs. Finally, ablation analyses show that optimizing causal reach improves performance on held-out perturbations, and the learned latent regulator activities track simulated protein dynamics, with median temporal correlations ranging from 0.79 to 0.99.

title: An integrated workflow for dual-guide CRISPR-Cas9 targeting and amplicon-based genotyping of Pla2g6 in primary mouse bone marrow-derived macrophages.
authors: Challa, Anil K; Nair, Rithvikha; Gurusamy, Arumugam; Huynh, Thi Yen Ly; Folmar, Jonathan R; Ahamed, Aaliya; Chowdarapu, Sriharsha; Ramanadham, Sasanka
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 editing in primary bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMD-Mɸs) requires coordinated assessment of cellular morphology, target modification, and sequence-level editing outcomes. We describe a workflow for dual-guide targeting of murine Pla2g6 that integrates guide design, ribonucleoprotein nucleofection, PCR-heteroduplex mobility analysis (PCR-HMA), and targeted amplicon sequencing. At 24 h after nucleofection, cells receiving ribonucleoproteins assembled with chemically synthesized single-guide RNAs preserved the elongated, adherent morphology, whereas cultures receiving in vitro -transcribed guides contained predominantly poorly adhered, rounded cells and appeared less densely populated; both guide preparations generated indels and deletions, so the difference observed was in cell appearance rather than in target modification. PCR-HMA provided a simple, qualitative screen for sequence heterogeneity and for a putative deletion product, which was subsequently characterized by sequencing. In two independent BMDM samples, one each from C57BL/6 and NOD mice, breakpoint-based analysis identified editing-associated indels in 54.7% and 44.5% of analyzed reads, compared with 0.28% and 0.07% in matched Cas9-only controls. Deletions spanning both target sites represented 33.1% and 26.2% of analyzed reads; none were detected among 4,383 analyzed control reads. The modal spanning deletion was 137 bp, the size predicted from precise joining of the two blunt Cas9 ends. Sequence interpretation depended on verified guide coordinates, deletion-aware analysis settings, and matched controls: scored permissively, the same control reads returned 22-23% apparent editing. Modest-depth Nanopore sequencing recovered the major editing classes, although low-frequency variants and small indels required additional caution. This workflow supports a simple and streamlined screening and sequence-based genotyping of edited BMDM populations, allowing the discernment of the comprehensive mutation spectrum arising from CRISPR-Cas9 gene targeting.

title: In situ single-cell CRISPR screens uncover context-dependent rewiring of glioma states and immune recruitment.
authors: Hou, Nicholas; Lia, Ioana-Teodora; Giglio, Ross M; Van, Bailey T; Pallais-Aks, Sebastian; Vaikunthan, Mathini; Lu, Vivian; Guo, Jonathan; Williams, Destinee; Nieto, Tiffany C; Shi, Lingting; Slater, Cody; Azizi, Elham; McFaline-Figueroa, Jose L
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: In vivo single-cell CRISPR screens can resolve perturbation effects in native tissues, but few combine cell-type-restricted delivery, somatic tumor initiation, and combinatorial perturbation. Here we developed an RCAS-TVA-based single-cell CRISPR screening approach coupling oncogenic transformation with single- or dual-guide perturbation in defined neural progenitors. In glioma, tumor suppressor loss produced distinct genotype-dependent transcriptional states, including an NF1 -loss-associated increase in mesenchymal programs. Introducing a fixed Cdkn2a (ARF) perturbastion altered malignant-cell state composition, immune-cell abundance, and the effects of additional tumor-suppressor perturbations, including increased representation of Pten - and Rb1 -deficient cells, suggestive of the relief of an ARF-dependent genetic barrier. These perturbations converged on transcriptional states resembling pharmacologic p53 activation in human glioblastoma. Across mouse tumors and human glioblastoma models, this response was associated with increased astrocyte-like state representation. These findings establish a framework for single-cell analysis of context-dependent somatic perturbations during tumor initiation in vivo .

title: Cell-in-drop genotyping detects megabase-scale loss of heterozygosity as a quantitative marker for CRISPR-Cas9 on-target toxicity.
authors: Medhi, Darpan; Mazutis, Linas; Jasin, Maria
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Targeted DNA double strand breaks catalyzed by CRISPR-Cas9 have been demonstrated to cause megabase-scale segmental deletions and whole chromosome losses in a wide variety of mouse and human cell lines. This raises safety concerns for CRISPR-Cas9 based therapeutics and highlights the need for scalable methods to assess its on-target genotoxicity in clinical contexts. In this report, we present cell-in-drop genotyping, as a high throughput approach that combines single cell encapsulation with droplet-based PCR genotyping of endogenous polymorphisms to detect loss of heterozygosity (LOH) at a targeted chromosome without any genome manipulation. With this approach, we detected megabase scale LOH induced by Cas9 DSBs, mostly frequently by segmental loss. This approach also detected LOH from loss of a critical DNA repair factor, BLM helicase, and LOH induced by other genotoxic conditions, in particular, the chemotherapeutic drugs Paclitaxel and Mitomycin C, which were demonstrated to induce LOH by different mechanisms. A modified version of the assay also captured rare local short range LOH arising from DSB-induced interhomologue recombination. Because it requires no genome manipulation, cell-in-drop genotyping offers a practical, scalable tool for evaluating genotoxic risk of CRISPR-Cas9 and other agents in research and clinical development.

title: Phenotype-genotype spectrum in CTNND2-related neurodevelopmental disease.
authors: Shahsavani, Mansoureh; Wincent, Josephine; Reiter, Ricarda; Soltysova, Andrea; Schuy, Jakob; Helgadottir, Hafdis T; Eisfeldt, Jesper; Ek, Marlene; Ficek, Andrej; Druschke, Lotta; Kusikova, Katarina; Hsieh, Tzung-Chien; Kirchhoff, Aron; Krawitz, Peter; Li, Jing-Mei; Webersinke, Gerald; Gorokhova, Svetlana; Missirian, Chantal; Riccardi, Florence; Pavinato, Lisa; Brusco, Alfredo; Mandrile, Giorgia; Trajkova, Slavica; Pintus, Francesco; Gagachovska, Biljana; Waisfisz, Quinten; van Hagen, Johanna M; Bedoukian, Emma; Izumi, Kosuke; Granger, Leslie; Petersen, Andrea; Oegema, Renske; Huibers, Manon; Demurger, Florence; Brischoux-Boucher, Elise; Julia, Sophie; Banneau, Guillaume; Zavala, M Jesus; Lagos, Catalina; Repetto, Gabriela M; Jouret, Guillaume; Kentros, Catherine; Ganapathi, Mythily; Chung, Wendy K; May, Halie; Hiatt, Susan M; Kelley, Whitley V; Forster, Alisa; Olfe, Lisa; Shillington, Amelle; Dauriat, Benjamin; Mercier, Sandra; Cogne, Benjamin; Engel, Camille; Dahlen, Eric; Rosenberger, Georg; Sauvigny, Thomas; Abdallah, Hamza Hadj; Courtin, Thomas; Stray-Pedersen, Asbjorg; Bernat, John A; Paolillo, Vitoria K; Viso, Florencia Del; Alaimo, Joseph T; Thiffault, Isabelle; Farrow, Emily G; Cohen, Ana S A; Weis, Serge; Duba, Hans-Christoph; Nordgren, Ann; Falk, Anna; Weis, Denisa; Lindstrand, Anna
abstract: Background Heterozygous variants in CTNND2 , encoding the brain-specific protein delta-catenin, are associated with a broad spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders, including dyslexia, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, intellectual disability, and autism. Despite its clinical significance, the full phenotypic spectrum of CTNND2 -associated disorders and the neurodevelopmental role of delta-catenin, a key component of the cadherin-catenin cell adhesion complex, remain poorly defined. Methods Through international collaboration, we assembled the phenotypic and molecular information for 57 individuals, 42 previously unpublished, carrying heterozygous CTNND2 variants. All individuals were evaluated by local clinicians, and the variants were identified through exome or genome sequencing, clinical microarray, or karyotyping. To investigate the effects of delta-catenin loss on early neurogenesis, we performed neural induction and transcriptomic profiling in three patient-derived neuroepithelial stem cell (NESC) lines and three isogenic CRISPR-Cas9-edited CTNND2 knockout lines. Transcriptomic changes were assessed across the patient-derived and CRISPR-edited models to identify shared and distinct transcriptional alterations, with particular focus on genes within the CTNND2 interactome and WNT- and cadherin-associated networks. Results We identified 41 distinct CTNND2 variants, including 28 novel variants comprising 18 predicted loss-of-function and 10 protein-altering variants. Among cases with parental testing, eight variants occurred de novo and 12 were inherited from an affected parent. The most common clinical features were developmental delay (90%), intellectual disability (74%), and behavioral abnormalities (79%). Neural induction revealed delayed neural rosette formation in one of the three patient-derived lines, whereas the remaining patient-derived and knockout lines showed apparently normal neural induction. Transcriptomic profiling revealed variable but partly convergent alterations across the patient-derived and knockout models, involving the CTNND2 interactome and WNT and cadherin signaling networks at both developmental time points. Conclusions This study defines CTNND2 -related neurodevelopmental disorders as a clinically recognizable but highly variable phenotype overlapping with other intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorders. Across cellular models, transcriptomic analysis identified variable and partly convergent changes involving interconnected networks associated with CTNND2, WNT, and cadherin signaling. The variability observed across both individuals and cellular models further highlights the influence of genetic background and other modifying factors on the consequences of CTNND2 disruption. These findings expand the clinical and molecular spectrum of CTNND2 -associated disorders and provide a framework for further investigation of the molecular consequences of CTNND2 disruption during early human neural development.

title: A high-throughput all-optical platform for mapping gene perturbations to electrophysiology.
authors: Zhang, Jinfan; Gong, Daozheng; Barrios, Alec M; Itkis, Daniel G; Sahni, Keemaya; Fandl, Hannah; Uenaka, Takeshi; Walton, Russell T; Plutkis, Sarah E; Lavis, Luke D; Blainey, Paul C; Wernig, Marius; Nehme, Ralda; Lee, Richard T; Fraenkel, Ernest; Farhi, Samouil L; Cohen, Adam E
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Electrical phenotyping remains a bottleneck in linking genes to cellular function. We developed a high-throughput all-optical electrophysiology platform combining an engineered human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) line, wide-field voltage imaging, and automated analysis. The hiPSC line integrates inducible NGN2, CRISPR interference, and degron-gated expression of Voltron2 and CheRiff, enabling neuronal differentiation, targeted gene knockdown, and optical electrophysiology. The microscope records approximately 1,500 spiking glutamatergic neurons at 800 Hz across a 4x4 mm field, with larger fields supporting approximately 3,000 neurons at 660 Hz. Automated analysis extracts single-cell voltage traces and quantifies firing patterns, action-potential waveforms, and subthreshold dynamics. Arrayed knockdown of five sodium- and potassium-channel genes produced distinct electrophysiological phenotypes. The engineered hiPSC line also supported optical electrophysiology recordings from motor neurons, astrocytes, and cardiomyocytes. These results establish a scalable platform for high-throughput electrophysiological phenotyping and functional genomics in hiPSC-derived cells.

title: Whole embryo barcoding reveals convergent origins of mesodermal cells during mammalian gastrulation.
authors: Secchi, Marine A; Martin, Peter J; Cornwall-Scoones, Jake; van Egeren, Debra; Dooley, Peyton J; Liu, Erica Y; Liu, Nianping; Masaltseva, Anastasiia; King, Hunter D; Jokhai, Rayyan T; Qiu, Xiaojie; Loh, Kyle M; Gottgens, Berthold; Camargo, Fernando D; Bowling, Sarah J
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Classical fate-mapping and recent single-cell trajectory studies have suggested that mesoderm diversification during gastrulation proceeds through progressive fate bias and branching lineage segregation. Here, we combine inducible CRISPR-based lineage recording with single-cell RNA sequencing to reconstruct clonal relationships across mouse embryos barcoded at primitive streak onset and analyzed at early organogenesis. Mesodermal clones diverged after streak formation, but their developmental outputs remained extensively overlapping, revealing a clonal architecture that is not a simple branching lineage tree. Using sampling-aware statistical models, we quantify distinct clonal origins of paraxial mesoderm across the anterior-posterior axis, show that endothelial cells arise from multiple mesoderm origins but demonstrate transcriptional differences that correspond to anatomical position and clonal lineage, and identify clonal sharing between extra-embryonic mesoderm and embryonic derivatives, including cardiac lineages and a shared hindlimb-allantois progenitor. In the heart, progenitors corresponding to classical heart fields remain multipotent, contributing both myocardial and non-myocardial cell types. Together, our findings support a model in which mesodermal diversity is assembled through spatially distinct, fate-biased progenitor pools whose descendants converge on shared cell states. Our findings challenge simple branching models of mesoderm diversification and provide a clonal framework for understanding how tissue diversity emerges in the embryo.

title: Time-resolved single-cell screening reveals the dynamic regulatory architecture of human cardiogenesis.
authors: Lindenhofer, D; Mikulik, K; Mantz, S; Jung, H; Ueltzhoffer, K; Kueblbeck, M; Rueda-Gensini, L; Munoz-Verdu, A; Haas, J; Meder, B; Schraivogel, D; Mall, M; Huber, W; Pettet, A; Reddington, J P; Clarke, B; Stegle, O; Steinmetz, L M
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Congenital heart disease (CHD) originates during early embryogenesis, yet when disease genes act cannot be determined from existing data. Human fetal heart atlases lack critical time points, and perturbation screens that systematically assess gene function currently profile at most a few time points. Here we combined single-cell CRISPR screening of 400 disease-relevant genes in cardioids, sampled daily over seven developmental days ( approximately 975,000 cells), with a matched multiome atlas. Perturbation phenotypes were strongly dependent on developmental stage. Perturbations that reshaped cell-fate allocation or gene expression were enriched for CHD-linked genes, and most acted already during progenitor stages. Timing was largely independent of the target gene's own expression, marking instead when a cell state became functionally dependent on it, and some effects persisted after expression declined. Consensus gene regulatory networks integrating perturbation and multiome data recovered stage-specific regulators and nominated HOXB2 and HOXB3 as candidate cardiac regulators. Many perturbations converged on shared downstream programmes, which were reorganised through differentiation. Effects correlated in progenitors were maintained in differentiated cells, split into distinct programmes, converged with other perturbations or disappeared entirely, indicating that gene function is highly context dependent. Beyond advancing our understanding of the developmental regulatory logic underlying CHD, our work provides a resource for developing context-dependent models for in silico prediction of perturbation effects.

title: Unbiased lineage tracing across the adipose organ decouples developmental origin from anatomical and transcriptomic identities.
authors: Inoue, Oto; Singh, Archana; Ginugu, Meghana; Ahn, Christopher; Secchi, Marine A; Bowling, Sarah J; Lim, Hee-Woong; Sanchez-Gurmaches, Joan
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: The developmental origins of individual adipose depots and whether embryonic lineage dictates adult function remain unresolved. Here, we apply in utero CRISPR-mediated barcoding lineage tracing to construct the first unbiased clonal map of adipose organ development in mice. The developmental hierarchy we uncover challenges several conventions. Remarkably, interscapular brown fat, used as the prototypical brown fat, is the most developmentally isolated brown fat; depots sharing Myf5/Pax3 lineage markers fail to cluster together; mesenteric white fat shares unexpected high clonal ancestry with brown fats despite a radically divergent transcriptome; and subcutaneous white adipose tissues converge transcriptomically despite distant developmental origins. These findings call for a reinterpretation of single-marker lineage tracing data across the adipose organ and propose that adipose depot identity is not solely encoded by embryonic lineage but is substantially shaped by the anatomical niche. HIGHLIGHTS: CRISPR barcoding simultaneously resolves lineage relationships among 12 fat depots.iBAT is the most developmentally isolated BAT.Visceral white fats are developmentally closer than the subcutaneous depots.Developmental origin and transcriptomic identity are largely decoupled across fat depots.

title: Perturbation-induced gene programs map the hidden regulatory architecture of complex diseases.
authors: Turhan, Berk; Lee, Hanbyul; Liu, Dingyu; Le, Ann; Ghosh, Arpan; Nandi, Dhruba; Mazumder, Rahul; Engreitz, Jesse M; Jin, Xin; Huangfu, Danwei; Dey, Kushal K
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Steady-state molecular profiles incompletely capture the regulatory programs through which genetic variation influences complex disease, particularly programs that emerge only when cells are perturbed. Here, we introduce Perturbscape, a computational framework that learns multiscale gene programs for individual perturbations in a CRISPR Perturb-seq screen using linear and nonlinear contrastive approaches alongside complementary program-learning methods, and integrates them with human genetics to prioritize disease-relevant genes, perturbations and downstream regulatory pathways. Across 15,859 perturbation-by-context profiles from 7 Perturb-seq systems and 53 complex diseases and traits (mean GWAS N=291K), perturbation-induced programs showed up to 4.3-fold higher heritability informativeness than analogous steady-state multi-tissue gene prioritization, and retained significant conditional heritability informativeness across all 34 matched cell system-trait comparisons after accounting for steady-state prioritization. Preserving perturbation-specific programs further yielded 2.5-5.3-fold higher trait relevance scores than programs derived from control cells, pooled perturbations or differential-expression summaries. In K562, Perturbscape-prioritized genes showed stronger enrichment for rare-variant burden genes than steady-state prioritization and were supported by orthogonal enhancer CRISPRi screens. In HepG2, LDL cholesterol-associated perturbation- induced programs specifically revealed statin-responsive pathways not significantly enriched by steady-state PoPS prioritization, supported by pharmacological transcriptional responses and population plasma proteomics. Perturbscape also recovered blood-related trait-conditioned trans-regulatory relationships that were specifically supported by population trans-eQTLs in IFN-gamma-stimulated monocytes (OR = 1.30, P=1.6e-05). Perturbscape further revealed developmental-stage-specific convergence between monogenic diabetes regulators and polygenic T2D risk during pancreatic islet differentiation, and neuronal-subclass-specific autism-associated regulatory programs in vivo . Together, these findings establish perturbation-induced gene programs as a complementary layer of disease-relevant regulatory information, revealing genetically informative pathways and context-specific regulatory relationships incompletely represented by steady-state molecular atlases.

title: ATF3 Preserves Macrophage Cholesterol Homeostasis during Metabolic Stress.
authors: Pearson, Amelia M; Barudi, Yusuf; Kang, Jihye; Williams, Langley; Vallez, Charles N; Ulanowicz, Cassidy J; Gokhale, Nandan S; Divanovic, Senad; Troutman, Ty D
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: BACKGROUND: Macrophages must coordinate immune activation with maintenance of cellular cholesterol homeostasis, yet the transcriptional mechanisms integrating these processes remain incompletely understood. Activating transcription factor 3 (ATF3) suppresses inflammatory and interferon responses and has been implicated in macrophage lipid metabolism, suggesting a role in coordinating immune and sterol-responsive transcriptional programs. METHODS: Wild-type and ATF3-deficient bone marrow-derived macrophages were analyzed by bulk RNA sequencing following Toll-like receptor stimulation and under conditions of sterol loading or depletion. Cholesterol content, cytokine production, and sterol-responsive gene expression were quantified. Human metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) datasets and Kupffer cell-specific ATF3 knockout mice were used to assess disease relevance in vivo. RESULTS: ATF3 deficiency enhanced inflammatory and interferon-responsive transcriptional programs while suppressing a sterol-responsive gene module enriched for SREBP2 target genes. This phenotype was conserved across diverse Toll-like receptor stimuli and accompanied by persistent Ch25h upregulation. Despite exhibiting elevated cellular cholesterol, ATF3-deficient macrophages retained transcriptional responsiveness to sterol loading and depletion while demonstrating reduced induction of SREBP2-dependent genes across conditions. IFNAR blockade reduced interferon-responsive gene expression but did not normalize Ch25h or sterol-responsive gene expression. In contrast, CRISPR-mediated reduction of Ch25h partially restored sterol-responsive gene expression in inflammatory ATF3-deficient macrophages. In human MASLD, hepatic ATF3 expression positively correlated with disease severity. In mice, ATF3 was preferentially induced in Kupffer cells during metabolic stress, and Kupffer cell-specific deletion of ATF3 increased liver injury and Kupffer cell lipid accumulation. CONCLUSIONS: ATF3 supports sterol-responsive transcriptional programs while restraining inflammatory activation in macrophages. ATF3 loss results in elevated cellular cholesterol, impaired SREBP2-dependent gene expression, and persistent derepression of Ch25h , which contributes to but does not fully explain the sterol phenotype. These findings identify ATF3 as a coordinator of macrophage adaptation to inflammatory and metabolic stress and support a protective role for Kupffer cell ATF3 during metabolic liver disease.

title: Correction to 'A new anti-CRISPR gene promotes the spread of drug-resistance plasmids in Klebsiella pneumoniae'.
Clinical validation of KIF11 overexpression in colorectal cancer and its potential association with the antitumor effects of nitidine chloride.
authors: Li, Hui; Lin, Rui; Wu, Ke-Jun; Li, Jin-Cheng; Wei, Long; Qin, Kai; Liu, Li-Min; Huang, Xiao-Jue; Mo, Liu-Hui; Li, Bin; Li, Dong-Ming; Li, Zong-Yu; Zeng, Da-Tong; Zhang, Wei; Gan, Lang-Ning; He, Rong-Quan; Chen, Gang; Zhang, Sen
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer mortality with few effective targeted therapies. Kinesin family member 11 (KIF11), a motor protein essential for mitotic spindle assembly, is frequently overexpressed in multiple cancers. We hypothesized that nitidine chloride (NC), a natural benzophenanthridine alkaloid with documented anti-tumor activity, might suppress CRC by targeting KIF11.Molecular docking predicted a strong interaction between NC and KIF11 (- 9.0 kcal/mol). RNA sequencing, quantitative RT-PCR, and immunohistochemistry confirmed that NC treatment markedly downregulated KIF11 expression. Meta-analysis across public datasets showed consistent KIF11 mRNA overexpression in CRC (standardized mean difference [SMD] = 1.33; AUC = 0.87), while in-house immunohistochemistry on 416 clinical specimens demonstrated even stronger protein-level elevation (AUC = 0.99) that correlated with larger tumor size and deeper invasion. Single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics further revealed that KIF11 is preferentially expressed in proliferative malignant epithelial cells. Through CRISPR-based knockout screening and lentiviral silencing, KIF11 depletion impaired the growth or viability of the examined CRC cell models. Public ChIP-seq data suggested RAD21 occupancy near the KIF11 regulatory region, whereas reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation supported an association between the RAD21 and KIF11 proteins. Among genes co-expressed with KIF11,a pronounced enrichment was observed in pathways governing cell-cycle progression. Following KIF11 knockdown, transcriptomic profiling showed reduced expression across cell-cycle, DNA-replication, and chromatin-cohesion programs, alongside a reciprocal increase in amino-acid metabolism and stress-response genes. At the functional level, KIF11 depletion suppressed cell proliferation and induced G2/M-phase arrest. Taken together, these in vitro and limited xenograft data indicate that NC restrains CRC growth chiefly through the RAD21-KIF11 axis; KIF11 represents a promising preclinical target, though comprehensive systematic in vivo pharmacodynamic and translational animal validation remains absent in the current study and requires further independent investigation.

title: Human iPSC-based modeling reveals coding and non-coding transcriptomic alterations associated with RFX3 deficiency in pancreatic islets.
authors: Elsayed, Ahmed K; Alnesf, Aldana; Aldous, Noura; Abohalawa, Bushra Yasin; Alajez, Nehad M; Abdelalim, Essam M
abstract: BACKGROUND: RFX3 is a transcription factor (TF) critical for pancreatic endocrine development. Its loss impairs beta-cell differentiation, promotes enterochromaffin cell (EC) generation, and induces apoptosis. However, the role of non-coding RNAs in mediating these effects remains poorly understood. METHODS: Using CRISPR/Cas9-derived RFX3 knockout (KO) human iPSC-derived pancreatic islets, we performed integrated transcriptomic analyses of coding and non-coding RNAs. Differentially expressed miRNAs (DEmiRs) and lncRNAs (DElncRNAs) were validated by RT-qPCR. Target prediction and competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) network analyses were conducted to explore potential regulatory interactions affecting key endocrine genes. RESULTS: RFX3 deficiency induced widespread transcriptomic changes in human iPSC-derived pancreatic islets. Core beta-cell markers and key pancreatic TFs were downregulated, alongside genes regulating ion channels, vesicle trafficking, metabolic sensing, and insulin secretion. Conversely, apoptotic and EC genes were upregulated. RFX3 KO islets exhibited significant alterations in miRNA profiles, including upregulation of miR-451a, miR-215-5p, miR-122-5p, miR-338-3p, miR-194-5p, miR-378a-3p, and the miR-29 family, which are predicted to target critical pancreatic endocrine genes. Several lncRNAs, including LINC00461, MIAT, RMST, and AC020916.1, were downregulated, potentially influencing miRNA activity via ceRNA interactions. Integrated analyses identified core regulatory axes, such as miR-4455/INS, miR-122-5p/ARX, and miR-660-3p/GHRL, while apoptosis-related genes, including CASP, TNFSF10, and TXNIP, were also predicted targets of dysregulated miRNAs. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings reveal widespread alterations in non-coding RNA networks associated with RFX3 loss, highlighting a potential layer of post-transcriptional regulation linked to impaired pancreatic endocrine development. These results provide insights into how RFX3 deficiency may reshape islet transcriptomes, influencing beta-cell maturation, function, and survival.

title: A comparative review of adaptive laboratory evolution in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Yarrowia lipolytica: mechanistic understanding, biotechnological applications, and industrial prospects.
authors: Syraji, Yonas; Dejene, Fitsum; Jeyaramraja, P R
abstract: Adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) is a powerful technique in yeast strain development, and it also helps in the understanding of microbial adaptations and development of robust strains for industrial biotechnology. Adaptive mutations enable strains to withstand stressors found in industrial processing, namely high ethanol concentration, temperature fluctuations, oxidative stress, high osmotic pressure, and presence of inhibitors. The yeast S. cerevisiae is still often linked to high-titer ethanol production and stress resistance, while Y. lipolytica has complementary advantageous characteristics mainly in lipid accumulation and ability to consume non-conventional carbon sources like glycerol and waste oils. The industrial applications of ALE consist of the production of biofuels, lipids, organic acids, and value-added biochemicals. These applications, therefore, strengthen the circularity principle of the bioeconomy by enabling the upcycling of waste streams through novel management practices. Hence, ALE serves as a versatile platform for analysis of genotype-phenotype correlations, promoting sustainable and economically viable processes in industrial bio-procedures. This review article provides a comparative and comprehensive study of ALE in S. cerevisiae and Y. lipolytica, which synthesizes evolutionary principles, strain properties, mechanistic understanding, and adaptive significance. Moreover, the progress achieved by ALE is also discussed in the context of industrial and biotechnological applications. Lastly, future directions are addressed, highlighting the integration of automation, standardization, machine learning, genome-scale modeling, and CRISPR-mediated rational engineering to mitigate major bottlenecks and make ALE less variable and more scalable.

title: Engineered hypoimmunogenic iPSC-derived mesenchymal stromal cells secreting high levels of functional FVIII ameliorate the hemophilia A phenotype.
authors: Tang, Qiyu; Chen, Yan; Tang, Wenjuan; Liu, Yating; Zhao, Junya; Wang, Zujia; Li, Zhixing; Zhu, Guanshan; Wu, Lingqian; Liang, Desheng
journal: Cellular and molecular life sciences : CMLS
abstract: Cell-based gene therapy represents a promising therapeutic avenue for genetic diseases such as hemophilia A (HA). However, clinical translation is limited by low transgene expression and host immune responses. Here, we describe a universally applicable hypoimmunogenic cell therapy. Using CRISPR/Cas9, we targeted a codon-optimized B domain-deleted F8 gene along with CD47 into the B2M locus in human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and differentiated these cells into mesenchymal stromal cells (iMSCs). The engineered iMSCs secreted functional FVIII at high concentrations (1271 ng/10(6) cells/48 h) and exhibited hypoimmunogenic properties. In immunodeficient mice, both intravenous and intramuscular administration were shown to be effective. Transplantation of engineered iMSCs into HA mice significantly increased plasma FVIII activity and ameliorated the bleeding phenotype. This study presents a combination strategy that integrates a designed hypoimmunogenic platform with targeted gene integration to enable effective potential allogeneic cell therapy for HA and other genetic diseases.

title: DNA CODEC: compressed obfuscated DNA encoding in cells for secure in vivo data storage.
authors: Kang, Taek; Zhou, Zikun; Mohammed, Shayan; Makris, Yiorgos; Bleris, Leonidas
abstract: DNA represents a compelling medium for data storage due to its density, durability, and compatibility with biological systems. Current in vivo DNA data storage strategies are largely restricted to single-population systems, limiting scalability and access control. Here, we present DNA CODEC, a multi-population in vivo DNA data storage platform that combines high-density encoding with molecular obfuscation across engineered human cell populations. CODEC uses 10-ary Huffman coding with degenerate bases to optimize compressibility while maintaining decoding accuracy despite biological and technical noise. Data payloads are stably integrated into the human genome using CRISPR-based targeted insertion. Obfuscation is introduced through heterogeneous populations containing decoy clones with structurally similar, non-informative masking sequences to conceal the true payload. CODEC stably maintains genomic payloads across extended cell culture, demonstrating robustness to replication errors and population drift. Together, these features establish a scalable framework for high-fidelity and secure DNA data storage in biological systems.

title: A receptor switch between discoidin domain receptors underlies orthobunyavirus entry and host range.
authors: Zhang, Yuyi; Wang, Fei; Gao, Zhichao; Yang, Lulu; Zhou, Jiayue; Wang, Xiaoyu; Zhao, Yubo; Huang, Doudou; Tian, Sicheng; Guo, Hongyuan; Feng, Fei; Zhan, Ran; Hu, Yingxin; He, Zhuohao; Cao, Sheng; Yuan, Zhiming; Xia, Han; Zhang, Rong
abstract: Orthobunyaviruses, an important group of arboviruses with broad vector and host ranges, pose a persistent global public health threat, yet their cellular entry and cross-species transmission remain poorly understood. Ebinur Lake virus (EBIV), a recently identified orthobunyavirus detected in multiple countries and hosts, demonstrates potential zoonotic and spillover relevance. Using a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify discoidin domain receptor 2 (DDR2) as an entry receptor for EBIV. Knockout and ectopic expression confirm that DDR2 promotes EBIV infectivity by facilitating viral binding and internalization. The discoidin (DS) domain of DDR2 directly interacts with EBIV particles at the Gc stalk region. A soluble DS decoy or anti-DDR2 DS antibody potently inhibits EBIV infection in cell lines and primary neural cells. The DS decoy or Ddr2 knockout protects mice from lethal EBIV challenge, significantly reducing viral loads. DDR2 homologs from diverse mammals and birds bind EBIV Gc and support infection, underscoring a broad host range. Notably, we demonstrate a receptor switch among phylogenetically related orthobunyaviruses: human-infecting Germiston virus (GERV) also utilizes DDR2, while Bozo virus (BOZOV) employs DDR1. These findings establish discoidin domain receptors as functional entry receptors for orthobunyaviruses, revealing a mechanism for broad host tropism and providing insights for antiviral strategies.

title: Deconvoluting the mode of action of antileishmanial aminopyrazoles through chemical mutagenesis.
authors: Ahmad, Rokaya; Van den Kerkhof, Magali; Leprohon, Philippe; Smiejkowska, Natalia; Wuyts, Ellen; Van Wielendaele, Pieter; Dufour, Sara; Devos, Simon; Baeza Garcia, Alvaro; Braillard, Stephanie; Mowbray, Charles E; Maes, Louis; Sterckx, Yann G-J; Ouellette, Marc; Caljon, Guy
abstract: Aminopyrazoles have emerged as a promising series of antileishmanial compounds. Molecular target deconvolution has been a major challenge because successive drug exposure failed to select for resistance. Chemical mutagenesis combined with aminopyrazole selective pressure and whole genome sequencing was used as an alternative approach. From the obtained panel of 28 resistant lines, an association was discovered between >10-49-fold resistance and multiple independent heterozygous mutations in the C-terminal FYVE Zn finger domain of LINF_180011100. LINF_180011100 gene overexpression and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing has independently confirmed the association with 10- to 30-fold aminopyrazole resistance. Genetic fusion with an N-terminal green fluorescent protein tag and partial colocalization with a C-terminal mCherry-tagged small GTPase Rab5 demonstrated that the functional protein primarily localizes in endocytic vesicles. In situ target engagement assays confirmed a selective effect of aminopyrazoles and its abrogation by introducing a resistance-conferring mutation. Finally, a direct interaction between the lead compound and recombinantly produced LINF_180011100 FYVE Zn finger domain was demonstrated through a biophysical assay. Hence, this work formally validates LINF_180011100 as a drug target and resistance determinant for several aminopyrazole leads and provides insights into the mechanism of action.

title: Context-dependent regulation and multidomain dynamics of HLTF.
authors: Helmer, Rebecca A; Chilton, Beverly S
abstract: The helicase-like transcription factor (HLTF) is a superfamily 2 translocase vital for maintaining genome integrity. As we discuss in this review article, recent breakthroughs show that HLTF alters its oligomeric state depending on substrate configuration, allowing it to coordinate mechanical DNA repair with epigenetic silencing. By anchoring its N-terminal HIP116 and Rad5 N-terminal domain directly onto exposed 3'-hydroxyl single-stranded DNA ends, HLTF operates as a monomer during nucleotide excision repair and post-cleavage CRISPR-associated protein 9 eviction to clear persistent protein roadblocks. Conversely, replication fork stress could promote self-assembly into an asymmetric homodimer to drive fork regression. Beyond physical DNA processing, HLTF resolves toxic G-quadruplex structures and stabilizes heterochromatin through its histone 3 lysine 23 ubiquitin ligase activity, exposing a targetable synthetic-lethal vulnerability in checkpoint-deficient tumors.

title: MR1-dependent MAIT cell activation is regulated by autophagy-associated proteins.
authors: Phalora, Prabhjeet; Ussher, James; Hester, Svenja; Hackstein, Carl-Philipp; Marchi, Emanuele; Mak, Jeffrey Yw; Fairlie, David P; Klenerman, Paul
abstract: The antigen-presenting molecule, MR1, presents microbial metabolites to MAIT cells, a population of innate-like, antimicrobial T cells. It also presents an unidentified ligand to MR1-restricted T cells in the setting of cancer. The cellular cofactors that regulate MR1 antigen presentation have yet to be fully defined. We performed a mass spectrometry-based proteomics screen to identify MR1-interacting proteins and discovered the selective autophagy receptor SQSTM1/p62. CRISPR-Cas9-mediated knockout of SQSTM1/p62 increased MAIT cell activation in the presence of Escherichia coli but not the synthetic ligand 5-OP-RU, whereas depletion of Atg5 and Atg7, key autophagy proteins, increased MAIT activation irrespective of the ligand used. This regulation appears to occur at an early step in the MR1 trafficking pathway. These data implicate distinct roles for autophagy-associated proteins in the regulation of MR1 activity and highlight the contribution of the autophagy pathway to regulation of cellular antigen presentation.

title: Engineering Cas Activity for Clinically Deployable CRISPR Diagnostics.
authors: Huang, Zhen; Lyon, Christopher J; Hu, Tony Y
abstract: CRISPR-based diagnostics have evolved from proof-of-concept nucleic acid assays to increasingly integrated platforms for streamlined canonical/non-canonical single or multiplex target detection with digital quantification. Here we review these advances according to their ability to regulate Cas activity and dissect key checkpoints of CRISPR activation. We also organize advanced CRISPR-based diagnostic systems by their use of four regulatory dimensions: activation-threshold control, reaction compatibility and temporal coordination, spatial organization, and catalytic signal transduction. This framework reveals common mechanisms and limitations underlying current engineering strategies and provides a conceptual foundation for predictable, standardizable, and clinically translatable Cas activity engineering.

title: A transgenic pig model for human metabolic disorders defines the relationship between the colon pathological phenotype of metabolic disease, the microbiota and the intestinal barrier.
authors: Yang, Yu; Xu, Jian; Miao, Jiakun; Du, Juan; Ma, Xiaohan; Xu, Shuang; Zhang, Kaiyi; Wu, Tianwen; Tao, Cong; Fang, Meiying; Wang, Yanfang; Yang, Shulin
abstract: Metabolic disorders are increasingly associated with intestinal dysfunction and colorectal diseases, yet the pathological characteristics and underlying mechanisms of intestinal injury under metabolic stress remain poorly understood. Here, we established a transgenic (TG) Bama pig model by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in of three humanized susceptibility genes and subjected the pigs to a high-fat, high-sugar diet (HFHSD) for 4, 8, or 12 months to investigate metabolic disorder-associated colonic dysfunction. HFHSD intervention induced marked alterations in serum biochemical parameters and disrupted colonic mucosal architecture, characterized by glandular disorganization and crypt distortion. Colonic tissues from TG pigs exhibited reduced populations of goblet cells, CD8(+) T cells, and CD79A(+) B cells, accompanied by pronounced activation of mitophagy, indicating impaired epithelial barrier integrity and mucosal immune homeostasis. In parallel, microbial diversity and IgA levels were reduced in the colonic contents of TG pigs, accompanied by an increased abundance of potentially pathogenic bacteria, particularly Escherichia-Shigella. Metabolomic profiling of colonic contents further revealed significant alterations in the intestinal metabolic landscape, including decreased levels of isobutyric acid and isovaleric acid and an increased level of myristic acid, a metabolite associated with autophagy-related processes. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that metabolic disorders are associated with coordinated alterations in colonic mucosal integrity, mucosal immunity, mitochondrial quality control, gut microbiota, and intestinal metabolism.
