Our findings support anti-FOLR1 ADC as a clinically actionable approach to overcome immune evasion and unlock immunotherapy efficacy in CRC.

title: Mechanistic insights into benzoxaborole activity against Cryptosporidium parvum: CPSF3 targeting genetically validated for AN3661, with implications for resistance.
authors: Wenker, Janine; Braun, Laurence; Swale, Christopher; Gouin, Axel; Pichon, Julien; Mariot, Julie; Lombard, Laura; Baty, Thomas; Dobrescu, Irina; Lalle, Marco; Hakimi, Mohamed-Ali; Bougdour, Alexandre; Laurent, Fabrice
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cryptosporidiosis is a major enteric disease affecting humans and animals worldwide, with severe consequences in young children and neonatal livestock, yet treatment options remain extremely limited. Benzoxaboroles have emerged as promising broad-spectrum antiparasitic compounds, but their mechanisms of action, molecular targets, and resistance pathways in Cryptosporidium spp. remain incompletely understood, limiting their optimal therapeutic deployment. We previously showed that the benzoxaborole AN3661 inhibits the endonuclease Cleavage and Polyadenylation Specificity Factor 3 (CPSF3) in Cryptosporidium hominis, likely by disrupting pre-mRNA processing and restricting parasite growth. Here, we further investigated the mode of action of AN3661 and compared it with two additional benzoxaboroles, AN13762 and AN7973. METHODOLOGY: Cell culture assays combined with imaging-based quantification were used to assess drug activity and determine the impact of treatment on parasite growth and development. CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing was used to introduce a point mutation into Cryptosporidium parvum CPSF3 and evaluate resistance to benzoxaboroles in vitro and in vivo. Nanopore sequencing was performed to examine the effects of drug exposure on parasite mRNA processing. PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: We identified a single mutation in C. parvum CPSF3 (Y385N) that conferred strong resistance to AN3661. In contrast, this mutation did not reduce sensitivity to AN13762 or AN7973, which are also suspected to target CPSF3. All three benzoxaboroles impaired mRNA processing, a process mediated by the CPSF machinery, and exhibited parasiticidal activity, with pronounced effects during late-stage maturation of first-generation meronts, including inhibition of parasite egress; two compounds also affected gametogenesis. Notably, AN7973 controlled severe infection in susceptible mice challenged with the AN3661-resistant C. parvum CPSF3 Y385N mutant. In Toxoplasma gondii, AN7973 remained active against strains resistant to AN3661 and AN13762, supporting a distinct mechanism of action. Finally, AN3661 and AN7973 were active against Eimeria tenella, and AN3661 against Giardia duodenalis. CONCLUSIONS/SIGNIFICANCE: Together, these results identify a resistance mechanism affecting AN3661 in Cryptosporidium, and highlight AN7973 as a promising alternative compound with broad antiparasitic activity and efficacy against AN3661-resistant parasites.

title: A Structurally Dynamic Chromosome 11 Locus from Oryza rufipogon Confers Recessive Resistance to Bacterial Blight in Rice.
authors: Li, Beibei; Shafique, Muhammad Sohaib; Huang, Weiqing; Wang, Chunlian; Liu, Yapei; Khan, Muhammad Faizan Anwar; Qiu, Xianjin; Ji, Zhiyuan
abstract: Bacterial blight (BB), caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Xoo), poses a major threat to global rice production as rapidly evolving pathogen populations overcome existing resistance genes. In this study, we characterized genetic resistance in the Oryza rufipogon accession Wild-173 (UP36), which exhibited broad resistance to diverse Xoo strains, whereas the susceptible cultivar Longjing-31 (LG31) displayed severe disease symptoms. Genetic analysis of an F(2) population derived from UP36(male symbol)xLG31(female symbol) indicated that BB resistance is controlled by a recessive locus, consistent with a 1:3 (R: S) segregation ratio (chi(2) test, P > 0.05). Bulked segregant analysis coupled with whole-genome resequencing (BSA-seq) identified a significant G' peak on chromosome 11. Fine mapping using InDel markers delimited the locus to an approximately 34 kb interval flanked by markers bb94 and bb26 on the long arm of chromosome 11. Within this interval, nine candidate genes were predicted. Two genes encoding a calmodulin-binding protein and an EAP30/Vps36 domain-containing protein showed sequence variation between UP36 and LG31 and were designated xa53-1(t) and xa53-2(t), while the remaining candidates were primarily retrotransposon-related. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of both candidate genes in a susceptible cultivar resulted in reduced lesion lengths, providing functional evidence for their roles in BB resistance. A high-quality PacBio HiFi assembly of UP36 revealed substantial structural variation and sequence divergence, including presence/absence polymorphisms and disrupted collinearity, indicating that this locus is distinct from previously cloned Xa genes. RNA-seq analysis of UP36 and LG31 following Xoo inoculation prioritized candidate genes and revealed transcriptional reprogramming associated with defense signaling, stress responses, and hormone-mediated immunity. Consistently, qPCR analysis showed stronger induction of defense-related marker genes (PR1a, PR1b, PR5, and PBZ1) in UP36 compared with LG31 after Xoo inoculation. Together, these findings demonstrate that UP36 harbors a novel recessive resistance locus on chromosome 11 conferring broad-spectrum BB resistance and provide valuable genomic resources for gene cloning and resistance breeding.

title: CRISPR/Cas9 knockout of N-acetyltransferase 1 influences mesenchymal transition in glioblastoma in a cell line dependent manner.
authors: Schroeder, Luke A; Habil, Mariam R; Newberry, Hannah M; Dillon, Phoebe K; Wise, James T F; Hein, David W; Hood, Joshua L
journal: Journal of cancer research and clinical oncology
abstract: PURPOSE: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common primary malignant brain tumor in adults and carries a poor prognosis despite standard of care treatment with surgical debulking, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy. Proneural to mesenchymal transition (PMT) is a key driver of GBM invasion and treatment resistance, yet its underlying molecular mechanisms remain uncharacterized. N-acetyltransferase 1 (NAT1) is implicated in the progression of several cancers, but its role in GBM is unknown. This study aimed to determine whether NAT1 regulated PMT phenotypic and transcriptional changes in GBM. METHODS: NAT1 knockout (KO) cells were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 lentiviral delivery in three GBM cell lines (U87, U118, and A172). Cell proliferation was measured via manual cell counts and PrestoBlue assays measured cell viability. Morphological changes were assessed via microscopy, and GFAP and nestin immunofluorescence. PMT associated gene expression was profiled using RT-qPCR arrays. TGF-beta1-treated control cells served as a positive control for PMT induction. RESULTS: NAT1 KO cells displayed altered morphology, characterized by decreased cluster formation. RT-qPCR array profiling revealed mRNA expression consistent with upregulation of IL1RN and MMP3 across U87 and U118 KO clones. However, overall gene expression profiles qualitatively suggested a mixed PMT phenotype for all three cell lines. CONCLUSION: NAT1 KO mediated induction of IL1RN and MMP3 indicates a conserved inflammatory and extracellular matrix axis that may broadly contribute to PMT in GBM. This raises important clinical considerations given glioma's limited treatment options. Consequently, therapeutically inhibiting NAT1 emerges as a promising strategy to target GBM PMT, with broader implications for other cancers.

title: Engineered Extracellular Vesicles (EVs) as Carriers for CRISPR/Cas9 Therapeutics: Recent Advances in Cargo Loading and Targeted Delivery.
authors: Zahid, Ayesha; Ismail, Hazrat; Qadeer, Abdul; Zahra, Memoona
abstract: The therapeutic potential of CRISPR/Cas genome editing has advanced the development of precision medicine; however, its clinical translation for many in vivo applications remains limited by challenges in achieving safe, efficient, and targeted delivery. Conventional viral vectors and synthetic nanocarriers are associated with challenges including immunogenicity, limited cargo capacity, prolonged nuclease expression, off-target effects, and manufacturing complexities. Engineered extracellular vesicles (EVs) are being investigated as alternative delivery carriers due to their biological origin, capacity for cargo encapsulation, and opportunities for surface functionalization. However, their biocompatibility, immunogenicity, and ability to cross biological barriers depend on vesicle source, formulation, and experimental conditions. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in the design of engineered EVs for CRISPR/Cas delivery, with a particular focus on strategies to improve cargo loading, targeting specificity, and therapeutic efficacy. We discuss the advantages and limitations of different CRISPR cargo formats, including plasmid DNA, mRNA, and ribonucleoprotein complexes, together with endogenous and exogenous loading approaches, hybrid EV platforms, and methods for enhancing intracellular delivery. Advances in EV surface engineering through genetic, chemical, physical, and biomimetic modifications are highlighted as strategies being investigated to improve tissue-specific delivery and functional cargo transport. The review also highlights emerging research directions, including CRISPR-EV theranostic platforms and the application of artificial intelligence to enhance CRISPR-EV therapeutic systems. Finally, key translational challenges, including scalable production, EV heterogeneity, cargo-loading efficiency, biodistribution, regulatory standardization, and quality control, are critically discussed. EV-mediated CRISPR delivery remains at an early preclinical stage, with clinical safety and therapeutic efficacy yet to be established. Further advances in EV engineering, cargo-loading strategies, and manufacturing standardization are needed to support its potential clinical translation.

title: CRISPR-Mediated PABPC1 Upregulation via ELF5 Binding Disruption Enhances Milk Protein and Lipid Biosynthesis in Goat Mammary Epithelial Cells.
authors: Zhu, Zhenliang; Wang, Haoxin; Liu, Yayi; Jian, Yangyi; Zhang, Yong; Feng, Rui; Liu, Jun; Gao, Yuanpeng
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: Post-transcriptional control of milk protein and lipid production in goats remains poorly understood. Here we combined ONT full-length transcriptome sequencing with RNA pull-down coupled to LC-MS/MS to identify RNA-binding proteins associated with milk protein mRNAs, and uncovered poly(A)-binding protein cytoplasmic 1 (PABPC1) as a central regulator. PABPC1 bound the 3'UTRs of casein and lipid-related transcripts such as CSN2, CSN3, LALBA, and FASN, stabilizing these mRNAs and promoting their translation, while dose-dependently modulating alternative polyadenylation (APA) site selection to reshape 3'UTR isoform usage. ELF5 directly bound the PABPC1 promoter, repressing its transcription. CRISPR/Cas9 editing of this binding motif relieved this repression, elevating PABPC1 levels and increasing casein accumulation and triglyceride synthesis in goat mammary epithelial cells. Our findings define an ELF5-PABPC1-APA regulatory module and nominate a tractable target for molecular breeding to enhance goat milk protein and lipid content.

title: Killers by Design: How Innovative Gene-Engineering Fine-Tunes NK Cells as Next Generation Immunotherapies.
authors: Kluge, Pia; Knapp, Lea Rebecca; Lai, Kuan-Yu; Sapre, Avani; Rasko, Tamas; Bexte, Tobias; Ullrich, Evelyn
abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells have emerged as promising candidates for adoptive immunotherapies. Their natural cytotoxic capabilities and low incidence of side-effects such as cytokine release syndrome and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity, render NK cells a favorable alternative to T cells. Incorporation of a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) has been shown to greatly enhance NK cell's antitumor capacity. Nevertheless, CAR-NK cell therapies still face several challenges, such as low in vivo persistence, low tumor homing of the transfused cells and the effects of the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Genetic modifications of key cellular mediators show great potential to overcome these hurdles. While well-established viral engineering strategies are currently the most commonly used techniques, biosafety concerns, high costs, and labour-intensive protocols have encouraged innovation toward nonviral strategies. In this review, we describe recently established viral and nonviral technologies used for NK cell engineering, focusing on their respective advantages and disadvantages. In addition, we highlight the most important functional refinements and mechanistic characterizations of NK cells and genetically optimized NK cells in the context of the TME and how these advances can be progressed toward therapeutic translation.

title: A KNOX-BELL-Lignin Module Regulates Leaf Rolling and Drought Tolerance in Rice.
authors: Qiao, Lei; Zhang, Zhongyu; Li, Qinying; Li, Jinrong; Da, Dingbang; Lin, Mingjia; Chen, Yuguo; Mi, Junhan; Li, Haifeng; Chen, Kunming; Li, Wenqiang
abstract: Leaf rolling is a critical agronomic trait in rice that directly shapes canopy architecture and photosynthetic efficiency, yet the underlying molecular mechanisms remain to be fully elucidated. Here, we identify RLC3 (OsBLH4), a BELL-type homeodomain transcription factor, as a key regulator of leaf rolling and drought tolerance. Genetic validation using rlc3-1, rlc3-2, and CRISPR/Cas9-generated rlc3-ko lines, supported by allelism tests, confirms the critical regulatory role of RLC3 in leaf rolling. Paraffin section analysis revealed that RLC3 loss-of-function mutations reduced bulliform cells (BCs) dimensions. Biochemical assays, ultrastructural observations and vascular permeability measurements further showed that these mutations disrupt lignin biosynthesis and secondary cell wall (SCW) formation, leading to aberrant midrib vascular patterning. This structural defect accelerates leaf water loss, which in turn ‌reduces BC turgor pressure, ultimately resulting in leaf rolling and reduced drought tolerance. Mechanistically, RLC3 directly binds to and activates the promoters of core lignin biosynthetic genes (OsCCR4, OsCAld5H1, OsPAL5, and OsCOMT5). Furthermore, RLC3 forms heterodimers with KNOX transcription factors OSH1/45/71, which differentially bind to and co-activate a subset of these targets: OSH1/71 specifically co-activate OsCCR4 and OsCAld5H1, whereas OSH45 additionally co-activates OsPAL5. Loss-of-function mutations in these KNOX genes result in leaf morphology alterations, with reduced lignin content and SCW thickness, ‌ which are partially consistent with the defects observed in rlc3 mutants‌‌. Together, our results reveal a KNOX-BELL-lignin regulatory module that connects transcriptional activation to SCW fortification and water loss regulation, enabling molecular design of drought-tolerant rice with balanced water retention and ideal plant architecture.

title: Fully modified SpyCas9 guide RNAs enable robust genome editing in cells and in vivo.
authors: Vu, Kim Anh; Zhang, Han; Amrani, Nadia; Devi, Gitali; Gaston, Nicholas; Lee, Jonathan; Maitland, Stacy A; Chen, Zexiang; Echeverria, Dimas; Liu, Pengpeng; Ponnienselvan, Karthikeyan; Hanlon, Matthew B; Lucas, Connor; Luk, Kevin; Sousa, Jacquelyn; Cooper, David; Srnka, Alyxandr; Rembetsy-Brown, Julia M; Ansodaria, Aditya Valji; Hedger, Adam K; Wagh, Atish; Bamidele, Nathan; Mir, Aamir; Yamada, Ken; Alterman, Julia F; Khvorova, Anastasia; Wolfe, Scot A; Sontheimer, Erik J; Watts, Jonathan K
abstract: Precision engineering of CRISPR/Cas9 components has advanced genome editing toward therapeutic applications. Fully chemically modified guide RNAs (gRNAs) have the potential to improve stability and broaden therapeutic delivery strategies. However, extensive chemical modification of CRISPR guides can compromise genome editing activity by disrupting gRNA-Cas9 interactions. Here, we employed an iterative, structure-guided optimization strategy to systematically evaluate chemical modifications throughout SpyCas9 gRNAs. Extending beyond commonly used nucleotide modifications, we incorporated 2'-amino-RNA, 4'-thio-RNA, and extended nucleic acid (exNA) to generate gRNAs in which 90%-100% of nucleotides are sugar- or backbone-modified. Although the performance of individual modification patterns varied among target sequences, we established a repertoire of guides that support robust genome editing in vitro and in vivo. Collectively, these findings provide a systematic framework for rational engineering of heavily and fully modified gRNAs using diverse nucleotide chemistries for nonviral CRISPR genome editing.

title: Loss of bmp15 gene function does not abolish fertility in male Atlantic salmon.
authors: Crespo, Diego; Fjelldal, Per Gunnar; Hansen, Tom J; Kjaerner-Semb, Erik; Ayllon, Fernando; Skaftnesmo, Kai Ove; Thorsen, Anders; Norberg, Birgitta; Edvardsen, Rolf B; Andersson, Eva; Schulz, Rudiger W; Wargelius, Anna; Kleppe, Lene
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Bone morphogenetic protein 15 (BMP15), a transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta) superfamily member, is well known for its crucial involvement in regulating female reproduction in mammals, and recently also in fishes. However, the biological function(s) of Bmp15 in male reproduction are largely unknown in vertebrates in general. METHODS: In this study, we used CRISPR/Cas9 technology to generate Atlantic salmon bmp15 mutants to investigate its potential role in testis development, spermiation rates and sperm motility. RESULTS: No apparent phenotypic differences were observed at either of the two sampling points (18 and 22 months of age) carried out prior to the spawning season, in any of the mutant groups. However, at 22 months of age, mutant males showed a higher frequency of individuals in the rapid testicular growth phase than wild-type (WT) controls (63.6% versus 33.3%). Then, males that remained sexually immature and homozygous for the frameshift mutations (bmp15 fs/fs) were significantly shorter and lighter than WT controls from 26 months of age (at spawning) onwards; they also exhibited a higher incidence of deformed vertebrae and significantly lower testicular transcript levels for two growth factors (amh, gsdf) when examined at the age of 26 months. Regarding testis maturation, 26 month-old fs/fs mutant males showed a higher frequency of spermiating fish than WTs. However, further analyses revealed variation in vgll3a genotype - linked to age at maturity - among the fish investigated, as well as a vgll3a genotype-dependent association with spermiation probability. No significant differences were found regarding the plasma levels of 11-ketotestosterone, the main androgen in fish, irrespective of the maturation stage. Also regarding sperm motility and trajectory, no significant differences were detected between mutants and WTs in the two following reproductive seasons, under the conditions of this study. CONCLUSION: This is the first mutant model in fish investigating Bmp15-mediated action in the male gonad and, similarly to the only other genetic model available in vertebrates to date-the pig -, no remarkable testicular phenotypes were revealed. Future studies will be required to determine whether these effects are evolutionary conserved across vertebrates, or whether distinct or additional phenotipic consequences emerge in other fishes or tetrapods.

title: The CRISPR-Cas system functions a regulatory module in diverse cellular processes in Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi and related Enterobacteriaceae.
authors: Villasenor, Tomas; Hernandez, Victor Manuel; Aguirre-Partida, Eira; Vazquez, Alejandra; Rivera-Ramirez, Abraham; Hernandez-Lucas, Ismael
abstract: The CRISPR-Cas systems have been traditionally viewed as adaptive immune mechanisms; however, increasing evidence indicates that they also perform broader regulatory functions. Here, we demonstrate that the Type I-E CRISPR-Cas system in Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi modulates the expression of key transcriptional regulators, including OmpR and TviA. Furthermore, the CRISPR-Cas system controls critical virulence-associated phenotypes including intracellular replication within human macrophages, bile salt resistance, biofilm formation, and motility. Comparative analyses across members of the Enterobacteriaceae family reveal species-specific contributions of CRISPR-Cas to bacterial physiology and virulence. In Salmonella Typhimurium, its role is largely restricted to bile salt resistance, whereas in enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EHEC) it additionally regulates, bile resistance, biofilm formation and motility. In contrast, no detectable CRISPR-Cas-dependent regulatory function was observed in Citrobacter rodentium or Escherichia coli K-12 under the conditions tested. Despite these differences, CRISPR-Cas systems consistently influence core physiological processes associated with host adaptation and pathogenicity. Collectively, our findings support a model in which CRISPR-Cas systems function as global regulatory module that enhance bacterial fitness and pathogenic potential by fine-tuning traits required for host colonization and environmental adaptation. This expanded functional paradigm underscores the importance of CRISPR-Cas in enteric pathogens and suggests that its contribution to virulence may be more widespread than previously appreciated.

title: A lactylation-associated transcriptomic signature predicts outcome and identifies CBX3 dependency in multiple myeloma.
authors: Hu, Qian; Tao, Yali; Wu, Daiqian; Xu, Jing; Pan, Hui; Liu, Yu; Niu, Ting
abstract: Lactate accumulation is associated with the progression of multiple myeloma (MM) and resistance to treatment, but the clinical implications of lactylation-associated transcription in MM are not yet fully understood. We integrated public transcriptomic, metabolomic, proteomic, and genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screening data to examine this relationship. A transcriptomic score derived from a curated set of 398 lactylation-associated genes increased across disease stages and adverse clinical groups. Six genes (CBX3, DDX21, GAPDH, HNRNPC, ILF2, and NUP133) associated with overall survival across four cohorts were retained as a fixed candidate panel. In the CoMMpass development cohort, a multivariable Cox model based on standardized expression yielded an optimism-corrected C-index of 0.648 (95% CI, 0.605-0.693). The continuous six-gene score remained associated with overall survival in the three replication cohorts (hazard ratios per standard-deviation increase, 1.33-1.58). Genome-wide CRISPR screening identified CBX3 as an MM-cell dependency. CBX3 knockout reduced cell proliferation and global lysine lactylation, whereas inhibition of lactate production reduced CBX3 protein abundance. These findings clarify the relationship between lactylation-associated transcription and MM pathophysiology.

title: Telomere-Targeting CRISPR-Cas9 Induces Distinct DNA Damage Responses.
authors: Choi, Hon Fung; Mak, Joyce P Y; Poon, Randy Yat Choi
abstract: Telomeres are essential for maintaining linear chromosome integrity, making their dysregulation in cancer an attractive target for DNA damage-mediated therapeutic interventions. Here, we explored the effects of targeting telomeric repeat sequences with CRISPR-Cas9 in human cells. At high expression levels achieved through transient transfection, telomere-specific CRISPR-Cas9 (TelCR), one of two possible telomere-targeting CRISPR-Cas9 constructs, triggered acute telomere loss, activated the ATR-CHK1/2-WEE1 G(2) DNA damage checkpoint, and promoted apoptosis in HeLa cells. Conversely, an inducible system delivering sublethal levels of TelCR resulted in progressive telomere attrition and an ATM-dependent DNA damage response. TelCR also induced chromosomal instability, characterized by the formation of multicentric chromosomes. Moreover, sublethal telomeric damage elicited a transcriptional program distinct from nonspecific DNA breaks, characterized by enrichment of pathways associated with metabolic adaptation, stress responses, and innate immune signaling. Collectively, these findings reveal distinct cellular and transcriptional responses to telomere-specific CRISPR-Cas9-mediated damage, highlighting its utility as a tool for inducing targeted telomeric damage.

title: GLOW-CRISPR: A G-Quadruplex Loop-Engineered Optical Workflow Combined with CRISPR-Cas12a System for SARS-CoV-2 Detection.
authors: Shi, Wenyang; Lin, Xiaodong; Li, Xiang; Pal, Tathagata; Liu, Benjamin M; Chen, Juhong
abstract: SARS-CoV-2 remains a serious public health threat, highlighting the need for rapid and accessible nucleic-acid diagnostics for decentralized testing. CRISPR-Cas systems are promising platforms for viral diagnostics because of their high specificity and compatibility with isothermal workflows. However, many CRISPR-based assays still rely on labelled reporters, dedicated fluorescence instrumentation, or single-mode outputs that increase cost and limit field deployment. Herein, we developed a label-free GLOW-CRISPR assay (a G-quadruplex loop-engineered optical workflow combined with the CRISPR-Cas12a system) to detect SARS-CoV-2. The assay provides fluorescence and colorimetric readouts in separate endpoint workflows through loop-engineered G4 reporters. Upon recognition of the SARS-CoV-2 target, activated Cas12a cleaves the loop-engineered G4 reporters, thereby suppressing both fluorescence and colorimetric signals. Using optimized conditions, the GLOW-CRISPR assay achieved limits of detection of 7.7 nM and 2.9 nM for fluorescence and colorimetric readouts, respectively. It also showed no detectable cross-reactivity with non-target respiratory viruses and correctly classified patient-derived nasopharyngeal samples in concordance with RT-qPCR results. Collectively, these results establish G4 loop engineering as a general strategy for label-free CRISPR-Cas12a signal transduction without probe labelling or specialized instrumentation. By expanding optical readout flexibility while reducing assay cost and complexity, the GLOW-CRISPR assay provides a practical framework for decentralized molecular diagnostics in resource-limited settings.

title: SPRINT-Cas12a: A Single Leading-Hairpin Probe-Enabled Dual-Pathway Activation Strategy for Sensitive miRNA Detection.
authors: Li, Qian; Liu, Junda; Xue, Mo; Wang, Jiahao; Zhang, Youfei; Huai, Luzhen; Zhu, Xingzhou; Liu, Xiaoyan; Wang, Jie
abstract: CRISPR-Cas12a possesses robust trans-cleavage activity and has emerged as a powerful tool for nucleic acid detection. However, the efficient integration of Cas12a trans-cleavage with direct miRNA recognition and signal amplification remains challenging, particularly because conventional assay designs often rely on multiple probes or a single activation pathway. Here, we developed SPRINT-Cas12a, a single-probe RNA-triggered integrated trans-cleavage platform for sensitive miRNA detection. In this design, a leading hairpin probe (L-HP) specifically recognizes the target miRNA and initiates polymerase-mediated cascade isothermal amplification, synchronously generating two structurally distinct Cas12a-activating products: an RNA-DNA complex and a long-chain micro-hairpin probe (L-MHP). These products provide complementary activation pathways for Cas12a, thereby promoting reporter cleavage and fluorescence signal generation. The single-probe architecture simplifies probe design while enabling synergistic signal amplification through dual-pathway Cas12a activation. The platform was successfully adapted for the detection of miR-21 and miR-122, two miRNAs with distinct sequences, demonstrating its modularity and sequence versatility. Using miR-192 as a hepatocellular carcinoma-associated target, the method achieved sensitive detection in serum samples and distinguished patients with hepatocellular carcinoma from healthy controls, with results consistent with stem-loop quantitative reverse-transcription PCR. In addition, the platform was coupled with a lateral flow assay to provide an instrument-free visual readout. Depending on the amplification and readout format, the assay could be completed within 90 min to 120 min using simple laboratory equipment. Overall, SPRINT-Cas12a provides a single-probe, dual-pathway strategy for Cas12a-mediated miRNA detection and shows promise for portable molecular diagnostics and point-of-care testing.

title: Fitness costs and effects on the peritrophic matrix associated with chitin synthase 2 gene knockout in Vip3Aa-resistant Helicoverpa zea.
authors: Heu, Chan C; Schutze, Inana X; LeRoy, Dannialle M; Wang, Yu-Hui; DeGain, Ben A; Carriere, Yves; Tabashnik, Bruce E; Fabrick, Jeffrey A
abstract: BACKGROUND: Genetically engineered crops producing insecticidal Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) proteins are used globally to manage key insect pests, including Helicoverpa zea (Lepidoptera: Noctuidae). In the United States, H. zea has evolved practical resistance to Bt corn and cotton producing crystalline Bt proteins and early warning of resistance to the vegetative insecticidal protein Vip3Aa has been reported. CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing that introduced disruptive mutations in the H. zea chitin synthase 2 (CHS2) gene facilitated creation of a strain (CHS2-KO) with 29 000-fold resistance to Vip3Aa relative to its parental susceptible strain, LAB-S. However, quantitative information about fitness costs associated with CHS2-mediated resistance remains limited. Here, we tested whether CHS2-KO exhibited costs affecting survival, development time, and pupal mass on diet without Vip3Aa, and examined direct effects on the peritrophic matrix (PM). RESULTS: Relative to LAB-S, fitness costs in CHS2-KO were 27.8% for neonate to adult survival, 23.2% for neonate to adult development time, and 17.8% for pupal mass. An intact PM was evident in LAB-S and F1 larvae, but not in CHS2-KO larvae. CONCLUSION: Mutations disrupting the CHS2 gene in the CHS2-KO strain of H. zea were associated with large fitness costs affecting survival, development time, and pupal mass when reared on diet under laboratory conditions. Also, no intact PM was evident in CHS2-KO. These results suggest that costs could oppose the spread of knockout alleles in the absence of Vip3Aa, although their magnitude on host plants and applicability to less disruptive CHS2 resistance alleles remain to be determined. title: Integrated QTL mapping and CRISPR screening in pooled iPSC-derived microglia reveals genetic drivers of neurodegenerative risk.
authors: Perez-Alcantara, Marta; Washer, Sam J; Chen, Yixi; Steer, Juliette; Gonzalez-Padilla, Daianna; McWilliam, Joe; Wille, David; Panousis, Nikolaos; Kolberg, Peep; Navarro-Guerrero, Elena; Alasoo, Kaur; Hall-Roberts, Hazel; Williams, Julie; Cowley, Sally A; Trynka, Gosia; Bassett, Andrew R
abstract: Mounting evidence implicates microglia in neurodegeneration, but linking disease-associated genetic variants to target genes and cellular phenotypes is hindered by the inaccessibility of these cells. We differentiated 261 human induced pluripotent stem cell lines into microglia-like (iMGL) cells in pools with phenotypic (differentiation, phagocytosis and migration) and single-cell transcriptomic readouts. Burden analysis of deleterious variants detected 36 genes influencing microglial phenotypes. Expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) analysis identified 7,121 eQTL-associated genes and 79 colocalizations across four neurodegenerative disease genome-wide association studies, half of which had limited prior evidence of causality. Integration of eQTL and phenotypic associations highlighted the role of disease-relevant variants, including LRRK2 and TREM2 acting through microglial phagocytosis. A coupled CRISPR screen identified a role for TREM2 in phagocytosis and highlighted the importance of cell type in the directionality of phenotypic effects. By contextualizing variant effects within iMGLs in different inflammatory states, we provide a comprehensive framework for interpreting the function of risk loci in neurodegenerative disorders.

title: Emerging gene and stem cell therapies for hereditary hearing loss: from molecular correction to regenerative reconstruction.
authors: Cheng, Yixin; Fu, Siqi; Qi, Jieyu; Chai, Renjie
abstract: Hearing loss is among the most common sensory impairments globally and remains a significant unmet clinical challenge. Current rehabilitative approaches, such as hearing aids and cochlear implants, provide partial functional compensation but fail to restore the structural and physiological integrity of the cochlea. This review summarizes progress in therapeutic development targeting key deafness-associated genes, including OTOF, GJB2, and SLC26A4, highlighting the rationale, current clinical evidence, and major translational challenges. We further discuss the potential of combining gene therapy with stem cell-based approaches to promote inner ear regeneration and restore sensorineural function. Emerging technologies such as CRISPR/Cas, adeno-associated virus, and induced pluripotent stem cell-derived otic progenitors have opened new avenues for causal correction and tissue reconstruction. Integrated therapeutic models that combine gene or stem cell therapy with cochlear implants are reshaping the treatment paradigm from symptom management to biological repair. Advances in gene editing, gene delivery, and stem cell technologies are establishing these approaches as promising treatments for hereditary hearing loss, with ongoing progress expected to accelerate clinical translation despite remaining challenges in delivery efficiency, immune responses, ethics, and long-term efficacy. Collectively, these advances mark a pivotal step toward personalized and regenerative interventions for hereditary hearing loss.

title: Fever-induced OR560 promotes antibacterial immunity through macrophage pseudopod formation and phagocytosis.
authors: Cai, Hong; Yi, Jun-Xi; Sun, Jing-Yi; Li, Jin; Feng, Min-Yi; Liu, Zhe-Han; Jiang, Shuai; Sun, Li-Ming; Zhang, Xin-Ran; Pan, Jie; Wang, Tong; Xing, Jia-Qing; Yi, Ya-Song; Qin, Ling-Mei; Zhou, Xue-Qing; Yue, Hui-Zi; Wang, Xue-Han; Yu, Liu-Bing; Liu, Chen-Xin; Chen, Ling; Han, Qiu-Ying; Zhao, Ming; Xia, Tian; Yu, Yu; Zhou, Tao; Zhang, Xue-Min; Li, Ai-Ling; Xue, Wen; Li, Tao
abstract: Fever is a conserved physiological response to pathogen infection. However, how fever promotes host defense remains poorly understood. Here we find that fever empowers antibacterial immunity by inducing olfactory receptor 560 (OR560) to promote macrophage phagocytosis. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we discovered that OR560 is indispensable for macrophage phagocytosis. Febrile temperature drives the serum response factor-dependent OR560 induction in macrophages to boost phagocytosis. OR560 responds to bacteria-derived peptides and plays an essential role in mediating pseudopod formation-a key step required for target uptake. Modulation of body temperature in mice showed that the immune-amplifying effect of fever depends predominantly on OR560. We further demonstrated that the genetic ablation of either Olfr560 or serum response factor (Srf) in mice not only abolished fever-potentiated macrophage phagocytosis but also led to catastrophic defects in bacterial clearance and increased mortality upon infections. Thus, our work reveals that OR560 is a pivotal regulator of fever-enhanced antibacterial phagocytosis and integrates both pathogen-derived and febrile signals to ensure a robust response to infection.

title: A multipathogen view of Epstein-Barr virus pathogenesis and tumorigenesis.
authors: Tang, Jiarui; Zhong, Ling; Yuan, Lie; Su, Di; Zhao, Qinjian; Krummenacher, Claude; Zhang, Xiao
abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infects more than 95% of the global population and contributes to multiple human cancers and autoimmune diseases. Co-infection with pathogens including Helicobacter pylori, human immunodeficiency virus, human papillomavirus, and Plasmodium falciparum can reshape host immunity and the EBV latency-lytic balance and, in some settings, promote reactivation. Collectively, these interactions may exacerbate chronic inflammation, immunosuppression, and epigenetic dysregulation to accelerate disease progression and tumor formation. Existing clinical treatments control only the active pathogens but fail to target latent EBV. Emerging strategies such as clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) gene editing and EBV-targeted immunotherapy aim to eliminate latent viral reservoirs. This review outlines the synergistic mechanisms of EBV co-infection in oncogenesis, highlighting that further research on pathogen interactions is vital for developing better prevention and treatment options.

title: Photo-controlled CRISPR/Cas12 systems: Molecular design evolution and applications in diagnostics and gene editing- A review.
authors: Fan, Ze; Yin, Xiaoyun; Tong, Zhaoyang
abstract: The CRISPR/Cas12 system has emerged as a powerful tool in molecular diagnostics and gene editing due to its high specificity, programmability, and robust trans-cleavage activity. Introducing optical responsiveness enables light-dependent regulation of CRISPR/Cas12 activity with improved spatiotemporal control, thereby expanding its utility in molecular diagnostics and gene editing. This review provides an overview of the latest advances in photo-controlled CRISPR/Cas12 systems, traces the technological evolution of their design strategies, elucidates the iteratively upgraded design schemes, and further discusses the applications of these light-activatable systems in in vitro diagnostics, gene editing, and cancer diagnosis. This review specifically organizes photo-controlled Cas12 systems according to the regulated molecular component and design evolution, and compares their effects on dark-state suppression, activation efficiency, assay integration, scalability, and application suitability, with particular attention to trans-cleavage-enabled molecular diagnostics. Finally, we separately discuss current technical challenges and future development directions, including UV-light dependence, irreversible activation, delivery efficiency, long-term safety, near-infrared responsiveness, reversible control, and clinical translation.

title: Pharmaceutical Aspects of Pichia pastoris: Optimizing Recombinant Protein Expression for Drug Discovery and Development.
authors: Fahim Shahriar, Md
abstract: Recently, researchers have observed multiple unique properties in Pichia pastoris, making it ideal for manufacturing pharmaceutical products such as enzymes, vaccines, and peptides. It exhibits rapid growth, is cost-effective to cultivate, and survives high-stress conditions; these attributes have made it a priority for researchers and pharmaceutical companies for potential applications in pharmaceutical manufacturing and product development. Since 2009, it has been used to produce pharmaceutical products and has obtained FDA approval. The FDA has approved several drugs and healthcare products derived from Pichia pastoris, including Kalbitor(R), Jetrea(R), Eptinezumab-jjmr, and human insulin. Although Pichia pastoris is considered safe, many disadvantages and safety concerns persist in its use for healthcare product development. Nonetheless, due to advantages such as protein modification and higher expression levels, researchers continue to address disadvantages, including high methanol induction, glycosylation-related complications, and codon optimization. Recent advances include effective genetic methods, such as CRISPR-Cas9, for precise genome modification in P. pastoris. It also highlights several research gaps in the application of Pichia pastoris in the pharmaceutical industry and proposes suggestions for future research.

title: CRISPR-Cas liquid biopsy for NSCLC: analytical evidence and laboratory translation.
authors: Porwal, Omji; Muhammed, Rozhan Arif; Visht, Sharad; Shaban, Sama Naziyah; Othman, Zainab Yalman; Amer, Alaa; Singh, Amit; Singh, Bimlesh Kumar
journal: Clinica chimica acta; international journal of clinical chemistry
abstract: In non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), plasma circulating tumor deoxyribonucleic acid (ctDNA) testing allows the detection of actionable mutations, such as epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations, including exon 19 deletions, L858R, T790M, and C797S. However, liquid-biopsy workflows primarily rely on centralized platforms, such as droplet digital polymerase chain reaction (ddPCR), quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), amplification-refractory mutation system polymerase chain reaction (ARMS-PCR), and next-generation sequencing (NGS), which may not enable rapid or decentralized testing. We reviewed the existing data on the use of Cas12a for plasma ctDNA detection and emerging Cas12a/Cas13a strategies for detecting exosomal microRNAs (miRNAs) and circular RNAs (circRNAs), distinguishing established plasma ctDNA testing from early CRISPR-Cas and exosomal RNA studies. Laboratory factors that impact implementation, such as specimen selection, preanalytical variability, matrix effects, reproducibility, quality control, clinically relevant decision thresholds, turnaround time, and cross-platform validation with established ddPCR and NGS workflows, are also highlighted. CRISPR-Cas biosensors demonstrate potential as a fast and specific method for EGFR genotyping during diagnosis and targeted testing upon progression in addition to validated molecular assays. Postoperative minimal residual disease surveillance remains investigational. Standard workflows, external test performance validation, clinically relevant cutoffs, and integration of the test into reflex molecular diagnostic workflows are necessary for clinical translation.

title: A Virus-like particle system based on parainfluenza virus PIV5-L for CRISPR-Cas9 and RNAi delivery.
authors: Ge, Xiaotian; Zheng, Lilan; Liu, Xiaoqing; Xu, Yifei; Wang, Ting; Du, Shujuan; Zhu, Caixia; Robertson, Erle; Wang, Yuyan; Wei, Fang; Cai, Qiliang
abstract: Nucleic acid-targeting technologies based on CRISPR-Cas or small-hairpin RNA (shRNA) are essential for functional genomics and therapeutic development, yet a delivery platform that simultaneously ensures high efficiency, safety, modularity, and broad cell compatibility remains lacking. Here, we report L-VLP, a virus-like particle platform derived from a B-lymphoma-isolated strain of parainfluenza virus PIV5-L. This single-cycle, replication-deficient VLP functions as a dual-mode delivery system, capable of carrying either Cas9/sgRNA for CRISPR-mediated gene editing or shRNA for RNA interference, and achieves effective target gene knockdown or knockout in both breast cancer and B-lymphoma cells. Notably, the sgRNA or shRNA cassettes in L-VLP can be readily exchanged for any sequence of interest without altering the core vector architecture, providing a modular and versatile design. Functional assays confirm that L-VLP-mediated UBR5 silencing significantly inhibits tumor cell growth in vitro and in vivo. Collectively, our work establishes L-VLP as a flexible and efficient platform for manipulating gene expression, with promising applications in both basic research and cancer target therapeutics.

title: Metabolic engineering of Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) for plasmid-free high-level production of ergothioneine via hybrid pathway and multicopy chromosomal integration.
authors: Ding, Xiaohu; Li, Yunxia; Yao, Hui; Dong, Miaomiao; Wei, Dongzhi; Wang, Feng-Qing
abstract: Ergothioneine (L-ergothioneine, EGT) is an antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and cytoprotective compound with high value in the food, cosmeceutical, and nutraceutical industries. Herein, an efficient microbial cell factory was developed by engineering a hybrid EGT biosynthetic pathway in Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) through the synergistic assembly of heterologous genetic modules of prokaryotic and eukaryotic origins. Systematic interrogation of gene combinations and transcriptional architectures identified sulfoxide synthase-mediated oxidative coupling as the pivotal metabolic bottleneck governing EGT biosynthetic flux. Addressing this rate-limiting step allowed the initial plasmid-bearing strain, EGT04, reaching an EGT titer of 156.35 mg/L during shake-flask fermentation. A multicopy chromosomal integration CRISPR-associated transposase strategy was implemented for stable multicopy chromosomal integration. This approach yielded a genetically robust, plasmid-free, and marker-free chassis, EGT15, which achieved an EGT titer of 287.14 mg/L, representing a 127.47% improvement over the initial prototype. Subsequent refinement of the fermentation landscape, integrating optimized glycerol feeding and strategic cysteine supplementation with a two-stage thermal control strategy (biomass accumulation at 37  degrees C followed by induction at 20  degrees C), further elevated the shake-flask titer to 353.69 mg/L. The final scale-up in a 5 L-fed-batch bioreactor culminated in a peak EGT concentration of 8.36 g/L with a volumetric productivity of 0.12 g/L/h. By eliminating the requirements for antibiotics and plasmid maintenance, this high-yielding and stable platform minimizes metabolic drag and enhances the industrial production potential. This study established a robust, plasmid-free, and resistance-free E. coli platform for sustainable microbial manufacturing of EGT, providing a scalable strategy for the high-level production of value-added sulfur-containing compounds.

title: CRISPR-cas systems in protozoan parasites: Genome editing, functional genomics, gene regulation and emerging applications.
authors: Ganguly, Nabanita; Thakre, Bhupendrakumar J
abstract: Protozoan parasites possess complex genomes, unusual DNA-repair mechanisms, multiple developmental stages, and, in several species, intracellular or vector-dependent life cycles that complicate functional genetic studies. CRISPR-Cas9 has become a central tool for functional genomics in these organisms, enabling targeted gene disruption, replacement, tagging, nucleotide modification and genome-wide functional screening. However, editing efficiency and outcomes vary substantially among parasite species and depend not only on Cas9-mediated double-strand break formation but also on target accessibility, guide design, delivery method, parasite stage, DNA-repair capacity, donor availability, selection and the biological cost of the induced lesion. This review focuses primarily on experimentally established Cas9-mediated genome editing in Plasmodium, Leishmania, Toxoplasma gondii, Trypanosoma, Babesia, Theileria and Cryptosporidium. We compare plasmid-based and transient expression, ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery, electroporation/nucleofection, stage-specific delivery, guide and donor design, selection strategies, editing outcomes, and molecular and functional validation. Particular emphasis is placed on homology-directed repair (HDR), canonical non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), microhomology-mediated end joining (MMEJ) and single-strand annealing (SSA), which determine whether editing results in indels, precise sequence replacement, tagging or larger genomic deletions. Species-specific differences are illustrated by efficient NHEJ-mediated disruption in Toxoplasma, donor-dependent repair in Plasmodium and Cryptosporidium, SSA-associated repair in Leishmania, efficient homologous recombination in trypanosomatids, precise editing in Babesia, and stage-specific delivery constraints in Theileria. The review further examines the progression from single-gene editing to marker-free manipulation, base editing, conditional approaches and genome-wide functional screens. Cas12a, CRISPRi/a, prime editing and related systems are discussed as emerging extensions. Overall, this repair- and delivery-centred framework explains why CRISPR editing differs among protozoan parasites and identifies the experimentally validated limitations that currently shape their genome-engineering potential.

title: Oncogenic histone hyperacetylation drives acute myeloid leukemia through enforced transcription initiation of leukemogenic genes.
authors: Cooper, Alexandra J; Zemlyanskiy, Grigory; Trakarnphornsombat, Watanya; Pena-Romer, Isabel; Sun, Lu; Willis, Hannah E; Burg, Jonathan M; Fan, Zheng; Valka, Valentina; Tajuddin, Rumaysa; Helin, Kristian; Keogh, Michael-Christopher; Radzisheuskaya, Aliaksandra
abstract: Histone acetylation is tightly correlated with active transcription, yet its causal roles and downstream mechanisms remain incompletely defined. Chromosomal translocations generating fusion proteins involving histone acetyltransferases (HATs) represent a powerful but underexplored system to dissect how dysregulated acetylation rewires transcriptional control. Here, we establish an endogenous mouse model of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) driven by a fusion between two HATs, KAT6A and p300, generated through CRISPR-mediated chromosomal rearrangement. KAT6A-p300 induces aggressive, transplantable AML and confers oncogene addiction. Mechanistically, the fusion establishes broad promoter-associated hyperacetylated domains. This hyperacetylation promotes recruitment and remodeling by the canonical BAF complex, increasing promoter accessibility and stimulating RNA polymerase II recruitment and transcription initiation. Fusion formation also redistributes wild-type p300, broadens its chromatin occupancy, and stabilizes its association with fusion-bound loci. Together, our findings establish histone hyperacetylation as a driver of transcription and reveal a direct mechanistic link between aberrant acetylation, chromatin remodeling, and leukemogenesis.

title: Dissecting the molecular machinery of CRISPR-associated transposons.
authors: Wang, Shukun; Singh, Juhi; Rice, Phoebe A; Chang, Leifu
abstract: CRISPR-associated transposons (CASTs) are naturally occurring mobile genetic elements that combine programmable RNA-guided DNA recognition with transposase-mediated integration, enabling site-selective insertion of kilobase-scale DNA without nuclease-induced double-strand breaks. Current structural and biochemical knowledge can be viewed in terms of three functional modules: the transposase module, which performs DNA cleavage and strand transfer; the AAA+ ATPase TnsC, which forms a recruitment and regulatory platform; and TnsD or CRISPR effector-TniQ targeting complexes, which position this platform at selected DNA sites. Here, we synthesize recent structural and biochemical advances in target recognition, recruitment, donor-end pairing, and strand transfer. Comparisons with Tn7 and phage Mu highlight conserved transposase and ATPase functions and system-specific differences in how these components are organized and regulated. We discuss the implications of these advances for engineering programmable DNA-insertion systems and highlight unresolved questions in CAST transposition.

title: Disruption of BnPHT5;1a reduces arsenic accumulation through Pi-dependent restriction of arsenate uptake in Brassica napus.
authors: Han, Bei; Jiang, Aosheng; Yan, Junjun; Wu, Tao; Zhang, Bingbing; Wang, Yajie; Yang, Xinyu; Wang, Sheliang; Zhao, Zhuqing; Shi, Lei
abstract: Arsenic (As) contamination threatens crop production and food safety, yet the role of vacuolar Pi transporters in arsenate [As(V)] acquisition remains unclear in polyploid crops. Here, we investigated BnPHT5;1a, a vacuolar Pi influx transporter in Brassica napus. Double mutants of the two B. napus homeologs BnA09PHT5;1a and BnC09PHT5;1a (BnPHT5;1a DM), generated by simultaneous CRISPR/Cas9 editing, exhibited enhanced As(V) tolerance. Under 400 muM As(V), mutant shoot and root fresh weights were 11.0-30.1% higher and root As concentrations were approximately 28% lower than those of wild-type W10. Heterologous overexpression increased As(V) sensitivity in Arabidopsis. Yeast growth assays provided no clear evidence of direct As(V) transport by BnPHT5;1a. Its disruption reduced the expression of several plasma membrane PHT1 genes and limited As(V) uptake under Pi-sufficient conditions, with these effects diminishing as external Pi availability decreased. Mutant plants displayed an attenuated transcriptional response to As(V), consistent with a lower As burden. These findings support an As(V)-avoidance mechanism in BnPHT5;1a DM and suggest possible functional differences between BnPHT5;1a and BnPHT5;1b, whose disruption was previously associated with increased As accumulation and shoot cell wall retention. This study highlights the role of vacuolar Pi partitioning in As(V) acquisition and provides a potential genetic target for breeding low-As rapeseed.

title: Precision immunopharmacology in xenotransplantation: integrating genome-engineered donors, organoid testbeds, and AI-guided translation.
authors: Ren, Tao; Fu, Gongbo; Duan, Shichao; Zeng, Min; Gao, Yi
abstract: Xenotransplantation is moving from isolated proof-of-concept procedures toward an engineered biotechnology platform for organ replacement. This review examines how genome-designed donor pigs, recipient-directed immunopharmacology, human-relevant in vitro testbeds, and data-driven decision systems can be integrated to address the remaining barriers to clinical translation. CRISPR-Cas-based engineering enables deletion of dominant carbohydrate xenoantigens, insertion of human complement- and coagulation-regulatory genes, modulation of innate and adaptive immune checkpoints, control of donor-organ growth, and inactivation of porcine endogenous retrovirus sequences. However, donor engineering does not eliminate residual T-cell, B-cell, antibody, complement, natural killer (NK) cell, macrophage, and inflammatory responses. Contemporary immunopharmacological strategies therefore increasingly combine costimulation blockade with complement inhibition, lymphocyte-directed therapy, and selected cytokine- or innate-immune interventions, with future regimens requiring closer integration of pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic monitoring with donor genotype and organ-specific risk. Organoids and microfluidic vascular systems may provide an intermediate testing layer by quantifying antibody binding, complement activation, endothelial injury, coagulation, leukocyte transmigration, cytokine responses, and tissue-specific function under controlled conditions before escalation to large-animal studies. Artificial intelligence may further support xenoantigen discovery, genome-editing design, donor-recipient matching, multimodal rejection surveillance, and ultimately clinician-supervised immunopharmacological decision support. We propose that these components should be connected through a traceable design-build-test-learn workflow linking computational prediction, donor construction, standardized functional testing, non-human-primate validation, and early human data. Durable translation will depend not on any single technological advance, but on reproducible donor manufacturing, precision immune control, validated human-relevant test systems, standardized longitudinal data, pathogen surveillance, organ-specific management, and transparent regulatory governance.

title: AS1411-targeted nanomedicines for precision cancer therapy: Advances, mechanisms, and translational perspectives.
authors: Mishra, Gaurav; Leharwani, Muskan; Alasmari, Tariq M; Osmani, Riyaz Ali M; Gupta, Garima; Goh, Khang Wen; Kesharwani, Prashant
abstract: Conventional cancer chemotherapy is frequently compromised by nonspecific biodistribution, dose-limiting systemic toxicity, inadequate tumor accumulation, and multidrug resistance, highlighting the need for targeted nanomedicines capable of improving tumor selectivity while preserving therapeutic efficacy. The AS1411 G-quadruplex DNA aptamer has emerged as a promising targeting ligand owing to its high affinity for nucleolin, which is aberrantly overexpressed on the surface of many malignant cells. AS1411-functionalized nanocarriers can exploit nucleolin-mediated endocytosis to enhance tumor-cell uptake, intracellular drug delivery, and therapeutic selectivity while minimizing off-target exposure. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in AS1411-engineered nanocarriers, encompassing polymeric nanoparticles, micelles, liposomes, inorganic and mesoporous nanostructures, as well as bioinspired platforms such as exosomes and cell membrane-coated nanoparticles. Particular emphasis is placed on rational nanocarrier engineering, including optimization of AS1411 surface density, PEGylation, physicochemical properties, and integration of tumor microenvironment-responsive mechanisms to achieve controlled and stimuli-responsive payload release. These platforms have been explored for the targeted delivery of conventional chemotherapeutics, nucleic acid therapeutics, and nonviral CRISPR/Cas systems, and increasingly incorporate multimodal therapeutic and diagnostic functions, including photothermal, photodynamic, sonodynamic, chemodynamic, and imaging-guided approaches. Despite considerable progress, clinical translation remains constrained by heterogeneous nucleolin expression, complex tumor microenvironmental barriers, limited endosomal escape and intracellular trafficking, potential off-target interactions, formulation stability, manufacturing scalability, and regulatory challenges. Future development should prioritize mechanistic understanding of AS1411-nucleolin interactions, standardized evaluation of targeting efficiency, and rational integration of multi-responsive, dual- and multi-ligand, and bioinspired architectures. Such advances may improve the translational potential of AS1411-based nanomedicines and support their further preclinical development.

title: AI-enabled phenomics of combined abiotic stress: Linking field signatures to plant multi-omics.
authors: Haq, Syed Ijaz Ul; Khan, Shahid Nawaz; Ibrahim, Muhammad; Wang, Guobin; Song, Cancan; Tahir, Muhammad Naveed; Lan, Yubin
abstract: Climate change is driving a rise in the frequency of simultaneous abiotic stresses in cropping systems, yet combined stresses elicit physiological and molecular responses that cannot be reliably inferred from single-stress studies. AI-enabled high-throughput phenomics offers a scalable means of detecting these responses in the field, but the biological meaning of AI-derived phenomic signatures and their relationship to underlying molecular processes remain insufficiently resolved. This review asks how phenomic signatures detected by AI/ML can be interpreted as physiologically meaningful readouts of combined abiotic stress and validated against molecular omics evidence. We synthesize evidence from 200 peer-reviewed studies selected through a structured literature search spanning 2010-2026, drawing on findings from high-throughput sensing, plant stress physiology, AI/ML-based phenotyping, and molecular omics. The evidence indicates that combined stresses generate context-dependent molecular and physiological responses that can produce overlapping as well as stress-combination-specific spectral, thermal, and structural phenotypes. AI/ML can help resolve these complex patterns and enable early, field-scale stress characterization; high predictive performance alone, however, does not establish biological or mechanistic validity. The principal bottleneck is the persistent disconnect between molecular omics generated predominantly under controlled conditions and phenomic measurements collected under heterogeneous field environments, compounded by limited combined-stress datasets, weak cross-environment generalization, and a lack of standardized phenomics-omics validation frameworks. Closing this gap is essential for moving AI-driven phenomics from accurate stress prediction toward biologically interpretable panomics and reliable selection of stress-resilient crops.

title: The OVCA1-A2BR-ROS axis drives gastric cancer aggressiveness and identifies an actionable precision target.
authors: Zhang, Dongwei; Wang, Dexu; Wang, Dong; Cai, Mengdi; Liang, Xiao; Xue, Yingwei; Fu, Songbin; Yu, Jingcui
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Gastric cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, underscoring the urgent need for novel therapeutic targets. Ovarian cancer gene 1 (OVCA1) has been implicated as a tumor suppressor in various malignancies; however, its clinical relevance and mechanistic role in gastric cancer progression remain poorly defined. METHODS: We assessed OVCA1 expression in a large clinical cohort (n = 616) and performed prognostic analyses (n = 417). The functional consequences of OVCA1 knockdown, overexpression, and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout were evaluated in gastric cancer cell lines. Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic profiling, together with in vivo xenograft and peritoneal metastasis models, were utilized to elucidate the downstream molecular mechanisms. Furthermore, the therapeutic potential of the selective adenosine A2B receptor (A2BR) antagonist BAY-545 was tested both in vitro and in vivo. RESULTS: Low OVCA1 expression was significantly associated with aggressive clinicopathological features and shorter patient survival. Functionally, OVCA1 loss promoted proliferation, invasion, and cell-cycle progression, whereas its overexpression reversed these phenotypes. Multi-omics integration linked OVCA1 deficiency to purine metabolism remodeling, marked by CD73/NT5E upregulation and selective elevation of the adenosine receptor A2BR. OVCA1-deficient tumors exhibited increased ROS accumulation and upregulation of MMP14 and VEGF. Notably, pharmacological A2BR inhibition with BAY-545 effectively mitigated the enhanced malignancy of OVCA1-knockout cells, suppressed ROS production, and significantly reduced tumor growth and peritoneal dissemination in vivo. CONCLUSION: Our findings identify a novel OVCA1-A2BR-ROS axis contributing to gastric cancer aggressiveness. Given that A2BR blockade robustly reverses OVCA1-loss-associated phenotypes, this study supports A2BR as a potential actionable target and provides a preclinical rationale for its further evaluation in OVCA1-deficient gastric cancer.

title: Single-cell transcriptomic analysis following CRISPR/Cas9 knockdown demonstrates a novel role for human T cell-intrinsic IL-1beta in determining T cell metabolic landscape.
authors: Kale, Kshitija; Vemulawada, Chakrapani; Rogers, Kai J; Crawford, Michael P; Heath, Jace; Karandikar, Nitin J
abstract: T helper 17 (Th17) CD4+ T cells are key mediators of autoimmune pathology. Interleukin (IL)-1beta is a potent proinflammatory cytokine known to promote Th17 differentiation and pathogenicity, in combination with other cytokines. Whereas recent studies have shown that T cells are capable of expressing IL-1beta themselves, the role of this T cell-endogenous IL-1beta is poorly understood. Using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of IL1B in naive human CD4+ T cells along with cytokine neutralization and IL-1 receptor blockade, we found that T cell-intrinsic IL-1beta is not essential for Th17 differentiation or effector resistance. Remarkably, single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that IL1B deletion profoundly rewires the transcriptional and metabolic landscape within the T cells, suppressing glycolytic and hypoxia-responsive pathways. These findings uncouple T cell-intrinsic IL-1beta from Th17 effector resistance while uncovering an important contribution toward sustaining metabolic roles. This refines our understanding of IL-1beta biology and informs therapeutic strategies in immune-mediated disease settings.

title: An engineered probiotic with integrated biocomputation and multi-molecular recording for precision theranostics of colitis.
authors: Zou, Zhen-Ping; Mi, Jing; Zhou, Shu-Qin; Mao, Ruichao; Shi, Xuan-Ren; Du, Wei; Zhang, Jingyu; Wang, Baojun; Zhang, Lixin; Ye, Bang-Ce; Zhou, Ying
abstract: Engineered therapeutic microbes capable of sensing and responding to diseases offer transformative potential for precision medicine. However, their capacity to intelligently process the complex and dynamic biomarkers of multifaceted diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) remains limited. Here, we design a probiotic system that executes logic computations through four stage-specific inflammatory biomarkers, enabling precise diagnosis and closed-loop treatment of colitis in mice. Integration with a CRISPR-based molecular recorder allows dynamic tracking of biomarker levels and converts inflammatory signals into quantifiable, site-specific base-editing events, thereby achieving precise diagnosis and analysis of disease progression within a living mammalian gut. We additionally develop a multimodal machine-learning classifier that utilizes both bioluminescent reporter signals and sequencing data to accurately stage intestinal inflammation with an accuracy of 0.83 +/- 0.05. Together, this work provides a robust platform for in situ biocomputation and marks a significant advance toward intelligent, precision theranostics for gastrointestinal disorders.

title: A universal platform for TCRalpha/beta removal enables safer and more potent TCR therapies and autoimmune modeling.
authors: Zanetti, Giorgia; Nikhat, Sameena; Legut, Mateusz; Chen, Austin; Fathi, Farshid; Suek, Nathan; Teteloshvili, Nato; Li, Hao Wei; Ding, Xiaolan; Traum, Daniel; Kaestner, Klaus H; Hoang, Ryan E; Sewell, Andrew K; Parent, Audrey V; Creusot, Remi J; Sykes, Megan; Khosravi-Maharlooei, Mohsen
abstract: Adoptive T-cell therapies using tumour-specific T-cell receptors (TCRs) are limited by competition with endogenous receptors, impairing efficacy and posing risks of off-target autoreactivity. Here we present a CRISPR-based platform that selectively eliminates both endogenous TCR-alpha and -beta chains without affecting transgenic TCRs, irrespective of codon optimization. This approach achieves >90% deletion efficiency in Jurkat and primary human T cells, enhancing expression and functional potency of transgenic receptors. Using an HLA-A*02:01-restricted DMF5 TCR, we show that dual TCR ablation boosts antigen-specific activation and cytotoxicity in vitro and enhances tumor clearance in vivo in human immune system (HIS) mice and prevents graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). Targeted locus amplification showed that CRISPR-induced double-strand breaks did not alter lentiviral integration profiles, supporting genomic safety. Extending this approach to four insulin-reactive TCRs demonstrated that endogenous receptor removal increased transduction efficiency and functional activity, with one (1E6) showing selective activation and infiltration of islet grafts (SC-islets) in vivo. This study establishes a universal, safe, and scalable genome-editing platform for generating functionally precise human T cells. By integrating cancer immunotherapy and autoimmune disease modelling within a single framework, it provides a preclinical rationale for dual endogenous TCR removal to improve specificity, safety, and therapeutic efficacy in TCR-based cell therapies.

title: Nanozyme-Catalyzed Lateral Flow Assay for the Simultaneous Detection of RNA and Protein Biomarkers.
authors: Park, Chaewon; Dissanayake-Perera, Schan; Ng, Ho-Cheung; Sadler, Christy J; Gallego Rubio, Cecilia; Nam, Keonwook; Prasad, Sanjay K; Stevens, Molly M
abstract: Molecular diagnostics have advanced rapidly over the past decade, driven by the demand for accessible and scalable testing solutions. However, current assays often focus on single biomolecule types, limiting their ability to capture the multifactorial nature of disease. Integrating distinct molecular readouts horizontal line such as transcriptomic and proteomic biomarkers horizontal line could provide richer diagnostic information and improve clinical decision-making. Here, we present MOSAIC (Multiplexed Orthogonal Sensing Assay Integrated with CRISPRZyme), a unified lateral flow assay that enables simultaneous detection of RNA and protein biomarkers using a shared nanozyme-catalyzed readout. The assay combines CRISPR/Cas13a-mediated RNA detection and antibody-based protein detection, with assay components optimized through antibody conjugation tuning, blocking agent optimization, and probe loading calibration to achieve balanced and cross-talk-free performance. Using cardiovascular disease as a model, the platform successfully detects NTproBNP and LIPCAR long noncoding RNA simultaneously from the same sample. The assay was further optimized for spiked human plasma, incorporating tailored pretreatment and recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) to maintain RNA stability and performance in complex biofluids. Extending its versatility, the same assay design was adapted to detect SARS-CoV-2 biomarkers, the spike (S) protein and ORF1ab gene, in pooled human saliva. To enable standardized interpretation of multiplexed readouts, we additionally developed a machine-learning-assisted computational workflow that automates strip localization, signal extraction, and calibration curve construction. Together, these results demonstrate a modular, paper-based diagnostic platform that unites transcriptomic and proteomic analyses within one assay architecture, offering a practical step toward accessible and multiplexed molecular diagnostics across diverse disease contexts.

title: Stable Anthocyanin Accumulation in Vegetable Crops: Multilayer Molecular Regulation, Edible-Tissue Constraints and Biotechnological Improvement.
authors: Murtaza, Ghulam; Wang, Yanzhou; Zhou, Xintong; Hussain, Hammad; Niu, Hangfan; Yan, Shixuan; Wang, Taotao; Sohail, Hamza; Li, Fu; Gao, Song; Liu, Touming
abstract: Anthocyanins are multifunctional flavonoid pigments that contribute to red, purple, and blue coloration, oxidative stress protection, nutritional quality, and market value in vegetable crops. However, their accumulation in edible tissues is often low, unstable, tissue-specific, and restricted to particular developmental stages, limiting their use in crop improvement and natural colorant production. This suggests that anthocyanin enrichment is not solely controlled by biosynthesis, but rather by the coordinated regulation of precursor flux, MYB-bHLH-WD40-mediated transcription, post-transcriptional and chromatin-based control, pigment modification, transport, sequestration, and degradation. Recent transcriptomic, metabolomic, and epigenomic studies have improved our understanding of how environmental signals, including light, temperature, nutrient status, and phytohormones, interact with these regulatory layers to shape anthocyanin accumulation and retention in vegetable crops. Biotechnological approaches, including CRISPR/Cas9, CRISPRa, metabolic engineering, and multi-omics-guided target discovery, provide new opportunities to improve pigment stability by targeting key biosynthetic and regulatory genes. This review synthesizes recent progress in vegetable crops, especially Solanaceae and Brassicaceae, with emphasis on the molecular constraints that limit stable pigmentation in edible tissues. We highlight that future improvement should move beyond darker phenotypes and focus on the coordinated regulation of synthesis, stabilization, vacuolar retention, and degradation control to develop anthocyanin-enriched vegetables with improved nutritional quality, climate resilience, and market value.

title: A chicken interferon-stimulated gene screen reveals limited genes restricting influenza virus replication.
authors: Barkhymer, Alison J; Becker, Jordan T; Shepherd, Frances K; Mickelson, Clayton K; Pross, Lauren M; Salnikov, Mark; Langlois, Ryan A
abstract: Avian influenza A virus (IAV) is a major global health threat. Not only does it cause significant economic losses to the agricultural industry, but it also presents a risk of spillover into the human population. However, several obstacles must be overcome for a successful cross-species transmission event to occur. One of these obstacles is the innate immunity of the host. While the innate immune response to IAV in humans has been well-studied, the innate immune response to IAV in birds is not as well understood. Here, we explore the interferon-induced immune response by identifying interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) in chicken, quail, and duck cells, and find that they are largely species-specific. Using this data, we performed a CRISPR knockout ISG screen against two strains of IAV, the mouse-adapted PR8, and the low pathogenicity avian IAV isolate WF10. We find that for PR8, IFITM3 is the dominant restrictor of viral replication with several additional hits with modest effects, consistent with previous work in mammals. For avian WF10, IFITM3 was also a hit; however, there were two additional hits absent for PR8, the HSP70 co-chaperone protein BAG5 and the deubiquitinase OTUD4. Overall, these findings confirm the divergence of interferon-mediated immunity between species and establish a screening system that can be used to identify ISGs important for viral restriction in avian species.IMPORTANCEWild birds, especially waterfowl and shorebirds, are the primary natural reservoir for influenza A viruses. These birds can transmit IAV to domestic poultry, where the spillover risk to humans increases. Chickens are the most common species of domestic poultry worldwide and frequently infected with avian influenza viruses. Despite this, relatively little is known about how their immune system responds to influenza infection. This lack of knowledge creates a barrier to finding ways of preventing or mitigating IAV infection in chicken flocks. In this study, we characterized the interferon-induced immune response to IAV in chickens and found that only a small subset of ISGs were responsible for restricting IAV in chicken cells.

title: Maternal Foxh1 loss reduces locus-specific H3K27me3 and disrupts lineage segregation.
authors: Cho, Jin S; Hendrickson, Clark L; Mar, Nathan; Blitz, Ira L; Fish, Margaret; Wang, Wenqi; Cho, Ken W Y
abstract: Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) establishes H3K27me3 marks to shape spatiotemporal gene expression during embryogenesis. How PRC2 is recruited to specific genomic loci remains debated, with a prevailing model favoring intrinsic chromatin affinity over recruitment by sequence-specific transcription factors. Here, we show that the maternally deposited pioneer transcription factor Foxh1 promotes PRC2 occupancy at specific genomic loci during zygotic genome activation in Xenopus. Foxh1 is a crucial mediator of Nodal signaling that pre-binds mesendodermal enhancers before signaling activation, facilitating enhanceosome assembly and coordinated mesendodermal gene expression in cooperation with other maternal transcription factors. Using maternal Foxh1-null embryos, we demonstrate that Foxh1 is also required for efficient Ezh2/PRC2 occupancy at a subset of Foxh1-bound loci. Loss of Foxh1 selectively reduces Ezh2 occupancy and associated H3K27me3 at these regions without substantially altering total Ezh2 levels. These findings support a dual-function model in which Foxh1 activates endodermal gene expression in endoderm, while promoting PRC2-associated repression of the same regulatory program in ectoderm. Thus, Foxh1 contributes to establishing spatially distinct epigenetic states that coordinate germ layer specification and lineage segregation during early embryogenesis.

title: ZmFLP Controls Symmetric Division of Guard Mother Cells and Associates with BZU2/ZmMUTE during Stomatal Development in Maize.
authors: Meng, Bolun; Li, Wenhui; Zhou, Yusen; Li, Qingzeng; Chang, Yuhua; Botella, Jose Ramon; Wang, Pengtao; Guo, Siyi
abstract: Stomata in grasses such as maize consist of dumbbell-shaped guard cells (GCs) produced by a single symmetric division of the guard mother cell (GMC), a process requiring strict regulation for proper function. Here, we show that the maize R2R3-MYB transcription factor ZmFLP is essential to terminate GMC division. CRISPR-Cas9 generated zmflp null mutants undergo additional longitudinal or transverse divisions after the initial symmetric GMC division, leading to aberrant GC clusters and abnormal subsidiary cells (SCs). As a consequence, mutants show elevated leaf temperature and seedling lethality. Transcriptome profiling revealed extensive changes in zmflp mutants, including upregulation of cell cycle and MAPK-associated genes and downregulation of key stomatal development regulators, including ZmFAMA, ZmSCRM2, and ZmTMM. ZmFLP physically interacts with the bHLH transcription factor BZU2/ZmMUTE in the nucleus, and dual-luciferase assays reveal that co-expression of BZU2 enhances ZmFLP transcriptional repression. Furthermore, introduction of an additional native-promoter-driven VENUS-BZU2 transgene reduced the frequency of abnormal stomatal complexes in zmflp mutants. Together, these findings establish ZmFLP as a key regulator of GMC division and suggest a functional link between ZmFLP and BZU2 in the final stages of stomatal development in maize.

title: A non-nucleotide activator reveals a second allosteric regulatory site in the type III CRISPR ribonuclease Csm6.
authors: Chen, Jingxuan; Chen, Xiaoyi; Sun, Jiehui; Li, Jinyu; Du, Liyang; Lin, Zhonghui
abstract: Type III CRISPR-Cas systems rely on cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) signaling to activate ancillary nucleases such as Csm6, which serve as core effectors in antiviral immunity. While cOA-mediated Csm6 activation has been widely harnessed for molecular diagnostics, its broader application is constrained by inherent limitations, including poor cellular permeability and susceptibility to degradation by ring nucleases. Here, we conducted a high-throughput fluorescence-based screen and identified DMPCH (7,8-dimethyl-4-phenylchroman-2-one) as a non-nucleotide allosteric activator of Thermus thermophilus (Tt) Csm6. DMPCH selectively stimulates TtCsm6 ribonuclease activity by binding to the higher eukaryotes and prokaryotes nucleotide-binding domain dimerization interface, leading to expansion of the catalytic pocket and remodeling of the R-X4-6-H catalytic motif. Moreover, DMPCH acts synergistically with cA4 to activate TtCsm6, enabling rapid and sensitive RNA detection in a Cas13a-Csm6 system. Cell-based assays confirm that DMPCH activates TtCsm6 ribonuclease activity in live bacteria cells. When combined with DMPCH, an engineered miniCsm6 fused to pyocin S2 (PyS2) exerts potent and specific bactericidal activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Our work establishes a framework for discovering non-nucleotide activators of CRISPR-associated ribonucleases and highlights their potential as chemical tools in cell-based research and as therapeutic agents against bacterial pathogens.

title: Programmable nucleases for nucleic acid detection: bridging the gap between analytical sensitivity and clinical adoption.
authors: Ding, Ronghua; Gao, Hui; Li, Yuanye; Li, Zhongyan; Mao, Hanjing; Gao, Shuhong; Long, Jinzhao
journal: Analytical methods : advancing methods and applications
abstract: Nucleic acid testing faces a persistent tension between analytical sensitivity and field deployability. Centralized qPCR relies on thermal cyclers and trained personnel, whereas isothermal amplification eliminates thermal cycling but often compromises sensitivity and stability.
