The COVID-19 pandemic intensified these constraints in primary care and point-of-care settings. Programmable nucleases offer a different detection logic: after guide-mediated target recognition, effector activity converts the recognition event into a detectable signal. Effector families such as CRISPR (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats), pAgo (prokaryotic Argonaute), and TnpB/Fanzor have yielded diverse assays, although TnpB has only recently been demonstrated, and Fanzor remains at the proof-of-principle stage. This review integrates effector mechanisms, engineering strategies, clinical evidence, and commercialization. It highlights three shifts: (i) an expanding effector toolbox with greater diversity in size, targeting requirements, and signal encoding; (ii) a transition from optimizing detection limits toward system-level capabilities, such as single-tube operation, multiplexing, absolute quantification, and robustness with unextracted or minimally processed samples; and (iii) a growing mismatch between analytical performance and regulatory maturity. Most CRISPR-based COVID-19 diagnostic products have been withdrawn, expired, or discontinued, likely reflecting commercial and regulatory factors rather than inherent technical limitations. In 2026, a CRISPR-based tuberculosis blood test received regulatory authorization in Colombia, extending the technology beyond respiratory virus detection. Bridging the laboratory-to-clinic gap now depends less on further sensitivity gains than on clear clinical indications, rigorous validation, and cost-controlled engineering. This review aims to guide assay selection and the development of next-generation diagnostics.

title: Friedelin in plants: metabolism, synthase engineering and production strategies.
authors: Cui, Qi; Shi, Chenglin; Li, Qiannan; Chen, Junyu; Xue, Zheyong; Shen, Xiaoxia; Liu, Juzhao
abstract: Friedelin (FD) is a pentacyclic triterpenoid with significant pharmacological potential and serves as the biosynthetic precursor to the anti-obesity drug celastrol. Despite its value, FD availability is limited by low natural abundance and the stereochemical complexity of chemical synthesis. This article critically reviews the state-of-the-art in FD research, spanning natural distribution, extraction methodologies, and the molecular basis of its biosynthesis. The structural evolution of friedelin synthases (FDSs), contrasting the mechanisms of multifunctional versus single-function enzymes, was analyzed. Furthermore, a comprehensive roadmap for sustainable production, integrating "Push-Block-Regulate-Store" metabolic engineering strategies with novel insights into transcriptional regulation, was provided. It is proposed that the convergence of AI-driven enzyme design, transporter engineering, and CRISPR-based precision breeding will overcome current yield bottlenecks, enabling the industrial-scale biomanufacturing of FD and its derivatives.

title: AI-guided CRISPR gene editing for cardiovascular disease: Current progress, transitional challenges, and future directions.
authors: Ghannam, Raja Bou; Danaf, Naseeb; Hamdan, Righab
journal: American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice
abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality despite major advances in pharmacological therapy, interventional cardiology, and lifestyle-based prevention. Although many current treatments reduce disease burden and improve outcomes, they often fail to address the underlying molecular and genetic mechanisms driving disease progression dot CRISPR hyphen-based gene- editing systems (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) have introduced the possibility of directly correcting, silencing, or modulating pathogenic genetic determinants involved in cardiovascular pathology. When integrated with artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled design, prediction, and optimization tools, an AI-guided CRISPR framework may assist in prioritizing editing strategies, predicting editing outcomes, and informing delivery design, although cardiovascular-specific validation of these applications remains limited. This narrative review examines the potential role of AI-guided CRISPR technologies in cardiovascular disease. It first outlines the major pathophysiologic mechanisms underlying CVD, then reviews molecular and genetic targets that may be amenable to editing. Current CRISPR applications in cardiometabolic and cardiovascular disorders are discussed, followed by an evaluation of how AI may support guide RNA design, off-target prediction, vector engineering, and therapeutic prioritization. Finally, major translational barriers are examined, including tissue-specific delivery, editing in non-dividing cells, long-term genomic safety, disease complexity, and regulatory implementation. Although early preclinical findings are encouraging, most cardiovascular applications remain in the experimental or early translational stage, and direct evidence for integrated AI-guided CRISPR applications in cardiovascular disease remains limited and largely preclinical. Progress in this field will depend on advances in delivery science, genome engineering, computational modelling, and long-term safety validation. AI-guided CRISPR should therefore be regarded as a developing precision medicine strategy with substantial future potential rather than an immediately deployable clinical solution.

title: [Immunologic Mechanism of the Synergistic Antitumor Effects of High-Dose Vitamin C and Oncolytic Adenovirus in Breast Cancer].
authors: Su, Xu; Zou, Yang; Jiang, Shuangju; Liu, Ningyi; Wei, Qingqing; Liu, Jinxing; Luo, Jun; Huang, Anliang; Yang, Fan
journal: Sichuan da xue xue bao. Yi xue ban = Journal of Sichuan University. Medical science edition
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To investigate the therapeutic effect of high-dose vitamin C (VitC) combined with oncolytic adenovirus (oAds) against breast cancer and to determine whether the combination therapy activates antitumor immune responses by inducing gasdermin E (GSDME)-dependent pyroptosis. METHODS: The 4T1 murine mammary cancer cell line and a BALB/c mouse tumor-bearing model were used. GSDME-knockout (GSDME (－/－)) cells were generated using CRISPR-Cas9. The 4T1 cancer cells and tumor-bearing mice were assigned to a control group, a VitC group receiving only VitC treatment (2 mmol/L), an oAds group receiving only oAds treatment (multiplicity of infection [MOI] = 10), and a combination treatment group. Western blotting was performed to assess GSDME cleavage and caspase-3 activation. Flow cytometry (annexin Ⅴ/propidium iodide [PI] staining) was used to differentiate pyroptosis and apoptosis. Immunofluorescence was performed to assess intratumoral CD8(+) T cell infiltration. ELISpot and flow cytometry were performed to determine the proportions of interferon (IFN)-gamma(+) CD8(+) T cells in the spleen. RESULTS: Combination treatment induced membrane rupture in 78.3% of 4T1 cells, activated caspase-3, and cleaved GSDME. After GSDME knockout, pyroptosis rate decreased from 65.4% to 6.2% (P < 0.001), shifting to apoptosis. In vivo, combination group tumor volume (454.3 mm(3)) was significantly smaller than control (1339.4 mm(3), P < 0.0001) and monotherapy groups (approximately 910 mm(3), P < 0.01), with median survival extended to 52 d. GSDME knockout partially reversed efficacy (tumor volume increased to 773.9 mm(3), P < 0.01; survival shortened to 43 d, P < 0.05). Combination significantly increased intratumoral CD8(+) T cell infiltration (212 cells/field vs. 58 cells/field, P < 0.0001) and splenic IFN-gamma(+) CD8(+) T cell proportion (15.8% vs. 7.3%, P < 0.0001); these effects were abolished by GSDME knockout. CONCLUSION: High-dose VitC combined with oAds induces GSDME-dependent pyroptosis, remodels the tumor immune microenvironment, and activates systemic antitumor immunity. GSDME is a key effector molecule in this combination treatment. These findings provide a new strategy for virus-immunotherapy combination treatment for triple-negative breast cancer.

title: BAP1 as a novel regulator of type I interferon signaling through transcriptional control of key response machinery components.
authors: Mortazavi, Yasaman; Zhang, Hanyue; Herrera, Robert; Cook, Ryan; Zhong, Bo; Lin, Dandan; Zhao, Yue
abstract: Type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling is critical for dual immunity, defending against microbial infections and augmenting anti-tumor immune responses. Research in the past few decades have identified the key machinery components and over 300 interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) that comprise the IFN-I signaling network. While cascade amplification mechanisms ensure robust pathway activation, appropriate expression of signaling components is essential for maintaining pathway sensitivity, enabling efficient signal amplification, and providing adequate host responses. Here, we identified BRCA1-associated protein-1 (BAP1) as a positive regulator of the IFN-I signaling pathway through a genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen in murine macrophage Raw264.7 cells stimulated with cGAMP. We confirmed both the enzymatic activity and nuclear localization of BAP1 were essential for this regulation. Our findings reveal that BAP1 regulates a broad transcriptional program essential for IFN-I responses, including IFNAR1 and IFNAR2. BAP1 deficient cells failed to mount an effective IFN-I response, showing markedly reduced ISGs and resulting in uncontrolled viral replication. These findings together highlight an essential role of BAP1 in controlling IFN-I signaling and antiviral responses.

title: Mobile group II intron reverse transcriptases: evolution, biochemical activities, and applications.
authors: Lambowitz, Alan M; Yao, Jun; Nottingham, Ryan M
abstract: Bacterial mobile group II intron-encoded reverse transcriptases are structurally similar to an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and may have evolved at the time of transition from an RNA to DNA world. Mobile group II intron reverse transcriptases remain prevalent in bacteria, where they diversified into different subtypes, as well as into chromosomally encoded reverse transcriptases that acquired a variety of cellular functions, including phage defense, RNA spacer acquisition in CRISPR systems, and host cell DNA double-strand break and oxidative DNA damage repair. Mobile group II intron and related reverse transcriptases have remarkably beneficial biochemical properties for biotechnological applications, including high-throughput RNA sequencing. Thermostable Group II Intron-encoded Reverse Transcriptases from bacterial thermophiles, the first of these enzymes shown to have such properties, were used to develop a comprehensive RNA sequencing method that enables simultaneous profiling of virtually all RNA biotypes in human cells, extracellular vesicles, and plasma. In recent studies, Thermostable Group II Intron Reverse Transcriptase sequencing identified a novel large class of short (<300 nt) largely structured Full-Length EXcised linear Intron RNAs in human cells and plasma; enabled parallel analysis of transcriptional and post-transcriptional gene regulation by mapping Thermostable Group II Intron Reverse Transcriptase sequencing reads to genome and transcriptome reference sequences and calculating intron/exon depth ratios; and detected numerous differentially expressed RNAs in inflammatory breast cancer patient tumors and peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Differentially expressed RNAs with high intron/exon depth ratios in inflammatory breast cancer patient tumors and peripheral blood mononuclear cells were correlated with pre-mRNA and intron RNA fragments detected in plasma and included the first potential inflammatory breast cancer biomarkers.

title: Higher Frequency and Precision of Target Site Integration Using TAHITI.
authors: Swanson, Ryan; Liu, Peng; Ratnayake, Sandaruwan; Gandhivel, Vivek Hari-Sundar; Diehl, Brooke; Hung, Yu-Hung; Duncan, Courtney; Edwards, Seth A; Hancock, C Nathan; Slotkin, R Keith
abstract: Efficient genomic target site integration, whereby the user selects the locus of transgene insertion, is a long-desired technology in plant biology. Sequence-based selection of the target site allows for the user to designate ideal genomic regions for transgene expression, durability, and downstream breeding, including the stacking of multiple traits. However, the efficiency of target site integration has traditionally been very low, requiring deep pipelines and screening. DNA transposable elements (TEs) naturally cut and paste themselves across genomes, and we previously coupled the activity of the rice TE mPing/Pong with CRISPR-Cas programmability and double-strand break formation, resulting in the targeted integration of the mPing TE and any associated internal cargo (traits). However, the natural activity of the TE generated a high rate of off-target mPing insertion. Here, we improve TE-mediated target site integration through engineering CRISPR-Cas to replace the role of the DNA cleavage activity of the Pong TE protein, providing improved on-target integration rates and reduced off-target rates. The combination of a deficient and immobilized TE system with CRISPR-Cas enables highly efficient DNA integration at a user-designated site, and we demonstrate higher accuracy and smaller junction scars compared to the previous version of the technology. We demonstrate additional methods to improve the rate of targeted integration, such as removing one of the two Pong proteins, intronizing coding regions, and heat-shocking plants. We demonstrate the next generation of TE-mediated target site integration, called Transposon-Assisted Homology-Independent Targeted Integration (TAHITI).

title: Genomic characterization of a novel Lactobacillus species from pangolin feces: phylogenomic placement and unique functional gene repertoire.
authors: Yu, Sijia; Hong, Peihang; Chou, Shyun; Liang, Tsui-Fang; Lin, Kuei-Shien; Lai, Cheng-Hung; Wang, Chao-Min
abstract: BACKGROUND: The genus Lactobacillus represents a phylogenetically and ecologically diverse group of lactic acid bacteria intimately linked to host gastrointestinal homeostasis and widely regarded as prime probiotic candidates. Pangolin conservation is severely challenged by high mortality rates driven by digestive tract diseases, yet their native gut microbial ecology, particularly the functional roles of resident lactobacilli, remains largely unexplored. RESULTS: In this study, a novel Lactobacillus strain, designated M44, was isolated from the feces of a wild Formosan pangolin, and its complete genome was resolved via whole-genome sequencing. Genome-wide taxonomic metrics (ANI, AAI, and dDDH) fell substantially below the established thresholds for known species. Phylogenomic reconstruction based on single-copy orthologs confirmed that strain M44 forms a distinct, novel evolutionary lineage clustering adjacent to L. psittaci, L. jensenii, and L. mulieris. Comparative genomic analysis revealed that while M44 shares a core of 936 orthogroups with these phylogenetically related peers, it maintains a unique repertoire of 207 strain-specific orthogroups. Multi-pipeline functional mining identified a robust gene cluster for exopolysaccharide biosynthesis, alongside an array of surface-anchored adhesins that support its strong mucosal colonization potential. From an antimicrobial defense perspective, genome mining identified no canonical bacteriocin gene clusters, while genes associated with organic acid and hydrogen peroxide biosynthesis were present. Metabolic pathway reconstruction identified genomic capacity for exogenous carbohydrate and peptide utilization, including catabolic pathways for trehalose and N-acetylglucosamine, as well as a comprehensive oligopeptide permease system and an extensive intracellular peptidase repertoire. Genomic safety screening confirmed the complete absence of acquired antimicrobial resistance genes and intact mobile genetic elements, reinforced by an active Type I-E CRISPR-Cas adaptive immune system. CONCLUSION: These genomic insights establish strain M44 as a novel Lactobacillus species with a functional architecture encompassing broad exogenous carbohydrate and peptide utilization capacity, enhanced intestinal adherence capabilities, and organic acid-mediated antimicrobial defense. The demonstration of a favorable genomic safety profile, combined with prior in vitro phenotypic screening, positions Lactobacillus sp. M44 as a scientifically compelling subject for wildlife microbiome exploration and a candidate worthy of further investigation for potential application in captive pangolin management.

title: Characterization of the SsdA deaminase-family for improved cytosine base editors.
authors: Lorenz, Paul J; Blome, Patrick; Schulz, Oliver; Boch, Jens
abstract: The choice of a suitable cytosine deaminase is a key decision when designing a base editor. Recently, bacterial toxins with cytosine deaminase activity have been established to build potent base editors for genome editing. Among those, SsdA gained considerable traction, being highly active and among the smallest established deaminases for cytosine base editors. The toxic nature of SsdA presents the major challenge, making wild type SsdA unsuitable for base editing. Although several modifications of SsdA are available, a comparison and deeper understanding of these modifications is still missing. Here, we investigate and compare the effects of several SsdA modifications. We enable a more educated choice for researchers by characterizing several improved SsdA variants for base editing. Amino acid substitutions at a key residue in SsdA suggest that steric alterations relieve its toxic effects. Indeed, the in vitro deaminase activity of SsdA was negatively linked to its in vivo performance. This indicates that base editing performance is highly compromised by toxic side effects, making less active deaminase variants the better genome editing tools. We further characterized a set of SsdA homologous proteins and showed that they were similarly toxic as SsdA. Two of them were confirmed to be cytosine deaminases and one of these allowed the construction of a new, highly functional base editing tool. This work deepens our understanding on DYW-family cytosine deaminases and broadens their use for genome editing.

title: A cilia-associated epithelial alteration axis nominates ERICH3 as an entry point to PI3K engagement in lung adenocarcinoma.
authors: Chen, Qiang; Wang, Yixuan; Zhang, Yang; Ying, Shuo; Feng, Huazhuo; Hou, Kai; Zhang, Li; Zhou, Xuexia; Li, Xuebing; Qin, Jianwen; Huang, Dingzhi
abstract: BACKGROUND: LUAD adopts heterogeneous oncogenic signalling states, and bias toward a PI3K-AKT-mTOR-engaged state is not fully explained by canonical pathway lesions. Because membrane-proximal spatial organization can tune receptor-proximal signalling yet is difficult to quantify in human tumours, we used cilia-associated epithelial programs as a hypothesis-generating entry point to identify convergently perturbed candidates and evaluate their relationship with PI3K engagement. METHODS: We performed intersection-based multi-omic prioritization in TCGA-LUAD, evaluated dependency directionality using DepMap/CCLE expression with CRISPR dependency profiles, and tested the functional relationship between ERICH3 loss and PI3K engagement by siRNA perturbation with PI3K-inhibitor rescue. We anchored tumour context using bulk co-expression, spatial transcriptomics, and single-cell analyses with ERICH3 stratified by transcript "detection", complemented by CellChat-based communication inference and structure/variant-informed hypothesis nomination. RESULTS: ERICH3 was prioritized through a cilia-informed screen as a convergently attenuated candidate, showed reduced protein in paired LUAD specimens (16/24, 66.7%; P = 0.014), promoter hypermethylation, and favourable survival association. An external DepMap dependency screen nominated PI3K-AKT-mTOR dependency directionality in ERICH3-low contexts (Hallmark NES = - 1.79; P = 1.04 x 10(-)(4)), which was subsequently evaluated functionally in LUAD cell lines. In LUAD cell lines, ERICH3 knockdown increased PI3K-AKT-mTOR phosphorylation and malignant phenotypes, which were attenuated by PI3K inhibition, supporting a functional relationship between ERICH3 loss and PI3K pathway engagement. Multi-scale transcriptomic analyses showed that ERICH3 transcripts were detected predominantly in a mucous epithelial compartment and non-tumour epithelium; CellChat suggested hypothesis-generating immune-interaction signals associated with ERICH3-detected mucous cells. Structural modelling and tumour-variant mapping nominated discrete membrane-proximal regions for mechanism-discriminating follow-up. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings support a testable model in which attenuation of ERICH3, identified through a cilia-informed epithelial framework, is associated with a PI3K-engaged malignant state in LUAD. The present study does not establish that ERICH3 directly regulates primary-cilium formation, ciliary protein localization, or ligand-induced ciliary signalling; the precise upstream membrane-proximal and/or cilia-related route remains to be defined.

title: Macrophage-specific IL-1beta ablation rescues tau burden via the reduction of macrophage infiltration into the central nervous system after systemic challenge.
authors: Yeung, Sherry Sin-Hang; Luo, Yong-Qi; Chan, Ho-Hin; Ng, Gar-Lee; Cheng, Ho-Ming; Chan, Wai-Hang; Savovic, Isidora; Chen, Xiang-Ke; Ma, Alvin Chun-Hang; Wong, Gordon Tin-Chun; Chang, Raymond Chuen-Chung
abstract: Systemic inflammation can initiate neuroinflammation, leading to abnormal tau hyperphosphorylation, a critical factor in the development of tau pathology and cognitive decline. Despite these associations, the mechanisms driving this process remain largely unexplored. This study demonstrated that sources of interleukin-1beta, specifically in macrophages, act as a key mediator of peripheral-neuroimmune crosstalk. In this study, systemic challenge was simulated in the zebrafish model via fin amputation (sterile inflammation) and intraperitoneal (i.p.) LPS (lipopolysaccharide) administration (non-sterile inflammation), both of which resulted in significant neuroinflammation characterized by macrophage infiltration and elevated IL-1beta expression. Using CRISPR-cas9, we generated a novel macrophage-specific IL1beta knockout (KO) model, where IL1beta was selectively ablated in macrophages only. Notably, macrophage-specific IL-1beta KO zebrafish exhibited significantly reduced neuroinflammation, as indicated by decreased microglial and astrocytic activation, along with diminished tau phosphorylation at the Ser396 site after fin amputation. Behavioral assessments further revealed that IL-1beta KO zebrafish showed improved cognitive performance and reduced anxiety, highlighting the potential of targeted IL-1beta inhibition to enhance cognitive outcomes and emotional well-being. Interestingly, fin amputation induced significant macrophage infiltration into the CNS via lyve1 + lymphatic vessels. These findings underscore the crucial role of macrophage-derived IL-1beta in mediating neuroinflammation and its impact on tau pathology and cognitive function. This study highlights the therapeutic potential of targeting IL-1beta in macrophages, paving the way for interventions aimed at mitigating neurodegenerative diseases and related cognitive disorders.

title: NtFLS1 disruption modulates flavonoid metabolic partitioning and promotes anthocyanin accumulation in tobacco.
authors: Chen, Yanchao; He, Xinxi; Chen, Long; Zhang, Xinyao; Chen, Kai; Huang, Pingjun; Yang, Xiaonian; Pu, Wenxuan; Wang, Shuaibin; Gao, Junping
abstract: BACKGROUND: Flower color in tobacco is largely determined by flavonoid and anthocyanin accumulation. Flavonol synthase (FLS) is a key branch-point enzyme in the flavonoid biosynthetic pathway that competes with dihydroflavonol 4-reductase for common substrates, thereby influencing the biosynthesis of flavonols and anthocyanins. However, the role of NtFLS1 in tobacco flower pigmentation remains unclear. RESULTS: To investigate the function of NtFLS1, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis was performed in Nicotiana tabacum. Compared with wild-type K326 plants, ntfls1 mutants exhibited markedly darker flowers at the full-bloom stage, with floral pigmentation changing from light pink to deep purple. Transcriptome analysis identified 7,052 differentially expressed genes between mutant and wild-type flowers, with significant enrichment in phenylpropanoid and flavonoid biosynthesis pathways. Expression analysis showed that CHS and CHI were downregulated, whereas COMT and F3'H were upregulated in ntfls1 flowers. Metabolomic analysis further revealed substantial accumulation of ( +)-trans-Taxifolin, Scopoletin, and multiple anthocyanins, including Cyanidin 3-O-glucoside and Pelargonidin-derived compounds. Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses suggested that NtFLS1 disruption altered flavonoid pathway partitioning and promoted anthocyanin accumulation in tobacco flowers. CONCLUSION: NtFLS1 is involved in the regulation of flavonoid biosynthesis and flower pigmentation in tobacco. Disruption of NtFLS1 was associated with increased anthocyanin accumulation and enhanced floral pigmentation, likely through redistribution of flavonoid pathway intermediates. These findings provide new insights into the molecular basis of flower color formation in tobacco and may facilitate molecular breeding of ornamental traits in Solanaceous crops.

title: Computational and experimental strategies for functional validation of non-coding variants in pancreatic cancer.
authors: Jenkac, Karla; Herlihy, Jane; Farinella, Riccardo; Guler, Murat; Unal, Pelin; Sever, Elif Arik; Giovannoni, Roberto; Campa, Daniele; Eustace, Alex J; Walsh, Naomi
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly aggressive malignancy characterised by extensive genomic heterogeneity and limited therapeutic options. Although recurrent coding mutations in key driver genes have been well researched, large-scale sequencing studies have identified a broad array of non-coding variants which may contribute to tumorigenesis by interfering with gene regulatory mechanisms. However, understanding the functional significance of these variants remains a major challenge due to their abundance and the complexity of non-coding regulatory structures. This review outlines current computational and experimental techniques to identify, prioritise, and functionally validate non-coding variants in PDAC. We discuss in silico methods including genome-wide association study (GWAS) fine-mapping, colocalisation, machine learning-driven functional annotation, and the use of established computational tools, in addition to epigenomic profiling technologies including, ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq, and CUT&RUN which define regulatory landscapes. We also emphasise new AI-based methods involving radiogenomics, AI imaging analysis and data integration, which provides novel potential to link genomic variation with phenotypic and imaging characteristics. Additionally, we highlight experimental validation techniques including reporter assays, electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA), chromatin conformation capture methods, and CRISPR-based perturbation systems used to study variant functionality. Together, these complementary approaches establish a framework for correlating non-coding variation to regulatory mechanisms in PDAC.

title: A CD7-targeted AAV variant enables efficient T and NK cell engineering in vivo.
authors: Hong, Lingjuan; Chen, Gennong; Liu, Yongjun; Cao, Yuanfang; Li, Xueting; Li, Weijie; Pan, Yumu; Wang, Huahe; Ru, Gaomeng; Yang, Siyu; Cheng, Ming; Lv, Tongtong; Zhu, Yunfan; Huang, Shan; Nian, Xiaoxiao; Ou, Hongling; Wang, Chengkun; Gu, Sean X; Lek, Monkol; Ye, Lupeng
abstract: Adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors have been applied for precise genome engineering in human T cells but poor tropism restricts their efficiency and translational potential. Here, through directed evolution of the AAV6 capsid in primary human T cells, we identified a family of variants containing an APR motif at residues 455-457. The lead candidate, AAV.APR31, enabled robust transduction of primary T and NK cells at nearly 100-1,000-fold lower doses than AAV6 and outperformed the human T cell-tropic capsid AAV-hT7. CRISPR screening identified CD7 as a lineage-specific entry enhancer alongside the canonical AAVR pathway and structural analysis suggested that the APR motif facilitates CD7 engagement. Unlike existing delivery systems confined to one engineering mode, AAV.APR31 enabled transient transgene delivery, site-specific knock-in and transposon integration in human T and NK cells, generating CAR-T cells functionally equivalent to lentiviral vector-manufactured products. Systemic administration of AAV.APR31-generated CAR-T cells in vivo resulted in potent tumor control in hematologic and solid tumor mouse models.

title: Joint single-cell capture of Cas9 edits and transcriptomes reveals on- and off-target effects on gene expression.
authors: Lorenzini, Michael H; Balderson, Brad; Lavalle, Shanna N; Sajeev, Karthyayani; Ho, Aaron J; Light, Madelyn; Usman, Olalekan H; Kurgan, Gavin; McVicker, Graham
abstract: A longstanding barrier in genome engineering with CRISPR-Cas9 has been the inability to measure editing outcomes and their functional effects at single-cell resolution. Here we present Superb-seq, which captures single-cell edits and transcriptome effects by integrating Cas9 editing, T7 in situ transcription and single-cell RNA sequencing. We performed Superb-seq on 35,000 cells from three cell lines. Using seven guide RNAs to target four chromatin remodeler genes in 10,000 K562 cells, Superb-seq detected 5,761 edited cells, all on-target sites and 36 off-target sites. Superb-seq improved estimation of downstream perturbation effects on gene expression compared to Perturb-seq. We compared Superb-seq to 4 bulk off-target detection methods and identified between 6 and 210 edit sites across 3 benchmarking guides. Nineteen off-target edits were associated with differential gene expression, nine of which were cell type-specific. In summary, Superb-seq illuminates the consequences of Cas9 genome editing by connecting single-cell edits with changes in gene expression.

title: Mapping the Tibetan Plateau microbiome across ecosystems provides a resource for biodiscovery.
authors: Liu, Yongqin; Yu, Tao; Ji, Mukan; Battin, Tom J; Dumont, Marc G; Yang, Yunfeng; Liu, Pengfei; Zhuang, Xuliang; Xing, Peng; Wang, Jianjun; Mao, Guannan; Deng, Yongcui; Hu, Anyi; Zhu, Yongguan; Jiao, Nianzhi
abstract: Microbial genetics can inspire innovations in biotechnology, but many microbial communities remain poorly understood. The genetic repertoire of high-mountain microbiomes remains largely untapped for biotechnology. Here we present the Tibetan Environmental Genome (TEG) catalogue, comprising 51,921 metagenome-assembled genomes from 1,698 environmental samples spanning 868 sites across 6 terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems of the Tibetan Plateau, Earth's highest and largest mountain region. The TEG spans 105 phyla encompassing 17,920 species, of which nearly 90% are previously uncharacterized. Importantly, TEG establishes a comprehensive repository for biodiscovery, revealing 44,719 biosynthetic gene clusters, 19,168 candidate antimicrobial peptides, 1,262 low-identity CRISPR-Cas systems and 1,077 candidate polyethylene terephthalate hydrolases. To validate these findings, 29 candidate antimicrobial peptides were synthesized and all exhibited inhibitory activity against at least 1 of 7 tested pathogens, with 5 showing broad-spectrum activity. This catalogue reveals a rich and previously inaccessible pool of enzymes, bioactive compounds and programmable molecular systems, establishing a foundational resource for discovery and application in biotechnology.

title: Retraction notice to "CRISPR-Cas and RNA sequencing reveal nutrient enhancement pathways in quinoa for plant-based athlete recovery diets and future food security" [Int. J. Biol. Macromol. 318 (2025) 144785].
authors: Bu, Guang; Ma, Xuelian; Jin, Hao; Wang, Lei

title: Genome architecture shapes clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat-Cas off-target potential.
authors: Soulard, Chloe; Mallet, Julie; Nogue, Fabien
abstract: Genome editing in plants is widely considered to be precise, yet genome architecture constrains its specificity. Across 47 plant species, genome size and ploidy shaped the predicted off-target landscapes of Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR) systems, highlighting the importance of incorporating genome architecture into the molecular characterization and case-specific evaluation of edited crops.

title: The Traitor Virus approach: A virus-driven CRISPR platform for discovery of antiviral factors and mechanisms.
authors: Pastorio, Chiara; Kirchhoff, Frank
abstract: Innate defense mechanisms and cellular features determine the outcome of pathogen exposure. Successful viruses, such as HIV-1, have evolved to counteract antiviral defense mechanisms and to manipulate their host cells for effective virus production. Although many restriction factors have been identified, additional antiviral proteins and cellular pathways that restrict viral replication remain to be discovered. Many current approaches involve manipulation of the cells prior to virus exposure, are limited to single-round infection assays, and focus on early steps of the viral replication cycle. To overcome these limitations, we developed the "Traitor Virus" approach, a screening platform combining the CRISPR/Cas9 technology with the replicative fitness of HIV-1. In this system, libraries of replication-competent HIV-1 constructs deliver sgRNAs into Cas9-expressing cells. sgRNAs that inactivate antiviral genes or mechanisms and convert the cells into more effective virus producers enhance HIV-1 replication and become increasingly enriched thereby revealing their cellular opponents by deep sequencing. This chapter discusses the conceptual basis, applications, limitations, and future perspectives of this strategy for dissecting virus-host interactions.

title: Polysaccharide-centered engineering of biomass-derived nanoparticles for precision medicine: From molecular assembly and structural deconstruction to therapeutic design.
authors: Li, Yumeng; Yang, Huan; Xiang, Wenchao; Yang, Xu; Tao, Lu; Jiang, Zhenyu; Han, Shiqi; Chen, Guoqiang; Jia, Haiyang; Liu, Qi
abstract: Polysaccharide-centered engineering of biomass-derived nanoparticles (BNPs) is emerging as a sustainable and biologically compatible strategy for precision medicine. Polysaccharide-derived nanoparticles offer renewable sources, structural diversity, tunable physicochemical properties, and intrinsic biological functions that enable their rational engineering for targeted delivery and therapeutic modulation. This review focuses on cellulose-, chitosan-, alginate-, and hyaluronic acid-based nanoplatforms and examines how their molecular and supramolecular characteristics govern nanoparticle construction, nano-bio interactions, and therapeutic performance. Selected protein-derived systems are discussed where they form hybrid architectures with polysaccharides or provide mechanistic insights directly relevant to polysaccharide nanoengineering. We integrate bottom-up molecular assembly and top-down structural deconstruction as complementary fabrication paradigms and analyze how BNPs navigate physiological barriers through mechanisms including receptor-mediated transport, tight-junction modulation, and stimulus-responsive structural reconfiguration. We further examine their applications in CRISPR-Cas9 delivery and precision immunotherapy, with particular attention to design principles, translational constraints, and opportunities for scalable manufacturing. By linking molecular structure, assembly behavior, biological transport, and therapeutic function, this review provides a polysaccharide-centered framework for the rational development of adaptive biomass-derived nanoplatforms for precision medicine.

title: Genetically encoded chemically controlled proximity switches: Molecular design, pharmacology, and therapeutic considerations.
authors: Nonomura, Tatsuki; Lakka, Neha; Price, Anna; Du, Danica; Lan, Tien-Hung; Huang, Yun; Zhou, Yubin
abstract: Genetically encoded chemically controlled proximity systems are chemogenetic tools that utilize small molecules to regulate protein association, higher-order assembly, and dissociation. Over the past three decades, an expanding repertoire of these systems has transformed the study of protein function and cellular signaling by enabling rapid, reversible, and tunable manipulation of protein localization, assembly, activity, and downstream physiological processes. As these technologies advance from experimental tools toward therapeutic applications, their translational potential depends not only on molecular switch performance but also on the properties of the chemical inducer and engineered protein components. In this review, we summarize the major classes and design principles of representative genetically encoded chemically controlled proximity systems, with particular emphasis on the pharmacological determinants that define their therapeutic operating window, including pharmacodynamic orthogonality, pharmacokinetics, tissue exposure, endogenous target engagement, and clinical readiness. We also examine how the biological origin and engineering of the chemogenetic modules influence immunogenicity and long-term compatibility. We further discuss exemplary applications, including pharmacological control of CAR-T cell activity, programmed cell death, CRISPR-based genome and epigenome engineering, and on-demand secretion of therapeutic proteins. Finally, we consider the delivery and coordinated expression of chemically regulated protein components as major remaining barriers to therapeutic implementation and highlight clinically compatible inducers, compact and minimally immunogenic protein modules, de novo protein design, and advances in viral and nonviral delivery as promising directions toward more reliable and pharmacologically tractable chemically controlled therapies.

title: An image-based CRISPR screen reveals RNA processing control of HP1alpha condensates.
authors: Wong, Matthew Man-Kin; Zhou, Shaopu; Rubio, Linda S; Priyadarshini, Monika; Carpenter, Christopher; Arya, Aishwarya; Rizvi, Aoon; Valbuena, Raeline; Carswell-Crumpton, Catherine; Wileveau, Amelie; Lopez, Gabriel L; Liu, Isabelle; Tycko, Josh; Yao, David; Spees, Kaitlyn; Maynard, Jason C; Bassik, Michael C; Goodarzi, Hani; Sanulli, Serena
abstract: Heterochromatin protein 1alpha (HP1alpha) is a core component of heterochromatin, forming subnuclear condensates whose regulation and function remain poorly understood. Although RNA has been implicated in heterochromatin organization, how RNA influences HP1alpha localization remains unclear. Here, we develop an image-based CRISPR screening platform to systematically identify regulators of HP1alpha condensates and identify RNA processing as a central pathway. Perturbations that disrupt RNA processing increase HP1alpha-RNA interactions and reduce its association with chromatin, leading to loss of silencing. These findings establish RNA processing as a post-transcriptional mechanism that regulates HP1alpha localization and heterochromatin by altering the composition and nuclear distribution of HP1alpha-associated RNAs. More broadly, our work reveals functional crosstalk between RNA processing and chromatin organization, providing a framework for how RNA metabolism can influence nuclear architecture and gene regulation.

title: The NADHX epimerase NAXE governs PARP1-DNA retention to maintain poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation homeostasis.
authors: Xiong, Yundong; Mao, Zuchao; Li, Xiaoman; Ruan, Xiaoyu; Chen, Kaiyu; Cui, Yilin; Li, Shiwei; Shen, Weiguo; Nie, Chen; Wang, Jian; Zhong, Lijun; Liang, Ling; Wang, Jing; Xu, Xingzhi; Wang, Weibin; Zhou, Xiao Albert; Wang, Jiadong
abstract: PARP1 is a crucial enzyme involved in DNA-damage repair and other biological processes through poly(ADP-ribose) modification (PARylation), but persistent activation can trigger parthanatos. Despite extensive research, the precise mechanisms governing PARP1 activity remain elusive. Here, through multiple CRISPR-Cas9 screens, we identified NAXE, an NADH hydrate (NADHX) epimerase, as a key regulator of PARP1 activity homeostasis. We show that NADHX inhibits PARP1-DNA binding, while NAXE lowers NADHX levels to promote PARP1 recruitment and DNA repair. PARP1 activation, in turn, induces PARylation that binds and inhibits NAXE, forming a negative feedback loop that restrains PARP1 aberrant activation. Notably, knockout of NAXE in mice and C. elegans disrupts PARylation homeostasis, leading to sustained DNA damage and PARP1 activation, ultimately resulting in parthanatos-driven catastrophic neural injury. These findings uncover a metabolite-mediated feedback mechanism that preserves PARylation homeostasis and highlight NAXE as a potential therapeutic target in PARP1-related neurological disorders.

title: Bridging traditional knowledge and modern technology: In-silico ethnopharmacology in herbal drug discovery.
authors: Redhu, Archana Kumari; Thaker, Kavita; Singh, Priyanka; Mehta, Raj; Kodolikar, Kshitij; Chandrani, Pratik; Gundeti, Manohar; Gota, Vikram
journal: Journal of Ayurveda and integrative medicine
abstract: The use of herbal medicines and phytochemicals has gained considerable attention due to their structural diversity, selective toxicity, lower incidence of adverse effects, and affordability compared to conventional chemotherapy. Nevertheless, their precise mechanisms of action and bioactive constituents remain insufficiently understood, limiting their clinical translation and highlighting the need for rigorous scientific investigation. This review provides an integrative perspective on herbal-based drug discovery, beginning with the intersection of traditional disease classification systems, such as Ayurveda, and modern frameworks such as the International Classification of Diseases (ICD), enabling the alignment of ethnomedical knowledge with contemporary biomedical standards. Relevant literature available up to May 2026 was identified through searches of PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar using keywords related to ethnopharmacology, phytochemicals, and computational drug discovery, with emphasis on recent advances while retaining key seminal studies. The review examines the application of network pharmacology and systems biology in elucidating the multi-target and multi-pathway actions of herbal medicines. Computational approaches, including virtual screening, molecular docking, and absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) profiling, are discussed for their roles in identifying and prioritizing bioactive phytochemicals. The utility of herbal databases, together with forward and reverse docking, Lipinski-based filtering, and drug repurposing strategies, is highlighted. Key challenges, including protein flexibility, phytochemical variability, and limited experimental validation, are critically evaluated. Emerging approaches integrating multi-omics technologies, CRISPR-based functional studies, and high-throughput sequencing are also discussed as future directions for accelerating herbal drug discovery. Therefore, rather than replacing experimental or clinical validation, these computational approaches primarily serve as hypothesis-generating tools that require further preclinical and clinical investigation.

title: PIK-75 suppresses SREBP-dependent sterol-synthesis genes in PIK3CA-altered small-cell lung cancer cells, but attribution to p110alpha remains unresolved.
authors: Movaqar, Aref; Yaghoubi, Atieh; Rezaee, Seyed Abdolrahim
abstract: BACKGROUND: Class IA PI3K isoforms are candidate therapeutic targets in small-cell lung cancer (SCLC). The transcriptional consequences of isoform-directed inhibitors in SCLC cells have not been compared genome-wide. METHODS: We re-analysed GEO series GSE40564, in which PIK3CA-altered NCI-H69 cells were treated for 24 h with vehicle, PIK-75 (p110alpha-directed) or TGX-221 (p110beta-directed), with three arrays per group. Differential expression used limma, with re-processing from raw files and spike-in-anchored normalisation as sensitivity analyses. Gene sets were tested with correlation-adjusted competitive tests (camera), including a direct comparison of the two compounds. The main finding was checked against LINCS L1000 signatures of selective PI3K inhibitors and an independent alpelisib RNA-seq dataset. Isoform dependency was examined in DepMap CRISPR screens, and a PIK-75 response score was tested in 81 primary SCLCs against matched random-signature nulls. RESULTS: PIK-75 changed 11,645 of 17,458 genes at FDR < 0.05; 316 decreased and 20 increased significantly beyond two-fold. Its clearest pathway-level effect was lower expression of SREBP-controlled sterol- and lipid-synthesis genes (SQLE, HMGCS1, HMGCR, LDLR, SCD; log2 fold-change -1.1 to -1.6). Cholesterol homeostasis was the only gene set that stayed significant after correlation adjustment (camera FDR = 0.02) and that differed significantly between PIK-75 and TGX-221 (FDR = 0.02). TGX-221 changed 358 genes, none two-fold, and its response depended on two of three replicates. In LINCS, the down-regulated genes of alpelisib and taselisib were enriched for SREBP targets (p  approximately  5 x 10(-)(6)), whereas those of TGX-221 were not, and alpelisib reduced several of the same genes in an independent dataset. PIK-75 also inhibits CDK9 and DNA-PK, and canonical FOXO targets were not induced, so the response cannot be attributed to p110alpha alone. SCLC lines depended more on PIK3CA than on PIK3CB in DepMap (median Chronos -0.38 vs -0.15), as did other lineages. In patients, the response score was not associated with survival beyond matched random signatures (empirical p = 0.12-0.14). CONCLUSION: To our knowledge, this is the first genome-wide comparison of isoform-directed PI3K inhibitors in SCLC cells. PIK-75, but not TGX-221, suppresses an SREBP-dependent sterol programme in NCI-H69 cells, and public data from selective p110alpha inhibitors point to PI3K signalling as its most plausible source. Because PIK-75 is not selective and TGX-221 exposure was not measured, the attribution to p110alpha and the apparent dispensability of p110beta remain preliminary.

title: Optimizing C-Terminal Gene Tagging Using CRISPR/Cas9 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae: From gRNA Design to Tag Incorporation.
authors: Mashkoor, Muneera; Grove, Anne
abstract: Protein tags are molecular tools for dissecting protein function by enabling detection and purification. N-terminal tagging can sometimes cause protein mislocalization or compromised function. As an alternative, a protein can be tagged at the C-terminus, a procedure that also retains expression from the endogenous promoter. CRISPR/Cas9 has emerged as a powerful tool for gene manipulation, including in vivo gene tagging strategies. Traditional yeast CRISPR design tools rely on static database lookups and provide limited guidance on predicting targeting efficiency, potentially resulting in hidden design limitations that can compromise precise gene editing. We harnessed the versatility of the pML104 expression vector and combined it with a dynamic, multi-parameter scoring gRNA design tool for seamless C-terminal tagging. We observed that certain sequence features, such as an extra guanine at the 3'-end of the PAM sequence, can affect cleavage efficiency, and that under suboptimal conditions, cells can evade homology-directed repair, resulting in an increased probability of false positives. Verification that the tagged protein is expressed and fully functional is critical, and it was achieved here using Western blotting and chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP). This framework provides an efficient blueprint and comprehensive guide for streamlining C-terminal protein tagging in S. cerevisiae.

title: Caspase-9 drives doxorubicin-induced inflammatory cell death, PANoptosis.
authors: Malireddi, R K Subbarao; Sharma, Bhesh Raj; Chadchan, Sangappa B; Chen, Wen; Tweedell, Rebecca E; Kanneganti, Thirumala-Devi
abstract: The anthracycline chemotherapeutic drug doxorubicin and the well-known compound staurosporine (STS) have long been regarded as prototypical inducers of the nonlytic cell death pathway apoptosis, with doxorubicin serving as a standard experimental tool for studying caspase-9-dependent intrinsic apoptosis. We recently showed that STS induces PANoptosis, a distinct lytic cell death pathway initiated by innate immune sensors and driven by caspases and/or RIPKs through PANoptosome complexes. Here, we asked whether doxorubicin similarly induces lytic cell death. Using CRISPR-Cas9 technology, we developed caspase-9-deficient immortalized bone marrow-derived macrophages to circumvent the embryonic lethality associated with germline deletion of caspase-9. We found that doxorubicin induced dose- and time-dependent lytic cell death-PANoptosis-in a caspase-9-dependent manner. Together with our previous findings on STS and caspase-8, these data demonstrate that classical inducers of nonlytic apoptosis also drive lytic, inflammatory cell death (PANoptosis) in innate immune cells, specifically macrophages. We further show that caspase-9 is a key driver of PANoptosis in response to doxorubicin and is required for the activation of caspase-1, caspase-8, caspase-3/-7, and gasdermin E, which are hallmarks of PANoptosis. These findings establish a role for caspase-9 beyond canonical apoptosis and suggest that PANoptosis and the downstream inflammatory response may contribute to the biological effects previously attributed to apoptosis for doxorubicin as a chemotherapeutic agent and for caspase-9 in other cancer and inflammatory disease settings.

title: Self-Supervised Denoising-Enhanced Dual-Site CRISPR Cascade Nanosphere Enables Amplification-Free Pathogen Detection.
authors: Zhou, Yang; Hu, Cong; Li, Kaitong; Lin, Hongbin; Chen, Rui; Hao, Xiaoqian; Wu, Long; Han, Sanyang
abstract: Foodborne pathogens pose a major threat to global public health, necessitating rapid, sensitive, and deployable detection methods. Despite their considerable promise, current CRISPR-based diagnostics remain constrained by mandatory preamplification steps and insufficient sensitivity, hindering point-of-care application. Here, we introduce a self-supervised denoising-enhanced dual-site CRISPR cascade nanosphere (SD-DCCN) biosensing platform for on-site detection. The SD-DCCN integrates a CRISPR cascade architecture that reactivates the dormant catalytic potential of Cas12a by employing a universal split crRNA motif with two full-length crRNAs to synergistically boost the trans-cleavage activity, coupled with a self-supervised denoising algorithm on a visualized nanosphere platform that converts the amplified signal into a high-contrast quantitative readout. Our strategy eliminates the need for preamplification and achieves detection of Salmonella Typhimurium with a limit of detection as low as 16 CFU/mL, representing a 62.5-fold improvement over conventional amplification-free CRISPR assays. In addition, by integrating smartphone-readable tube analysis with qPCR-comparable sensitivity, the portable SD-DCCN presents a practical approach for rapid and on-site food safety monitoring. Furthermore, we quantify viable bacteria in diverse real food samples and validate the detection results against qPCR benchmarks. This platform holds great promise for CRISPR diagnosis of foodborne diseases, especially in resource-limited settings.

title: Protocol for CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing of murine neutrophils for in vitro and in vivo mechanistic studies.
authors: Siwicki, Marie; Engblom, Camilla; Manguso, Robert; Pittet, Mikael J; Bolli, Evangelia
abstract: Neutrophils' short lifespan and resistance to genetic manipulation have limited mechanistic interrogation of gene-specific functions in these cells. Here, we present a protocol for gene targeting in murine neutrophil-lineage cells using two complementary CRISPR-Cas9-based strategies. First, we describe steps for an ER-Hoxb8-based system for scalable gain- and loss-of-function studies. We then detail procedures for a Lineage- Sca-1+ cKit+ (LSK) progenitor cell-based hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell-targeting strategy for stable genetic perturbation of endogenous neutrophils. For complete information on the generation and use of this protocol, please refer to Bolli et al.(1).

title: Nanoparticle therapeutics for infectious diseases integrating AI-guided design, crispr delivery, phage synergy, and immune modulation.
authors: Mehmood, Muhammad Shahid; Javaid, Fariha; Afroz, Eeman; Saleem, Muhammad; Ullah, Hikmat; Moh'd, Amir Majdi; Shahid, Iqra; Nazari, Mohammad Jalal
abstract: Infectious diseases continue to pose a global health challenge, intensified by antimicrobial resistance and limitations of pharmaceutical countermeasures. Nanotechnology offers a promising front against these barriers using intelligent, multifunctional systems. This review explores the convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), CRISPR gene editing, bacteriophage therapy, and immune modulation within the framework of second-generation nanoparticle therapeutics. AI-guided modelling enables predictive optimization of nanoparticle design on the basis of size, charge, and surface proteins, targeting specific pathogens and providing enhanced stability. Consequently, nanoparticles serve as precision nanocarriers and protective delivery vehicles for the CRISPR-Cas system, shielding nucleic acid cargo from enzymatic degradation and enabling targeted intracellular delivery via pH-responsive endosomal escape mechanisms. The nanoparticles not only provide protection but also enable tissue-targeting and infection-site-specific delivery of the CRISPR-Cas system, facilitating precise genome editing to reverse resistance in specific pathogens such as HIV and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Phage nanoparticle hybrids further expand antimicrobial potency by enhancing phage stability, delivery, and host range. Moreover, engineered nanoparticles modulate the immune system via immunosuppressive and immunostimulant strategies for reducing hyperinflammation and enhancing pathogen clearance, respectively. Despite such encouraging laboratory outcomes, the clinical translation of AI-integrated nanoparticle platforms still faces a number of obstacles. Large-scale manufacturing, scalability, and reproducibility pose a significant challenge. Regulatory approvals for such multi-modal nano-drugs seem to get bogged down due to vague and scarce exemplary proofs. Furthermore, safety and efficacy apprehensions, unpredictable and complex host-phage interactions, cost-effectiveness, and equitable access remain a subject matter of concern. Conclusively, the convergence of advanced nanotechnology, artificial intelligence, and synthetic biology marks the dawn of a transformative era in infectious disease therapeutics where treatment is not only intelligent and adaptive but also ethically and globally inclusive.Clinical trial registrationNot applicable.

title: Engineering BHK-21 cells by dual knockout of host-restriction factors Cav1 and HDAC6 achieved a marked increase in FMDV titers for scalable vaccine production.
authors: Nokhwal, Alka; Khandelwal, Nitin; Kumar, Garvit; Kamboj, Himanshu; Chander, Yogesh; Bhattacharya, Supriya; Verma, Assim; T, Riyesh; Kilari, Sreenivasulu; Kumar, Naveen
abstract: Foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV) vaccine production depends on BHK-21 cells, but the high antigen dose required for biannual mass vaccination campaigns using an inactivated vaccine limits global vaccine supply. In this study, a targeted small-molecule screen identified baicalein (caveolin-1 inhibitor) and tubacin (HDAC6 inhibitor) as potent enhancers of FMDV replication in BHK-21 cells. Cav1 was shown to act as an early restriction factor: its inhibition increased the viral entry and consequently produced a sixfold higher virus yield. Cav1 inhibition also primed p53-dependent intrinsic apoptosis, raising p53 phosphorylation and BAX/BIM transcripts, shifting cells into early apoptosis, and promoting cytolytic spread. HDAC6 was shown to function as a post-entry restriction factor: its inhibition elevated alpha-tubulin acetylation, enhancing viral RNA and protein expression and producing four to six times titer boost. Finally, using CRISPR/Cas9, we generated Cav1/HDAC6 double-knockout (dKO) BHK-21 cells, targeting two host restriction factors that impose entry and post-entry barriers to FMDV replication. The engineered BHK-21 cells in both adherent and suspension culture formats produced 10- to 20-fold higher virus titers across field FMDV serotype "O" and FMDV vaccine strains of serotypes "O," "A," and "Asia 1." Reintroducing either factor restored restriction, confirming their roles as host restriction factors. These findings reveal a dual-layer host defense mechanism and establish an engineered, high-yield BHK-21 cell line for enhanced viral production and improved vaccine manufacturing efficiency.IMPORTANCEFoot-and-mouth disease (FMD) imposes substantial economic losses on livestock-producing countries through reduced animal productivity and trade restrictions. Control relies on biannual herd vaccination, generating a demand for vaccine that often exceeds current manufacturing capacity. FMD vaccine antigen is conventionally produced in BHK-21 cells; however, limited viral yields increase production costs and constrain supply. Here, we identify caveolin-1 and HDAC6 as host restriction factors for foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV) in BHK-21 cells. Caveolin-1 restricts FMDV at the entry stage, whereas HDAC6 acts at a post-entry step. Knockout of these factors enhances viral yields by 10- to 20-fold across FMDV serotypes O, A, and Asia 1-the three serotypes included in India's trivalent vaccine program. These findings indicate that BHK-21 cells deficient in caveolin-1 and HDAC6 could substantially improve FMDV propagation and provide a scalable, cost-effective platform for vaccine manufacturing.

title: T-cell clonality and TCR repertoire dynamics during germinal center responses: A comprehensive review of regulatory mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities.
authors: Sirati Moghaddam, Parsa; Mirzajani Sarvandani, Mandana
abstract: T-cell receptors (TCRs) are pivotal for antigen recognition within germinal centers (GCs), which are essential for B-cell maturation and high-affinity antibody production. Although the role played by T follicular helper (Tfh) cells in supporting B cells is established, the mechanisms driving the expansion and maintenance of distinct T-cell clonotypes in the GC perifollicular region remain poorly understood. This review aims to synthesize current knowledge on the differentiation, migration, and clonal expansion of T cells within GCs, with emphasis on Tfh-B-cell interactions. Findings from immunohistochemistry, flow cytometry, single-cell RNA sequencing, multiphoton microscopy, and CRISPR/Cas9-based approaches indicate that clonal expansion of T cells carrying defined TCR clonotypes is a regulated process driven by cognate Tfh-B-cell interactions. These interactions promote both B-cell affinity maturation and the concomitant selection and clonal expansion of T cells. The reviewed studies reveal that the TCR repertoire within the GC perifollicular region is refined over time, contributing to the development of long-lived memory and effector cells. The collective results underscore a dynamic reciprocity where T cells shape the antibody response while themselves undergoing antigen-driven selection. Key challenges include clarifying TCR signaling networks, improving in vivo analysis of cellular interactions, and identifying strategies to therapeutically modulate these processes without disrupting immune homeostasis. Overcoming these hurdles will require interdisciplinary approaches and the application of emerging technologies. Future research focused on these areas will be critical for advancing fundamental immunology and developing novel therapeutic strategies for vaccines, autoimmune diseases, and cancer.

title: An ultra-multiplex CRISPR/Cas9 system for simultaneous editing of 29 genes reshapes the nutritional profile of soybean.
authors: Bai, Mengyan; Lin, Jieni; Zhang, Jieping; Feng, Xiangchi; Zhang, Yaru; Zhong, Hai; Kuang, Huaqin; Peng, Chunyan; Zhang, Chunlei; Lin, Wenxin; Zhou, Yufan; Hazaisi, Hanipa; Kong, Fanjiang; Guan, Yuefeng
abstract: Simultaneous editing of dozens of genes has been a long-standing goal in plant biotechnology. However, this approach faces major technical hurdles, including reduced editing efficiency with increasing numbers of sgRNAs, vector instability caused by repetitive Pol III promoters, and limited capacity of single-transcript-unit systems. These challenges collectively hinder the engineering of complex traits. Soybean is a vital source of plant protein and oil, but anti-nutritional factors and unpleasant flavors degrade its seed quality, and conventional breeding fails to pyramid favorable alleles to eliminate undesirable ones. To resolve these bottlenecks, we developed the Multiple SgRNA Array (MSA) system, a modular and scalable architecture for expanded sgRNA loading while maintaining cloning flexibility and high editing efficiency. Hairy-root assays validated its capacity to edit 46 targets via 32 sgRNAs simultaneously. We deployed MSA in stable soybean transformation to knock out 29 genes across three functional modules: anti-nutritional-factor reduction, flavor refinement, and nodulation optimization. Multi-generation screening generated the rnp-29m mutant with loss-of-function mutations in all 29 genes. This mutant shows enhanced seed traits, elevated oleic acid, decreased allergens and anti-nutrients, improved digestibility, and attenuated beany flavor, with no significant yield penalty. Our modular MSA system enables high-capacity sgRNA assembly and ultra-multiplex editing, providing a robust tool for rapid trait pyramiding and elite soybean germplasm with superior nutrition.

title: Suspending the Question: China and the New Geopolitics of Immunity "After" COVID.
authors: Alexander, Travis
abstract: Although immunologic rhetorics from the global north have cohered historically on a characterization of the global south as an inevitable ecosystem of disease (e.g., HIV/AIDS), the west's response to COVID-19 evinces a new episteme, evident in two competing origin stories: wet market vs. lab leak. In light of China's biomedical advance, which includes vigilante CRISPR experimentation, the western imaginary is impelled not to resolve its competing theories, holding them both in indefinite suspension- a strategy that presents an ultramodern yet reassuringly backward China, marking a pedagogy for a new immunity and sovereignty optimized for an age of flexibility.

title: A genetic engineering toolkit for the probiotic yeast Saccharomyces boulardii.
authors: Dong, Huaming; Xiao, Chunqiao; Zhang, Yanfei
abstract: Saccharomyces boulardii (S. boulardii) is the only yeast probiotic widely used in clinical practice and consumer products. It combines gastrointestinal robustness, intrinsic antibiotic tolerance and eukaryotic protein-processing capacity, making it an attractive chassis for engineered probiotics, in situ biomanufacturing and live biotherapeutic delivery. However, host-specific characterization of regulatory elements, candidate genomic integration sites, and multicopy integration strategies remains limited in the clinically used S. boulardii CNCM I-745 background. Here, using S. boulardii CNCM I-745 as the host, we developed and characterized a genetic engineering toolkit that integrates transcriptional control elements with genome-integration strategies. We first quantified the activities of 20 endogenous constitutive promoters, two inducible promoters and six terminators. We then established a markerless CRISPR-Cas9 workflow and evaluated 10 chromosomal integration loci; six of which showed Editing efficiency above 80% while supporting comparable transgene expression without detectable growth penalties. Finally, we constructed an rDNA-repeat-based multicopy integration system that increased transgene expression by 9.8- to 22.6-fold relative to single-copy integration and revealed a significant positive but non-proportional association between estimated copy number and reporter output. Together, this toolkit provides S. boulardii with a set of tunable promoters and terminators, candidate chromosomal integration sites compatible with a markerless CRISPR-Cas9 workflow. These resources expand the genetic accessibility of this probiotic yeast and provide a foundation for developing engineered S. boulardii strains with enhanced probiotic, therapeutic and biomanufacturing functions.

title: Redesigning photoprotection: nature-inspired and synthetic biology strategies to enhance crop productivity.
authors: Guardini, Zeno; Barera, Simone; Pinnola, Alberta
abstract: Photosynthesis captures solar energy and carbon dioxide to fuel life on Earth by providing food and oxygen. When light intensity exceeds photosynthetic capacity, resulting in the saturation of the electron transport chain, photosynthetic organisms protect themselves by activating photoprotective non-photochemical quenching (NPQ), which dissipates excess energy as heat. Despite the importance of NPQ in plant physiology, its slow activation and relaxation may cause substantial yield losses in field-grown crops. For this reason, qE, the fastest component of NPQ, has become a central biotechnological target for crop engineering. While pioneering approaches, such as the "VPZ strategy" involving the overexpression of both xanthophyll cycle and PSBS proteins, have successfully enhanced field productivity, their efficacy varies across species, highlighting current biotechnological bottlenecks. This review discusses the molecular bases and activation models of qE in different clades, describing the transition from LHCSR- to PSBS-dependent strategies and the central role of the xanthophyll cycle, while highlighting open debates and unresolved questions. Further, it outlines the future of NPQ engineering, exploring nature-inspired solutions, including the heterologous expression of LHCSR or alternative xanthophyll cycles in crops. Finally, this review discusses how CRISPR-Cas9-driven precision breeding and the application of Artificial Intelligence, and de novo protein design will guide future biotechnological intervention toward developing high-yielding, better resource-efficient crops.

title: Idh2-alpha-KG axis dysregulation disrupts epigenetic landscape and imprinted genes, inducing placental hypertrophy in somatic cell nuclear transfer Bos taurus.
authors: Zhao, Xiao-Yu; Yun, Yuan; Liao, Hong-Yi; Tao, Shao-Ying; Wu, Shan-Shan; Gao, Yu-Xin; Bo, Chun-Jie; Yang, Lei; Liu, Xue-Fei; Song, Li-Shuang; Bai, Chun-Ling; Li, Guang-Peng; Su, Guang-Hua
abstract: Placental hypertrophy is a major cause of pregnancy failure in somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) animals, with metabolic-epigenetic crosstalk proposed as a key regulatory node, yet its molecular mechanism remains elusive. Isocitrate dehydrogenase 2 (Idh2) is a critical mitochondrial metabolic enzyme that controls the production of alpha-Ketoglutarate (alpha-KG), a central regulator of epigenetic modifications. Abnormally elevated alpha-KG levels were found in SCNT Bos taurus placentomes and derived placental mesenchymal cells. Further functional experiments in these cells suggested that elevated alpha-KG levels were associated with significant increases in 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) and the active histone marker H3K4me3, as well as decreases in the repressive markers H3K9me3 and H3K27me3, accompanied by altered expression of ten-eleven translocation (TET) dioxygenases and lysine demethylase (KDMs). This ultimately led to the dysregulation of key imprinted genes associated with placental development, including upregulation of Insulin-like growth factor 2 receptor ( Igf2r) and Zinc figer protein 597 ( Znf597), and downregulation of Pleckstrin homology-like domain family A member 2 ( Phlda2), Paternally expressed gene 10 ( Peg10), and MAGE family member L2 ( Magel2). Further analysis revealed that Idh2, a key enzyme for alpha-KG synthesis, was significantly upregulated in SCNT B. taurus placentas, with its promoter region exhibiting hypomethylation, increased H3K4me3 modification, and enhanced chromatin accessibility. Targeted knockdown of Idh2 via CRISPR-Cas9 or inhibition of alpha-KG production using specific inhibitors effectively reversed these epigenetic abnormalities and improved the placental hypertrophy phenotype. In Mus musculus validation experiments, maternal alpha-KG supplementation during pregnancy induced placental hypertrophy, whereas inhibiting Idh2 activity completely rescued this phenotype. This study is the first to elucidate the molecular mechanism by which Idh2-alpha-KG axis regulates placental development through a "metabolism-epigenetics" axis, providing novel strategies to improve cloning efficiency and potential intervention targets for treating placenta-related diseases (e.g., placental macrosomia).

title: Genome-wide analysis of Phoebe zhennan CADs identifies PzCAD4 as a key contributor to drought response via lignin biosynthesis.
authors: Chen, Beibei; Yu, Lingfan; Liao, Zhenqi; Luo, Yingxuan; Gu, Yunjie; Wang, Lihua; Li, Yuan; Ye, Min; Ding, Zhongbiao; Liu, Weiyi; Huang, Shengjia
abstract: BACKGROUND: During drought stress, one of the physiological challenges plants face is the embolism and collapse of xylem vessels. Lignin biosynthetic enzymes form complexes during lignification to facilitate metabolic channeling. Although cinnamyl alcohol dehydrogenase (CAD)-mediated lignin biosynthesis is essential for reinforcing cell wall mechanical strength and maintaining water transport capacity under stress, the molecular mechanisms by which CAD genes confer drought tolerance in the valuable timber species Phoebe zhennan remain elusive. RESULTS: In this study, we identified six PzCAD genes within the P. zhennan genome, characterized by an uneven chromosomal distribution and a localized tandem duplication event on chromosome 2. Phylogenetic and structural analyses revealed that these members are distributed across three distinct evolutionary clades and exhibit significant exon-intron divergence, while their promoters are universally enriched in stress- and hormone-responsive elements. Protein interaction assays, including yeast two-hybrid (Y2H), bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC), and luciferase complementation imaging (LCI), demonstrated that PzCAD2-1 and PzCAD2-2 assemble into stable homodimers. Structural and transcriptional analyses showed that while virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) of Clade I (PzCAD1) and Clade II (PzCAD2) members failed to alter bulk lignin accumulation, the Clade IV orthologs (PzCAD4-1, PzCAD4-2, PzCAD4-3) were profoundly upregulated under PEG-simulated drought. Comprehensive in planta functional validations in transgenic hairy root systems revealed that overexpressing the PzCAD4 clade markedly enhanced drought tolerance by augmenting lignin deposition, elevating antioxidant enzyme activities, accumulating osmoprotectants, and attenuating reactive oxygen species (ROS) bursts. Additionally, the overexpression lines synergistically accumulated defense-associated phytohormones (salicylic acid and jasmonic acid) alongside moderately elevated H(2)O(2), which more likely functioned as a signaling molecule under drought stress. In stark contrast, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockouts of individual PzCAD4 genes severely repressed lignin biosynthesis, exacerbating cellular oxidative damage and precipitating pronounced drought responses. CONCLUSIONS: We conclude that PzCAD4 is a key positive regulator of lignin biosynthesis under drought stress that improves PEG-induced drought tolerance mainly by reinforcing secondary cell walls, accompanied by coordinated changes in antioxidant metabolism and defense phytohormone accumulation. These findings comprehensively elucidate the functional landscape of the P. zhennan CAD gene family, providing theoretical foundations and genetic targets for the molecular breeding of drought-resilient timbers.

title: Construction of an all-in-one doxycycline-inducible Cre/loxP marker recycling system in Aspergillus species.
authors: Yakabe, Shun; Hamaguchi, Ayuki; Noguchi, Masayuki; Kakihara, Kosuke; Sasano, Yu; Futagami, Taiki; Oka, Takuji; Kadooka, Chihiro
abstract: Aspergillus features numerous species with diverse characteristics, and efforts to identify the genes responsible for these traits are ongoing worldwide. Advanced multi-gene knockout technologies are required to analyze the functions of these genes. Although CRISPR/Cas9-based gene disruption methods have become widely used in many organisms, conventional homologous recombination remains the most reliable method for multiple-gene disruption in Aspergillus species. Here, we report the development of a novel marker recycling cassette for Aspergillus spp. This system enables highly efficient gene disruption and marker recycling by combining a doxycycline-inducible Cre/loxP system with a uracil biosynthesis pathway and counterselection using uracil analogs. Using the model filamentous fungi Aspergillus nidulans and the human pathogen Aspergillus fumigatus, we disrupted genes involved in conidial pigment biosynthesis and amino acid and vitamin biosynthesis. This system is expected to facilitate and accelerate functional genomic analyses in Aspergillus spp.

title: Toll-Like Receptor-Driven Neuroinflammation in Neurological Disorders: Signaling Crosstalk and Therapeutic Opportunities.
authors: Sharma, Akhil; Singh, Gurkirat; Mannan, Ashi; Subramaniyan, Vetriselvan; Dua, Kamal; Singh, Thakur Gurjeet
abstract: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) serve as pivotal mediators bridging innate immunity and neuroinflammation, orchestrating pathological cascades that drive neurological disorders. Beyond their sentinel role in pathogen recognition, aberrant TLR activation triggers intricate and destructive signaling networks, including activation of NF-kappaB, MAPK, JAK/STAT, and PI3K/AKT, alongside IRFs and type I interferon responses that converge on chronic neuroinflammation and subsequent neuronal damage. This review dissects TLRs' multilayered contribution to neuropathology, emphasizing their regulation of secondary inflammatory mechanisms, including NLRP3 inflammasome priming and activation, mTOR-driven metabolic dysregulation, SOCS-mediated feedback inhibition, inflammasome activation, and pyroptotic cell death. Critically, these signaling pathways create a pathological intersection with oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, amplifying a self-perpetuating cycle of neuronal injury that underlies conditions like Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), Huntington's disease (HD), and Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Stroke, Multiple sclerosis (MS), Epilepsy and Traumatic brain injury (TBI). Against this neuropathological landscape, this review systematically evaluates emerging therapeutic strategies targeting TLR-mediated neuroinflammation, encompassing small molecule TLR antagonists, intracellular adaptor protein inhibitors targeting myeloid differentiation primary response 88 (MyD88) and TIR-domain-containing adapter-inducing interferon-beta (TRIF), biologic therapies including monoclonal antibodies and fusion proteins, natural phytochemicals and nutraceuticals, Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based genomic interventions, and cell-based immunomodulatory therapies, collectively representing a mechanistically diverse arsenal aimed at recalibrating the dysregulated innate immune response to achieve durable neuroprotection across the full spectrum of TLR-mediated neurological disorders.

title: Stress memory and adaptive intelligence in plants from signaling networks to crop improvement under climate change.
authors: Chauhan, Jyoti; Behera, Partha Pratim; Jha, Rintu; Rana, Amit; Singhal, Rajesh Kumar; Ahmed, Shahid; Zimik, Masochon
journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
abstract: Plants, as sessile organisms, have evolved sophisticated decentralized signaling networks that enable perception, integration, and memory of environmental stresses despite lacking a nervous system. This review examines current understanding of plant intelligence, stress memory, and adaptive plasticity, highlighting how these processes enhance survival and productivity under increasingly variable climates. Key mechanisms include sensory receptors for diverse stimuli, rapid signaling via calcium, reactive oxygen species (ROS), electrical, and hydraulic waves, and extensive hormonal crosstalk Abscisic acid (ABA), Jasmonic acid (JA), Salicylic acid (SA), Ethylene (E). Stress memory operates through epigenetic modifications (DNA methylation, histone changes, chromatin remodeling), transcriptional reprogramming (Type I sustained and Type II hyper-induced patterns), and metabolic adjustments that create primed states for faster responses upon recurrent stress. These processes underpin cross-tolerance, systemic acquired resistance (SAR), induced systemic resistance (ISR), and transgenerational inheritance. In crops, priming, microbiome recruitment, and phenotypic plasticity, such as root foraging, shade avoidance, improve resilience to combined abiotic and biotic stresses. Advances in multi-omics, AI-driven phenomics, and systems biology are accelerating the identification of memory-associated genes and regulatory networks. Translational strategies such as seed priming, CRISPR-based editing, and epigenetic-informed breeding offer promising tools for developing climate-resilient varieties with enhanced yield stability. Integrating stress memory and adaptive intelligence concepts offers a comprehensive framework for sustainable agriculture. Future research should prioritize multi-environment field validation, quantification of fitness trade-offs, and integration of multi-stress networks to translate these mechanisms into robust crop improvement strategies.

title: Beyond off-target editing: the emerging landscape of Cas9 cytotoxicity and immunogenicity across biological systems.
authors: Awais, Muhammad; Sadaqat, Sahar; Iftikhar, Noreen; Arslan, Muhammad; Fatemi, Ehsan; Yasmeen, Aneela; Shahid, Naila; Wang, Zhi; Rao, Abdul Qayyum
abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 has transformed agricultural biotechnology, microbial engineering, and human therapeutics within a decade, yet biosafety assessment remains focused on editing accuracy and off-target cleavage. A second, neglected question is what the high-molecular-weight Cas9 effector protein does to expressing systems. This review integrates evidence from eukaryotic cell lines, microbial hosts, transgenic mammals, and dietary exposure models. In isolated cells Cas9 injures the host by three routes, only one requiring DNA cleavage: TP53-dependent genotoxic stress at susceptible loci, modified by cell sex and p53 status; guide-independent binding to ribosomal proteins that activates the PI3K-mTORC2 axis; and promiscuous association with host transcripts inducing a p53-linked stress programme. In GC-rich bacteria, PAM density and limited double-strand break repair make basal expression lethal. Intact mammals tolerate tissue-restricted Cas9 expression, although nervous system and germline compartments are exceptions, and dietary exposure carries no measurable toxicological or allergenic risk. Pre-existing anti-Cas9 immunity is the dominant translational barrier. Proteasomal, SUMO-regulated and autophagic pathways together set Cas9 half-life. Transient ribonucleoprotein delivery, anti-CRISPR, degron-based control, and lower-toxicity orthogonal nucleases each narrow this exposure window. We conclude that Cas9 toxicity is not intrinsic but contingent on expression kinetics, delivery format, host repair, proteostatic capacity, and immunological history. Biosafety is therefore a tunable design parameter, and this review provides a mechanism-based framework for matching nuclease, delivery route and temporal control to the intended application.

title: Large scale CRISPR genome engineering reveal principles of single nucleotide microhomology in precision editing
authors: Shi X; Li C; Li J; Liu Y; Wu Q
abstract: The CRISPR/Cas9 system has emerged as a revolutionary tool with diverse applications in genome engineering; however, the role of nanoscale hydrogen bonds between single nucleotides in precision editing remains unknown. Here we systematically compared A-rich and G-rich PAM-recognizing Cas9 editors through comprehensive analyses of ~37,000 targeting sites with about half million libraries of ~0.36 billion types of editing outcomes. We showed that the A-rich Cas9 editors exhibit stronger editing outcome predictability in comparison with the conventional Cas9 editor of the G-rich PAM. In addition, the A-rich Cas9 editors induce a higher frequency of staggered cleavages, resulting in predictable editing with donor-independent templated insertions. Moreover, we identified distinct DNA sequence motifs for predictable insertions with the A-rich Cas9 editors. In particular, we revealed single nucleotides at the -4 position as MMEJ microhomologies in precision engineering via two or three hydrogen bonds with A-rich or G-rich PAM, respectively. Furthermore, we found that PolQ plays a key role in enhanced random insertions. Finally, we developed a discrete-space diffusion model CRIfuser of deep learning for predicting editing outcomes with staggered cleavage. Together, these findings establish PAM-dependent cleavage geometry as a tunable determinant of Cas9 editing outcomes and provide a framework for predictive and precision genome engineering.
